title: Tube-sized tunnel under London gets a power boost – with help from its own monorail
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Tube-sized tunnel under London gets a power boost – with help from its own monorail
A 20 year old tube-train sized tunnel under north-west London is getting an upgrade to help it carry more electrons, and the engineers might be able to use a monorail to carry out the work.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2016/10/london-electricity-tunnels-04.jpg)
The Elstree–St John’s Wood cable tunnel forms a key part of National Grid’s newly launched North West London Upgrade (NWLU), a programme to increase the amount of electricity that can be carried into London and provide connections for new developments.
As part of the project, engineers will upgrade the existing tunnel and its headhouses before installing a new 400kV cable circuit along its length.
Working in such a long tunnel presents an obvious logistical problem, so contractor Hochtief-Murphy Joint Venture (HMJV) may use the engineers’ monorail inside the tunnel to move people, equipment and materials along the underground route while the upgrade and cable installation work takes place.
At the moment, the final decision hasn’t been taken, and a spokesperson confirmed that they are still “assessing the condition and suitability of the existing infrastructure” as part of their design process, adding that the “exact approach to cable installation, including the use of any existing tunnel infrastructure, will be determined during the design phase.”
Around 60km of new cable infrastructure will be installed inside the tunnel, which stretches from Elstree in Hertfordshire to St John’s Wood in London.
The tunnel was built in the early 2000s and already carries what National Grid says are the longest alternating current (AC) transmission cables in England and Wales. Helpfully for the latest upgrade, it was designed from the outset with enough space for an additional cable circuit to be installed if extra capacity was needed in the future.
That spare capacity will now be put to use.
The tunnel work is part of a much larger upgrade stretching from Sundon substation in Bedfordshire through Elstree and into London. More than 200km of existing overhead line will be upgraded along the 35km Sundon–Elstree route, while substations at Sundon, Elstree and St John’s Wood will also be upgraded.
National Grid will also build a new 132kV gas-insulated switchgear substation at Letchmore Heath, next to the existing Elstree substation to provide connections for five new data centres with a combined electricity demand of around 1GW.
National Grid says the overall programme will strengthen the resilience of electricity supplies while providing additional capacity for homes, businesses and digital infrastructure across North West London and surrounding areas. The company says increasing network capacity should also help reduce electricity constraint costs, which arise when limitations on the transmission network mean cheaper electricity cannot be moved to where it is needed.
Several major contractors have been appointed to carry out the programme. HMJV will be responsible for the tunnel upgrades and cable installation, while Laing O’Rourke will carry out substation works at Letchmore Heath, Elstree and St John’s Wood.
Hyundai Electric will supply and install major electrical equipment, including transformers, and Siemens Energy will provide shunt reactors for the Elstree substation.
The North West London Upgrade joins two other major National Grid projects in the capital — London Power Tunnels 2 and the North London Reinforcement scheme — as the electricity network is expanded to cope with rising demand.
summary: National Grid is upgrading the 20-year-old Elstree–St John’s Wood cable tunnel under north-west London as part of a major programme to increase electricity capacity. Contractors are considering using an existing internal monorail to transport personnel and materials during the installation of a new 400kV cable circuit. The broader project also includes upgrading overhead lines, expanding substations, and constructing a new substation to support data centres and local power resilience.
key_points: The Elstree–St John’s Wood tunnel is receiving an upgrade to install a new 400kV cable circuit.
Engineers may use an internal monorail system to move people, equipment, and materials through the tunnel.
The work forms part of National Grid's North West London Upgrade to increase electrical capacity and supply new developments.
Additional components of the wider project include overhead line upgrades, substation improvements, and a new gas-insulated switchgear substation.
Contractors such as Hochtief-Murphy Joint Venture, Laing O’Rourke, Hyundai Electric, and Siemens Energy have been appointed for the programme.

title: This north London neighbourhood has been named one of the best places to live in the UK – and it’s home to an iconic clocktower and a whole host of celebrity residents
author: Katie Forge
content:
![A clocktower in Crouch End with a row of terraced houses behind](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/26101127/shutterstock_1875107896-1024x683.jpg) 
I certainly make no secret of the fact that I have a fairly sizeable soft spot for this big, bright city of ours. And despite having lived here for the best part of two decades, there are still very few things that I enjoy more than discovering new corners of the capital to fall in love with. But with desirable neighbourhoods found at each turn and every tube stop, it sure is tricky to pinpoint the very best places to live. And so I guess it’s pretty darn handy that the lovely lot over at Muddy Stilettos, have – once again – done the hard work for us.
Every year, the leading lifestyle publication have us on the edge of our moquette-covered seats, waiting for the highly-anticipated arrival of their annual ‘Best Places to Live’ guide. From busy towns to teeny-tiny villages, the trusty team scour the length and breadth of the entire country to create this catalogue of the best places to reside. 260 lovely locations managed to earn themselves a comfy spot on the 2026 iteration of the list; eight of which are here in London. And topping the charts as one of the very best places to live in the country is – drum roll, please… Crouch End.
Seamlessly blending a hip-and-happening city location with a quaint-and-quiet village vibe; Crouch End really does have the best of both worlds. Filled to the brim with things to see, do, eat, and drink, it’s certainly not too hard to see why the legendary likes of Alan Carr, David Tennant, Katherine Ryan, and Simon Pegg all call this north London locale home.
![Row of identical English terraced houses in Crouch End](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/25125044/shutterstock_1801600948-1-1024x683.jpg)
The neighbourhood is picture-perfectly perched in the London Borough of Haringey, and has a (rather iconic) 19th-century clocktower slap-bang in the middle of it. According to Muddy Stilettos, the area boasts ‘an elegant, laid-back vibe more akin to a market town than a city’. The lack of tube station certainly adds to the village-like feel of the place, but Highgate is just a hop, skip, and a 20 minute walk away – and residents can also hop on a train to London Bridge from the nearby Crouch Hill station.
Just a stone’s throw from Alexandra Palace, there’s no shortage of green space nearby – and there’s also a plethora of independent shops, pubs, restaurants, and bars dotted around the area. Crouch End boasts some pretty gorgeous Victorian and Edwardian houses but – as I’m sure you can imagine – they don’t come particularly cheap. The average cost of a flat in Crouch End is £552,331, whilst a semi-detached house will set you back a rather eye-watering average of £1,447,756.
The best places to live in London (according to Muddy Stilettos):
- Crouch End
- De Beauvoir Town
- Greenwich
- Herne Hill
- Teddington
- Walthamstow
- Wandsworth
- Wimbledon
If you’re interested to know where else in the UK was named among the best places to reside, you can peruse the full list here.
summary: Crouch End in north London has been named one of the best places to live in the UK by Muddy Stilettos in its 2026 guide. The neighbourhood combines a city location with a village vibe, featuring an iconic 19th-century clocktower, Victorian and Edwardian houses, and numerous independent shops and green spaces. It is also home to several celebrity residents and maintains a relaxed market-town atmosphere despite lacking its own tube station.
key_points: Crouch End was featured as a top place to live in the 2026 Muddy Stilettos guide.
The area is known for its village-like feel, 19th-century clocktower, and lack of a tube station.
It offers plenty of independent shops, restaurants, pubs, and nearby green spaces like Alexandra Palace.
The neighbourhood is home to notable celebrities including David Tennant, Alan Carr, Katherine Ryan, and Simon Pegg.
Housing is expensive, with flats averaging £552,331 and semi-detached houses averaging £1,447,756.

title: New Superloop Route: SL12 Launches In September
author: Will Noble
content:
![A Superloop bus](https://assets.londonist.com/uploads/2026/08/i875/tfl_image_-_sl12.jpeg) 
The latest Superloop bus route launches in September.
The SL12 — running between Gants Hill and Rainham — becomes part of London's network of express bus routes on Saturday 5 September, marking the Superloop's expansion into the borough of Havering.
The full SL12 route is:
🚌 Gants Hill
🚌 Newbury Park
🚌 King George Hospital
🚌 East Road
🚌 Romford
🚌 Queen's Hospital
🚌 Elm Park
🚌 Rainham Ferry Lane
Currently, the journey time on a bus between Gants Hill and Rainham is slightly over an hour. On the SL12, this will be shaved down to around 40-45 minutes. The route also takes in two hospitals; Central, District, Overground and Elizabeth line stations; and links up with the SL2 Superloop at Gants Hills. (Gants Hill itself, of course, is home to a resplendent Tube station).
The SL12 will operate between 5.30am and 12.30am daily — every 12 minutes during the day on Mondays to Saturdays, and every 15 minutes every evening and all day on Sundays.
![The new route on the map](https://assets.londonist.com/uploads/2026/08/i730/sl12-superloop.jpg) 
SL12 buses are brand-new electric, zero-emission vehicles with air con and device-charging points. As an added bonus for passengers, the first week of travel on the SL12 is free (you'll still need to touch in).
Since launching in July 2023, the Superloop bus has accommodated some 81 million trips — although many of the routes are tweaked versions of existing ones.
summary: London's new SL12 Superloop express bus route will launch on September 5, operating between Gants Hill and Rainham. The route will reduce travel time to around 40-45 minutes and serve various transport hubs, hospitals, and stations. The service will use brand-new electric vehicles, with the first week of travel offered for free to passengers.
key_points: The SL12 launches on Saturday 5 September, expanding the Superloop into the borough of Havering.
Travel time between Gants Hill and Rainham will be reduced from slightly over an hour to 40-45 minutes.
Buses will operate daily from 5.30am to 12.30am, running every 12 minutes during the day (Mon-Sat) and every 15 minutes in the evenings and all day Sundays.
The route will use brand-new electric, zero-emission vehicles equipped with air conditioning and device-charging points.
The first week of travel on the SL12 will be free, though passengers will still need to touch in.

title: Professor Green's fast food restaurant is coming to London
author: Alice Saville
content:
[title]
Music’s biggest names can’t seem to stay away from the food biz. Eminem has a Detroit restaurant called Mom’s Spaghetti, Snoop Dogg is forever popping up in Just Eat ads, Blur’s Alex James now makes artisanal cheeses, and Ed Sheeran has his very own hot sauce, unappealingly named ‘Tingly Ted’s’. Now, London rapper Professor Green is getting in on the act, with a brand-new fast food restaurant launching in Soho in mid-September.
Called ‘Proper Good’, this isn’t your standard burger or fried chicken joint. Instead, it’s a build-your-own-meal concept that sounds ideal for anyone who likes to customise their food to the max. There’s already a first branch of PG Fast Food in Glasgow, which lays out the rough format. There are four adventurous base meal options: potato puffs, a South Korean-inspired UFO sub, loaded rice, or a loaded salad. Then, you can pile ’em high with toppings including miso salmon, pot roast beef, cheesy beans or pickled red chilli peas. There are also tons of dips and side options, including probiotic slaw, yoghurt ranch dressing, or spicy chimichurri.
The restaurant’s loosely Asian influence shows up in drinks including mango matcha and blueberry boba. And in a fun healthy touch, you can get frozen grapes for dessert, with kooky flavours including ‘unicorn’ or ‘upside down cheesecake’.
The Glasgow spot seems pretty popular, with TripAdvisor reviews praising its unusual, healthy choices: ‘a taste explosion...meeting Professor Green out of the blue was a nice surprise’ said one satisfied visitor.
Cracking the busy central London market could be a challenge, but Proper Good will have its location in its favour. The restaurant’s new spot on 3 Soho Street is on an underserved thoroughfare between Oxford Street and Soho Square, making it an easy spot for shoppers to pop into, whether they’re craving a matcha, ravenous for a sandwich, or just treating the kids to some unicorn frozen grapes.
Proper Good, 3 Soho Street, W1D 3QF.
In search of more adventurous flavours? Cult vegan sandwich spot Coven of Wiches has moved to a new location

Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: London rapper Professor Green is opening a new fast food restaurant called Proper Good in Soho this mid-September. Following the success of its first branch in Glasgow, the restaurant features a build-your-own-meal concept with bases like potato puffs and South Korean-inspired UFO subs. The menu also offers unique toppings, Asian-influenced drinks, and healthy desserts such as flavoured frozen grapes.
key_points: Proper Good is set to open its new Soho location at 3 Soho Street in mid-September.
The restaurant offers a build-your-own-meal format with four base options: potato puffs, UFO subs, loaded rice, or loaded salad.
Menu items include adventurous toppings, dips, Asian-influenced drinks like mango matcha, and flavoured frozen grapes for dessert.
The new Soho location is situated on an underserved thoroughfare between Oxford Street and Soho Square.

title: Dolly Parton's love affair with London
author: Isobel Lewis; Holly Bishop
content:
Dolly Parton's love affair with London, from her first trip overseas to her charity project in the capital
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Dolly Parton tours iconic London landmarks in 1983 HBO special ‘Dolly in London’](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/11/2.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![The Weekender](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_weekender_embed_desktop.png)
While Dolly Parton will always be associated with Tennessee – her place of birth, the home of country music and her theme park Dollywood – the singer has a long-standing connection to and love for London.
The “Jolene” performer, who died on Tuesday 25 August aged 80 after a “brief battle with cancer”, first visited the UK more than 50 years ago, and maintained a love affair with the capital for decades.
In 1975, one year after the release of “I Will Always Love You”, Parton performed in the UK for the first time ever at the Festival of Country Music at Wembley Arena.
It was a special experience for Parton, the singer revealed in a 2023 interview, as this was her first ever trip abroad.
![20th May 1977:  Country music queen Dolly Parton is back in London after performing at the King's Theatre, Glasgow, at a Scottish Royal Jubilee Television Special in the presence of the Queen, she now commences on a tour of Britain and the continent.  (Photo by Keystone/Getty Images)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2023/07/04/17/newFile-1.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Parton explained that she “loved England”, saying: “I couldn’t believe that there was a world like that. Imagine, we used to read about the kings and queens in books. I loved all that royalty stuff. I was always impressed by the robes and jewellery – the stories were like fairy tales to me.
“But then, when I actually saw castles and churches and all the stuff I had in my mind, it was amazing. We don’t have stuff like that in the United States.”
Parton continued: “I took the tour of Buckingham Palace and all those places where they tell you the stories of dungeons and things like that. To see it for real, all the history and buildings that are hundreds of years old, was fascinating to me. It was all so beautiful.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/10/5.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
In March 1983, Parton made a trip to the capital to perform a legendary show at the Dominion Theatre, which was broadcast as a televised special on HBO.
Dolly In Concert saw the star perform some of her most famous hits, including “Baby I’m Burning”, “Jolene”, and “9-5”.
Welcoming the bustling crowd, Parton said: “The most exciting and beautiful city in the world and the sweetest people I’ve ever known.”
Read More
Alongside performing her musical hits, Parton even treated fans to her best attempt at a London accent while on stage.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/41/4.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The special also offered a glimpse of the country legend taking in some of the capital’s iconic sights. She could be seen taking a ride on a red double-decker bus, meeting the Horse Guards and flirting with a police officer and planting a kiss on his cheek.
In a press conference, also broadcast as part of the special, Parton explained why country music appealed to Brits, saying: “I think it’s probably the same reason as the US. It tells a real story about ordinary people, and I’d like to think in my case, told in an extraordinary way.”
Just two months before her death, Parton shared footage of the show on her social media as she looked back on the iconic night. “Dolly in Concert wasn’t only a success, it was as fun for me as it looked!” she wrote.
Philanthropy has always been a huge part of Parton’s life, with her Imagination Library programme allowing her gift books to children around the world in their pre-school years.
The programme launched in the UK in 2007, and Parton came to London to meet kids from around London at the Savoy Hotel at the time.
Parton last played a London tour date in 2014, when she performed two nights at the O2 Arena on her Blue Smoke world tour.
The shows came just days after her Legends slot performance at Glastonbury, when Parton wowed a huge crowd on the Pyramid Stage.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/26/10/01M0YQSNPG6HW8AHMWX3F9RS51.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Looking back on the show in the wake of Parton’s death, festival organiser Emily Eavis described Parton as an “absolute delight”.
“I will never forget her coming here in 2014 and bringing her incredible songs, overflowing joy and wonderful spirit to Worthy Farm,” she wrote.
“There was a vast crowd in the field for her slot, the sun shone, and when she walked out on to the Pyramid Stage she reigned supreme. It was just magic. Thank you for it all, Dolly.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/53/Screenshot-2026-08-26-at-10-29-13.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
However, Parton returned to the UK in 2019 for the opening night of 9 to 5: The Musical, the stage production of her hit 1980 comedy film of the same name.
The production ran at the Savoy Theatre, with Parton drinking tea out of a Union Jack mug in a video announcing the West End show. Speaking about the revival, Parton said that the show was finding a “new life and a new reason and a new purpose” in London.
summary: Dolly Parton maintained a lifelong love affair with London, beginning with her first overseas trip and performance in the UK in 1975. Over the decades, she returned frequently to perform landmark concerts, sightsee, launch charitable projects like her Imagination Library, and support West End productions. Her enduring connection to the British capital remained a cherished part of her career until her passing.
key_points: Dolly Parton first visited the UK in 1975 to perform at Wembley Arena, marking her first trip abroad.
She filmed a famous HBO television special in London in March 1983, which featured iconic sights like riding a double-decker bus.
Parton brought her Imagination Library literacy programme to London in 2007 to gift books to pre-school children.
She performed her last London tour dates at the O2 Arena in 2014, shortly after playing the Glastonbury Festival.
In 2019, Parton returned to London for the opening night of 9 to 5: The Musical at the Savoy Theatre.

title: The south east London neighbourhoods with the best and worst GCSE results
author: Poppy Huggett
content:
Several south east London boroughs have recorded some of the highest GCSE results in England this year, with Southwark coming out on top locally.
New figures published by Ofqual show the proportion of GCSE entries awarded a grade 7 or above – equivalent to an old-style A grade or better – across local authority areas in 2026.
Southwark's figure remained almost unchanged from last year, edging up from 33.2 per cent in 2025.
Bromley also saw an increase, rising from 27.4 per cent to 28.3 per cent, while Greenwich increased from 23.3 per cent to 24.2 per cent.
READ MORE: Kent florist shortlisted for two national awards after double nomination
Lewisham's proportion of top grades rose slightly from 22.7 per cent last year to 23.1 per cent in 2026.
Bexley was the only south east London borough in the figures to see a fall, dropping from 30.6 per cent in 2025 to 29 per cent this year.
How south east London boroughs compare
- Southwark: 33.3 per cent (33.2 per cent in 2025)
- Bexley: 29 per cent (30.6 per cent in 2025)
- Bromley: 28.3 per cent (27.4 per cent in 2025)
- Greenwich: 24.2 per cent (23.3 per cent in 2025)
- Lewisham: 23.1 per cent (22.7 per cent in 2025)
Across England, Cambridge had the highest proportion of GCSE entries awarded grade 7 or above at 53.5 per cent, up from 50.3 per cent in 2025.
Richmond upon Thames was second nationally at 43.4 per cent, followed by Sutton at 43 per cent and Kingston upon Thames at 42.5 per cent.
At the other end of the table, Tamworth in Staffordshire had the lowest proportion of entries receiving a grade 7 or above at 6.7 per cent.
The figures provide a picture of GCSE attainment across local authority areas, but do not necessarily reflect the performance of individual schools.
The City of London has been excluded from the rankings because of its small population size.
summary: Newly published Ofqual data reveals GCSE results for local authority areas across south east London. Southwark recorded the highest proportion of top grades locally, while Bexley was the only borough in the region to experience a decrease from the previous year. Nationally, Cambridge achieved the highest proportion of grade 7 or above entries, whereas Tamworth recorded the lowest.
key_points: Southwark led south east London with 33.3 per cent of GCSE entries achieving a grade 7 or above.
Bexley was the only south east London borough to see a drop, falling from 30.6 per cent in 2025 to 29 per cent.
Cambridge recorded the highest proportion of top GCSE grades nationally at 53.5 per cent.
Tamworth had the lowest proportion of top grades in England at 6.7 per cent.
The data reflects local authority attainment overall and does not necessarily indicate the performance of individual schools.

title: What is the future of Notting Hill Carnival? Inside the battle for survival
author: Niva Yadav
content:
What is the future for Notting Hill Carnival? Inside the battle for survival for Europe’s biggest street party
World-famous street party finds itself at a crossroads as it battles rising costs and safety fears as it celebrates its 60th anniversary
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Notting Hill Carnival almost didn’t happen in 2025.
Months of costume design, float construction, and rehearsals nearly collapsed after the carnival struggled to secure adequate funding following an independent safety review reporting “critical public safety concerns.”
London’s City Hall and the local councils of Kensington & Chelsea and Westminster were forced to step in with an emergency £1million bailout to save the Carnival in July last year, signalling the escalating battle over Europe’s largest street festival.
Just eight months later, Sir Sadiq Khan wrote another cheque totaling £4.66 million ahead of this year’s carnival, which mark’s the world-famous event’s sixtieth anniversary. The festival finds itself at a crossroads as it battles rising costs, safety concerns, and an onslaught of negative publicity.
Born out of British-Caribbean resilience and resistance to racism, CEO of Notting Hill Carnival Ltd Matthew Phillip argues the event is still “the biggest celebration and example of diversity” in Britain.
Yet as the event attracts more than two million attendees each year, it is now facing scrutiny over its operational budget, policing requirements, and public safety record.
The £21 million question: Escalating costs and public bailouts
The total cost for the three-day event has surged from approximately £6million in the early 2000s to a staggering £21million in 2025. These costs cover stewarding, policing, clean-up, and security, including additional costs for third-party contractors.
“It’s absolutely eye-watering the amount it costs,” she says. “It costs us an absolute fortune. Why should we have to pay for this?”
![Notting Hill Carnival 2025](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/12/09/10/37/Notting-Hill-Carnival-2025-3mlywy49.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
But for carnival organisers like Mr Phillip, it is an “investment” rather than a “burden” or a “drain”. According to research commissioned by the Voice Newspaper in 2024, JN Bank economist James Williams found that “total direct or net economic impact of Europe’s largest street festival is over £396 million annually”, as well as bringing in some 160,000 tourists and supporting 3,000 full-time jobs.
“It’s an investment in what it brings back to society,” Mr Phillip adds, explaining that carnival began “as a reaction” to marginalisation and deprivation, but created a way “to bring people together to celebrate things we have in common.”
“It’s a feeling of pride and a feeling of belonging,” he says. “No matter what our skin colour or religion, we’re all human beings.”
Leroy Logan, a former police superintendent and founding member of the Black Police Association, says carnival contributes a great deal into “empowering young people to know about their identity”, giving them a sense of “hope and aspiration”.
“There is that opportunity to pass on a positive legacy from generation to generation,” he says.
It is not just the cost of Notting Carnival that is rising; costs across London events have been on the rise. City Hall’s funding package for Pride in London rose from an initial £500,000 five-year contract in 2013 to a £625,000 five-year contract in 2023, while the budget for the annual New Year’s Eve fireworks display increased to approximately £4million in 2024 - even after the introduction of ticketing a decade earlier.
Policing, crime stats, and safety concerns
The rocketing costs faced by Carnival include policing, paid for by the Met Police each year. In 2025, the force spent £15.7million on the event - up from £11.7million in 2024. The expenses include accommodation, catering, and officer overtime.
In contrast, the Met Police spent just over £10 million on policing the 133 Premier League football matches hosted in London across the entire 2024-2025 season.
Tensions at carnival truly came to a head in 2024 when Cher Maximen was stabbed in front of her three-year-old child with a zombie knife - a story which shook London. But also a story which provided the vitriol for many to brand Notting Hill Carnival as a “violent” and unsafe event in desperate need of resolution.
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/15/17/FotoJet-(7).jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
“There is violence every single year at this particular event,” says Cllr Hall, pointing out that since 2016, more than 75 people have been stabbed. Last year, 528 people were arrested, four people were stabbed and 18 people were arrested for sexual assault.
But the reality is more, with the Met Police reporting a decline in serious violence in recent years - aided by facial recognition technology - and the majority of arrests stemming from drug offences rather than possession of offensive weapons.
Mr Philip insists that knife crime is a problem across the capital and not just at carnival.
“Any crime is not tolerable or acceptable in our view,” he says. “Carnival doesn’t cause crime. We are victim[s] of crime like everyone else.”
Some of Carnival’s mas band leaders have claimed that official figures are inflated by nearby, unrelated incidents - such as the 2024 murder of Mussie Imentu in Queensway, which took place outside the Carnival’s footprint.
Others have added that it is seldom the parade participants who are involved in the violence, rather the participants.
Colin Julien, owner of Caribbean Sessions mas band, explains as a participant of the parade, he has never seen the violence portrayed in the headlines. Pauline, band leader of Funatik Mas, agrees that she always feels safe at carnival as part of the band.
A Met Police spokesperson said: “We already distinguish between arrests at the event and arrests made on the approaches to it. For example, last year there were 528 arrests overall and we explained in our public statements that 135 were on the approaches to Carnival while the majority (393) were inside the event footprint.
“Arrests on the approaches are still very relevant, as a key part of the policing operation involves doing all we can to keep people safe by identifying and intercepting people intent on committing crime before they get into the busy crowds at the event.”
Beyond the monetary expense, the event can also place heavy strain on police services, forcing officers from surrounding counties and constabularies to work across bank holiday weekend.
“The police have got to go. Their holidays are stopped. They are obliged to go,” says Cllr Hall.
“I don’t like the way police are treated during it. They’re kicked at, they’re spat at, they’ve broken arms over time.”
According to Met Police figures, seventy-eight officers were injured while policing Notting Hill Carnival last year, while 100 were injured or assaulted in 2024.
“Carnival has been viewed in a prism of crime and violence”
Leroy Logan
A report by the Metropolitan Police Federation, representing 30,000 rank and file officers, recorded that 88.66% of officers said they felt unsafe while working at carnival. In one section of the report, an officer described the carnival as a “war zone” where “officers are treated as lambs to slaughter."
But Mr Logan has warned against framing the event as a “them vs us” narrative.
“Carnival has been viewed in a prism of crime and violence,” Mr Logan said, adding that the black community is frequently labelled as “violent and troublemakers,” with several organisers expressing frustration at the carnival’s negative perception in the press.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/15/18/Screenshot-2026-08-21-at-16-51-39.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Logan called on the Met Police to issue outcomes following arrests, including whether the suspects were charged or cautioned to provide context to the raw statistics.
He also condemned the Met’s use of tactics such as kettling, instead advocating for pre-emptive arrests and interventions to manage potential fallout at Carnival.
“I did that as a superintendent in Hackney. I’d go to certain areas where I built good relations, speak to [suspects], speak to youth workers, or even elders in the neighbourhood,” he said.
Responding to claims about a “them vs us” narrative, a spokesperson for the Met said: “We don’t recognise this characterisation of the present-day policing of Carnival. We’ve been very clear that the vast majority of people attending are there for all the right reasons – to have fun and enjoy a celebration.
“Our aim is to ensure they can do so safely by relentlessly targeting the small minority who are there to be violent, to put women at girls at risk or to commit other offences”
The festival has grown exponentially since its beginnings in the 1960s. From 500 residents in 1966 to more than 2 million expected in 2026. For many, the route, which has never expanded since its inception, is no longer fit for purpose and has led to criticism about overcrowding and “pinchpoints.”
“It’s a disaster waiting to happen with the crushing. It is absolutely rife for a crush” says Cllr Hall. “You’ll end up with a Hillsborough situation.”
“The joys of ticketing is you’d know how many people were there. You could arrange policing and all sorts of things in a better way. Secondly, it would start to pay for itself,” she said.
Organisers have been resolute in their plans to keep Notting Hill Carnival on the streets of W1, pointing out that Hyde Park’s largest licensed event, British Summer Time, caps daily capacity at 69,999 - a fraction of the attendance at Carnival.
Mr Philip argues that carnival must be “maintained as a free event which doesn’t have any barriers to participation, honouring the event’s founding principles as a place of inclusivity and community.
Long-term funding and cultural preservation
But organisers do have an alternative plan as they plot to “approach the Arts Council in the future so that Notting Hill Carnival can become a National Portfolio Organisation,” meaning the company could secure additional grant packages.
Without it, the carnival’s future does hang in the balance, with organisers agreeing that a more permanent solution must be found. Dr Debbie Weekes-Bernard, London’s Deputy Mayor for Communities and Social Justice, said in a statement that the mayor was “proud” to step in to ensure this “fantastic celebration of Caribbean culture” took place in its 60th year. But it remains unclear whether City Hall will continue to provide Notting Hill Carnival with the funding it needs.
A Kensington and Chelsea Council spokesperson said: “Our priority is to support the organisers in putting on a safe, successful and memorable Carnival for everyone.”
The statement added that the council would support traders and sound systems, providing more than 1,000 toilet facilities and teams would be deployed to clear around 300 tonnes of waste from the streets.
Besides the financial returns that Carnival brings to the capital annually, “it would be virtually impossible to measure the social impact [that Notting Hill Carnival] has in the kinds of well-being, self-pride, feeling of belonging,” says Mr Philip.
“You can’t put a price on that,” he says. And band leaders, sound systems, and steel pan bands all agree. From memories of playing mas for the first time, to honouring those who lost their lives at Grenfell, Notting Hill Carnival has brought together communities and has served as a vital tool for empowerment, especially amongst young people.
The event is one of only occasions in the London calendar which sees multiple generations celebrating together, one band leader tells the Standard. Another adds that carnival “puts the unity in community.”
![Dancers performing during the Notting Hill Carnival celebrations](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/08/25/13/35/SEI263295762.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Crucially, the organisers want to invest more of the funding into the people “at the heart of the event”, including the sound systems, mas bands, Brazilian bands, and steel bands.
By bolstering the cultural relevance of the event, organisers believe they can protect the carnival to ensure it is treated as a piece of heritage, and not just a giant street party.
“Those communities are the artistic and cultural lifeblood of the event,” says Mr Philip.
He adds that recognising Carnival as “the force of good” that it is will be the first step in ensuring it lives on to see another 60 years and more.
Amid a backdrop of racial tensions and hostility, carnival organisers continue to see the event as a symbol of diversity and a cause for celebration.
“It’s a big message to those people that seek to find division and rift in our communities. Everyone that comes to carnival is not here for that.
“This is us coming together to show solidarity.”
summary: Europe's Notting Hill Carnival is facing significant challenges regarding its future as it celebrates its 60th anniversary, driven by escalating operating budgets, safety concerns, and heavy policing costs. City Hall and local councils recently provided emergency bailouts to secure the event's continuation, though debates persist over public safety, crime statistics, and whether the festival should remain free and un-ticketed. Despite these financial and security pressures, organizers and supporters emphasize the event's profound economic and cultural impact, generating hundreds of millions of pounds and fostering community pride.
key_points: The total cost of hosting the three-day Notting Hill Carnival surged to £21 million in 2025, with policing expenses alone reaching £15.7 million.
London's City Hall and local councils intervened with emergency financial bailouts, including a £4.66 million package ahead of the 60th-anniversary event.

While critics and a police federation report highlight concerns over violence, injuries to officers, and large crowds, organizers and supporters argue that crime is not caused by the carnival and point to its £396 million annual economic impact.

Organizers remain committed to keeping the festival free and accessible without ticketing barriers, while exploring potential future funding avenues such as becoming a National Portfolio Organisation with the Arts Council.

title: Revealed: The surprise Londoners backing Nigel Farage's Reform
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Farage says Labour and Tories 'wiped out' as Reform win first London borough](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/06/d818f16f675553392e5ece071789cda6Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg2NzY5NjAx-2.85221085.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) So, who are the Londoners backing Mr Farage’s party? More male than female voters are supporting Reform. The perception is also that older people lean Reform. But the survey showed by far the biggest group of voters in London turning to this party is 45 to 54-year-olds. Reform picked up 38% of this age group in voting intentions for London mayor, compared to 22% for those aged 55 and over. Dr Eoghan Kelly, a postdoctoral researcher in British Politics at Queen Mary University of London, said: “Reform voters are older than average, but the party hasn't broken through amongst the oldest age groups who are sticking with the Conservatives. “It is predominantly people in their 40s, 50s and 60s who are opting for Reform. They are mostly white, male, less well off, and less well educated. “There isn't a big Inner/Outer split, but Reform are bigger in the eastern half of London especially as you approach Kent or Essex.” ![

ROMFORD, ENGLAND - MAY 08: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage poses with winning councillors outside Havering Town Hall following the 2026 local election results on May 08, 2026 in Romford, England. Voters went to the polls yesterday in the local elections across England. Results counted overnight show widespread losses for the Labour Party. Several key Labour councils have surrendered their majority as Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats make significant gains. (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/05/08/11/2275131541.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Thirteen per cent of this age group would vote for Ms Cunningham, the survey suggested, as would 11% of Londoners aged 24 to 35, and 18% of those 35 to 44. The age group results, and some other categories, need to be treated with some caution given the small sample sizes in a poll of 1,036 adults. But the findings on Inner London, long a Labour stronghold, and Outer London, where Reform did best at the local elections winning control of Havering, should be more robust given there are just two categories rather than four or five. The poll showed Reform getting 21% of the mayoral vote in Inner London and 20% in outer boroughs. A more detailed geographical breakdown put it on 23% of the vote in eastern boroughs, 21 in the west, 19% in the south, 18% in the north and 16% in central areas. Reform is picking up 30% of the vote among white people, and 8% from ethnic minority communities. One in five single people (19%) would vote for Mr Farage’s party in the mayoral contest, 17% of those who are married or in couples, and 44% of individuals who are separated, divorced or widowed. Read More Eighteen per cent of lesbian, gay or bisexual Londoners would vote for Ms Cunningham, according to the poll, as would 21% of heterosexual/straight people. Nearly a quarter of Londoners (23%) without children say they would vote Reform, compared to 18% with children. Reform gets more than double the support from people who have not been to university, 33%, compared to 14% of graduates. A third of London voters (32%) living in social or council housing back the party, more than the 22% for Labour, as would 18% of tenants renting privately, 19% of homeowners with or without a mortgage, and 16% of those living at home with their parents. One in four Londoners with household income below £30,000 favour Reform, compared to 18% for the £30,000 to £49,999 category, and 20% for those on £50,000 or more.
summary: A survey reveals the demographic profile of Londoners supporting Nigel Farage's Reform party, showing higher backing among men, individuals without university degrees, and those living in social housing. While Reform is often perceived as a party for older voters, the poll indicates its strongest support comes from 45 to 54-year-olds rather than the oldest age groups. Regionally, the party performs strongly in eastern London boroughs and shows consistent support across both Inner and Outer London.
key_points: Reform's largest age demographic of supporters in London is 45 to 54-year-olds at 38%, compared to 22% for those aged 55 and over.
Supporters are predominantly male, mostly white, less well off, and less well educated.
The party receives more than double the support from non-graduates (33%) compared to university graduates (14%).
A third of London voters (32%) living in social or council housing back Reform.
Geographically, Reform polls highest in the eastern boroughs of London at 23%.

title: Thunderstorms warning in force for London as rain sweeps capital
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Rain showers sweep across London amid fears of flash flooding](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/01M0FGM7PFKA584505TS8Y08EH.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Forecasters at the Met Office had predicted “a band of heavy showers and thunderstorms” hitting the capital on Wednesday morning and further showers, with further stormy weather hitting in the afternoon.
But current weather forecasts on the BBC and Met Office for Wednesday forecasts predict rain showers during parts of the day - but not thundery downpours. Rain is set to fall during morning rush hour.
A yellow warning for thunderstorms has been issued from 3am to 10pm on Wednesday across much of England including London and the South East, the Midlands, East Anglia, and parts of the North West, South West, as well as eastern parts of Wales.
The Met Office warned that showers and thunderstorms on Wednesday afternoon “may be intense”, with 20-30mm rain falling in less than an hour and 40-50mm being possible in two to three hours in a few spots, leading to some surface water flooding.
The London Mayor urged Londoners to prepare for possible torrential downpours.
“From 3am, London is at risk of severe flash floods,” he posted on X.
“Intense downpours could see up to 50mm of rainfall arrive in the space of just a few hours - almost the total average rainfall for August.”
The yellow thunderstorm warning remains in place until 10pm on Wednesday.
Yellow flood warnings mean that there is a small chance that businesses and homes could experience flooding.
The Met Office also warns where flooding or lightning strikes occur, there is a chance of delays and some cancellations to train and bus services.
Read More
Spray and sudden flooding could lead to difficult driving conditions and some road closures.
There is a slight chance that power cuts could occur and other services to some homes and businesses could be lost
This could lead to cancellations of public transport services and some road closures.
The hard ground after the sustained hot weather is expected to increase the risk of flash flooding.
The rainfall will be welcomed by many after London was declared to be under a drought after the record dry summer.
It has left London under a hose pipe ban and the capitals’s parks brown and dried out.
summary: A yellow weather warning for thunderstorms and heavy rain is in force for London and large parts of England and Wales until 10pm on Wednesday. Forecasters warn that intense downpours could bring up to 50mm of rain in a few hours, creating risks of flash flooding, transport disruptions, and power cuts. The rainfall follows a record dry summer that placed London under a drought and a hosepipe ban, leaving parks brown and dried out.
key_points: A yellow thunderstorm warning is in place from 3am to 10pm on Wednesday.
Intense downpours could bring 40-50mm of rain in two to three hours, increasing flash flood risks due to hard ground from hot weather.
The severe weather may cause travel delays, road closures, public transport cancellations, and potential power cuts.
The rain follows a record dry summer and drought in London that resulted in a hosepipe ban.

title: London's income tax bill hits record £80 billion as PM doesn't rule out more levies
author: Nicholas Cecil; Luke Reevey
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Andy Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises: 'Whatever I do will be carefully thought out'](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/22/c27eff905c6232167f1f0952a9acc9cfY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzE4NTk3-2.85564291.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Hundreds of thousands of people in London and its commuter belt have been dragged into paying the basic and higher rates of income tax by the threshold freeze which Rachel Reeves extended for a further three years until 2031. The 20% basic rate of income tax is paid on income from £12,571 to £50,270, and the 40% higher rate on income from £50,271 to £125,140. He has signalled that he may increase levies on the better off to fund measures to ease the cost of living for millions of households struggling to make ends meet. ![

Property prices are falling in Inner London

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/04/22/13/2197616128.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The Office for National Statistics data details how the capital contributed almost £240 billion in taxes to the Treasury in 2024/25, but benefited from only £165.5 billion in public spending. Read More After items such as capital expenditure and depreciation are taken into account, London's "fiscal surplus" for the Government totalled an all-time high of £48.8 billion, up from £45.3 billion the previous year. Only one other region, the South East, also makes a net contribution to the Exchequer. All other English regions, as well as Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, receive more in public spending than they contribute in tax. The biggest net recipient is the North West, the region that includes Mr Burnham's Manchester heartland and Makerfield constituency, which had a fiscal deficit of £39.5 billion in 2024/25. By contrast Mr Burnham's North West received a net subsidy equivalent to £5,162 per head.
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people in London and its commuter belt have been pulled into basic and higher income tax rates due to a threshold freeze extended until 2031. Office for National Statistics data shows London contributed nearly £240 billion in taxes in 2024/25 while receiving £165.5 billion in public spending. This resulted in London's fiscal surplus reaching a record £48.8 billion.
key_points: Income tax thresholds have been frozen until 2031 by Rachel Reeves.
London contributed nearly £240 billion in taxes to the Treasury in 2024/25.
London's fiscal surplus reached a record high of £48.8 billion.
Only London and the South East make a net tax contribution to the Exchequer, while other regions receive more in spending than they contribute.

title: East Midlands Railway passengers complain about unviable service
author: Katy Prickett
content:
![Picture of the front of a train - the class 810 - on a railway line.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1200/cpsprodpb/526b/live/c5cf8430-89c5-11f1-a501-d9a9d2e9b6c1.jpg)
Regular train users have written to the Corby MP about the "unreliability" of East Midlands Railway (EMR) as strike action looms
- Published
"East Midlands Railway either don't have the rolling stock or they don't have the staff," says regular rail traveller Matthew Aldridge.
He is among train users on the Corby to London St Pancras line who have contacted their MP Lee Barron complaining about the unreliability of the service.
Aldridge, from Thrapston, Northamptonshire, said his daughter has often been stranded at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, or Bedford, requiring him to collect her.
A train company spokesperson said "extreme hot weather and a number of infrastructure issues over the wider rail network" meant its performance has fallen below the standard expected.
![A head and shoulder shot of Matthew Aldridge standing against a wall. He has greying dark hair and a grey beard. He is wearing a maroon T-shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/5f23/live/e7ba2370-a08b-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Matthew Aldridge describes East Midlands Railway's north to south services as useless
Aldridge said: "It just seems, more and more, that chances are you're going to have no service available to you - and if there is one available, the others around it will have been cancelled and so the train will be absolutely chock-a-block with other people whose service has been cancelled."
His family used to regularly travel to London for work or for an evening out, "but it's just not viable anymore".
"We're going on holiday in a few weeks, we're flying from Luton, but we're not going to take the train because we can't risk there being no train - we're going to have to drive down and put the car in the car park," he added.
![A close up of the side of an East Midlands carriage. It is branded in purple colour and has E M R written on its side in capital letters. It is sitting at a platform, which can just be seen on the left.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/959f/live/7d105240-a09c-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Regular London commuter Rachel Wilson agrees and wonders if the solution is to move closer to a better train line
Rachel Wilson, who lives in Irthlingborough, also wrote to Barron, the Labour MP for Corby and East Northamptonshire.
"I think over the last probably five, six months, it's become almost unusable," said the charity worker, who has commuted to London two days a week for five years.
She cited delays, cancellations, broken air conditioning and too few carriages for the number of passengers, while train ticket prices continued to go up.
"This year in particular has been just impossible," she said, adding she is wondering if it would be simpler to move nearer a better commuter line.
"I'm late for meetings, I'm late home. I've had to be collected from Northampton, from Bedford, from Milton Keynes - I'm very lucky that I have a husband that will come out sometimes in the middle of the night to collect me so that I'm not completely stranded."
Both passengers said complaints to EMR resulted in an automated reply including the delay repay link.
![A head and shoulder shot of Lee Barron. He has black-framed glasses and is wearing a mid blue jacket over a light blue open necked shirt. Behind him is grass, a path and a children's play area behind a fence.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/070e/live/e74a13d0-a09c-11f1-8a1f-314a01485cf4.jpg)
Lee Barron has told the railway company his constituents expect a reliable, professional service and instead endure disruption, uncertainty and inconvenience
Barron has written to the company, saying: "For many constituents, this route can no longer be considered a reliable transport option.
"Confidence in the service has steadily eroded, and my constituents have also reported having to book overnight accommodation in London because they cannot rely on being on time for early morning work appointments."
An EMR spokesperson said: "We're sorry to customers who have been affected by recent disruption on EMR Connect.
"We recognise the frustration that disruption causes and are working closely with our industry partners to improve reliability and minimise the impact on customers."
It has also invested Â£30m to transform its fleet, they added.
Union members working at EMR plan to strike for 48 hours from 30 August - the bank holiday weekend - over "safety concerns" with its new fleet of Aurora (Class 810) trains.
Do you have a story suggestion for Northamptonshire? Contact us below.
summary: Regular passengers on the East Midlands Railway (EMR) Corby to London St Pancras line have contacted their MP to complain about severe unreliability, cancellations, and overcrowding. Commuters report being frequently stranded and state the service has become unviable for work and leisure travel. EMR apologized for the disruption, citing extreme hot weather and wider infrastructure issues, while union members also announced upcoming strike action over safety concerns with new trains.
key_points: Train users have written to Corby MP Lee Barron regarding the unreliability of EMR services.
Passengers report frequent delays, cancellations, overcrowding, and broken air conditioning.
EMR stated that extreme hot weather and wider infrastructure issues have negatively impacted performance.
Union members working at EMR plan a 48-hour strike starting 30 August over safety concerns regarding new Aurora trains.

title: Murder investigation launched as young man dies after stabbing at council HQ
author: Helen William
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/18/5d37a3c6b8845e16a0c3e7b46060ad85Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NzY0MjE4-2.85657870.jpg?crop=8:5,smart&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
A murder investigation has been launched after a young man died after a stabbing at a council headquarters building.
He was found with stab wounds and treated by paramedics but pronounced dead at the scene.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/18/43d88f4f9d4676262d90900da9f68826Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NzY0Mjcz-2.85657869.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Some staff, residents and visitors saw the fatal attack take place, according to Brent Council leader Muhammed Butt, who said the area had been left “shaken” by the incident.
The civic centre was evacuated and is now shut until further notice as police search for the killer.
Police have imposed a Section 60 order, granting officers enhanced powers to stop and search people and vehicles.
The order covers the Wembley Park, Barnhill, Tokyngton, Stonebridge, Roundwood, Dollis Hill, Willesden and Welsh Harp ward areas of Brent.
Superintendent Chris Clarke, lead for emergency response policing in the area, said: “This is an awful incident in which someone has tragically lost their life.”
No arrests have yet been made and police are “urgently” trying to identify the victim and inform his next of kin.
Mr Clarke added: “An investigation is under way to establish exactly what has taken place and trace those responsible.
“We recognise the concern this incident will cause within the local community and are committed to keeping residents informed as our inquiries progress.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/18/f43b1b3e1e18b481f58e13e5a8611511Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NzY0MzUw-2.85657841.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“In light of the incident, we have authorised additional stop and search powers to help prevent further violence, support our investigation, and keep people safe.
Read More
“There will be an increased police presence in and around the area in the coming hours while our officers continue their investigation.”
Mr Butt urged people to stay away, saying: “Today, Brent has been shaken by an appalling and deeply tragic incident at the civic centre, in which a person has lost their life.
“Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim, their family and loved ones, as well as the staff, residents and visitors who witnessed what happened.
“The civic centre has been evacuated and will remain closed until further notice.
“I would urge people to avoid the area and allow the police and emergency services to carry out their work.
“There is an active police investigation under way – please do not speculate or repeat any unverified claims online.”
There had been a “swift response” from the emergency services to the incident and council officials are now “working closely” with the Metropolitan Police, he added.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/18/0b6e6869c8dcd0ac82674787953100f0Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NzY0NjU5-2.85657871.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Butt said council staff had also shown “professionalism, compassion and calm” in dealing with the “most difficult of circumstances”.
A London Ambulance Service spokesman said: “We were called at 2.25pm today to reports of a stabbing at Brent Civic Centre, Wembley, HA9.
“We sent an ambulance crew, paramedics in fast response cars and an incident response officer.
“We also dispatched London’s Air Ambulance.
“Sadly, despite the best efforts of our crews, a patient was pronounced dead at the scene.”
A statement later appeared on the council website saying: “The Brent Civic Centre and Wembley Library are currently closed due to an ongoing incident.
“Please avoid visiting the building at this time.
“We’ll share updates as soon as we can.”
summary: A murder investigation has been launched after a young man was fatally stabbed at Brent Council's headquarters. The civic centre was evacuated and remains closed while police search for the killer and work to identify the victim. Authorities have implemented a Section 60 stop and search order covering multiple ward areas in Brent.
key_points: A young man died from stab wounds at a council headquarters building after being treated by paramedics at the scene.
The civic centre and Wembley Library have been closed until further notice following the incident.
No arrests have been made, and police are urgently trying to identify the victim and notify his next of kin.
A Section 60 order has been enacted, granting police enhanced stop and search powers across several areas in Brent.

title: London Playbook PM: On the home front
author: Emilio Casalicchio
content:
Good afternoon. This is Emilio Casalicchio.
TUESDAY CHEAT SHEET
— Ministers are batting off complaints that Andy Burnham watered down a social housing pledge.
— Kemi Badenoch is plotting a post-recess mini-reshuffle to manage some HR logistics.
— Labour infighting about their next HQ boss continues.
— Nigel Farage said there’s a “risk” small boat migrants could form an army to rise up against Brits.
— Conservative and Labour frontbenchers got into a spat about the A66 crash.
DRIVETIME DEBRIEF
ON THE HOME FRONT: Ministers are dismissing criticism about Andy Burnham backing off his Makerfield campaign pledge for all new council homes to be for social rent. As Playbook noted this morning, the government confirmed overnight that just 60 percent of the first £10 billion in funding from the Social and Affordable Homes Programme will be for social rents — about the same level as the Keir Starmer administration had planned.
The excuse is: “The proportions of money going to social rent in this programme dwarf anything that previous governments have done,” Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told Sky this morning. So that’s OK then. He added to BBC Breakfast: “Burnham said in the by-election that he wanted to see more money spent on social rent on council housebuilding. That’s exactly what we’re doing through this initial wave of funding.” Critics would argue he said he wanted all cash spent on social rent. Which is not what the government is doing.
Ah well: It’s an initial No.10 lesson for Burnham on making promises that can’t be kept — a lesson politicians never seem to learn. The Greens lashed out at the “massive backtrack.”
The other political fight around this housing announcement … is the suggestion from Shadow Communities Secretary James Cleverly that new council homes won’t need to be built until 2039. But government officials pointed out that 2039 is the hard stop for the final homes to be built under the plan, and some being built right now will be finished before the end of this parliament.
DON’T SWEAT THE SMALL SHUFF: Playbook PM can confirm the Tony Diver report in the Telegraph about a mini-Conservative reshuffle coming after recess. Kemi Badenoch needs to cover Claire Coutinho’s looming maternity leave, mirror the government merger between the business and science departments and replace Solicitor General Helen Grant, who wants to stand down. Diver hears newbies including Katie Lam, Harriet Cross and Aphra Brandreth could be promoted, and details some of the amusing infighting over shadow cabinet talent (or lack thereof).
Further reading for those who love the infighting: The latest write-up of the coming Anthony Seldon book about Rishi Sunak reveals allegations that Badenoch plotted to depose him. It’s in the Independent. Seldon is on the News Agents podcast tonight.
Not wanting to feel left out: The Labour scrap over who gets to be its next general secretary continues. This thread from activist Emily Pomroy-Smith supporting Claire Reynolds was being shared around WhatsApp following reports that Joe Fortune is the Burnham pick. One Labour MP argued that Burnham had “sacked the first female chancellor and replaced her with a white man. He then got rid of the two chief of staff members at No.10 who were both women and replaced them with a white man. Now we hear he’s replacing the woman we had as Gen Sec with … guess what … another white man!” The person said they were “furious I was fooled by [Burnham’s] false promises.”
And over in camp John Lehal: Another Labour MP texted in that it was a “sad day for the Labour Party to lose the great talent of John Lehal.” Worth waiting for the actual confirmation about the gen sec role, of course.
BULLEH PAYERS: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh suggested there could be further tweaks to green levies in energy bills at the coming budget. Rachel Reeves moved some levies (which pay for net-zero infrastructure and consumer support) into tax last November. “We have already started doing this,” Fahnbulleh wrote during a Reddit ask-me-anything this afternoon, adding: “We’ll keep looking at how these costs are recovered in the fairest way.”
FIGHT THEM ON THE BEACHES? Nigel Farage said there’s a “risk” small boat migrants form an army to rise up against Brits. He told Reform conference host Jeremy Kyle that arrivals are “aggressive, dangerous young men,” adding: “There are some who say ‘could some of them turn into a force within this country, perhaps even an army in this country, that’s against us at some point in the future?’ I don’t think we’re there yet but the risk remains.”
Elsewhere in the softball Talk interview … Farage dismissed the report in the Times overnight that Georgia Meloni told Kemi Badenoch not to form an electoral pact with Reform. “I don’t see a single quote from Georgia Meloni herself,” Farage said about the account. “I see what Kemi Badenoch tells us Georgia Meloni said.” My POLITICO colleague Hannah Roberts writes in from Rome that team Meloni insists she never made the suggestion to Badenoch. An official for the Fratelli d’Italia party said the PM has no hostility to Farage or Reform but does not intend to get involved in domestic political dynamics or the relationships between British parties.
On which note … the Reform pact line from the Times tale appears to have been scrubbed from the internet.
BEANS FOR BRITAIN: The government is preparing a campaign telling Brits to store tinned food and bottled water in case of emergencies from extreme weather or hack attacks, according to the FT. It comes as ministers accelerate work on a “war book” manual about defending against external threats.
WHAT ELSE THE GOVERNMENT WANTED TO TALK ABOUT: Some £70 million to help restart production at the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon, with the government pledging to ringfence 50 percent of production for use in Britain. The mineral is used in steel, electronics and aerospace. Explainer from the great Ed Conway here.
IPSA FACTO: IPSA opened an investigation into DUP MP Gregory Campbell over office cost claims linked to printed constituency cards and signage. The expenses watchdog won’t publish further info until the investigation has concluded.
WHAT THE LIB DEMS WANTED TO TALK ABOUT: MP Charlie Maynard (who once took Thames Water to court) complained about reports that Andy Burnham won’t take the firm into special administration.
SOCIAL (MEDIA) AFFAIRS
TWITTER RAGE BAIT FIGHT OF THE DAY: Conservative frontbencher Nick Timothy and Home Office Minister Anna Turley have been squabbling about her response to the A66 crash at the weekend that killed seven people, including two police officers. Timothy accused Turley of having “put two police officers on a par with the thugs who killed them” in a Facebook post she published after the incident. But she shot back in a letter the Mail put online that no one knew the identities of the non-police victims when she published the post, which contained zero equivalence. “The fact that you have sought to create media hits and political points out of this horrendous event is beneath contempt,” she wrote.
BEYOND THE M25
A MATTER OF LIFE AND DEATH: The number of babies born in Scotland fell to a record low for the third year in a row, with just 45,067 live births recorded in 2025, 696 fewer than 2024. The 61,726 registered deaths also marked the eleventh consecutive year of more deaths than births. The Scotsman has a write-up.
OH, CANADA: Canada will launch 50 percent retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. across 700 products, following Prime Minister Mark Carney’s vow to match Donald Trump’s duties “dollar for dollar.” The new tariffs will be imposed from September 8. The Guardian has a live blog.
CHINESE WHISPERS: Beijing has vowed to protect its interests after the U.S. widened economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners. Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China opposed “illegal unilateral sanctions” and would take “all necessary measures” to protect its rights. China is currently the biggest buyer of Iranian oil. The BBC has more.
Back in the Strait of Hormuz: Trump claimed “all mines” have been removed or detonated from within the waterway. Writing on Truth Social, the U.S. president said Tehran has been told “any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed.”
GERMAN CONCERN: Friedrich Merz warned Germany is “facing very real threats” after explosive drones were found near Leipzig airport earlier this month. The German chancellor didn’t ascribe responsibility for the attack but said his team is “working intensively on that together with the security agencies, and we will present our findings and comment on them shortly.” My colleague Jules Darmanin has further info.
WHATSAPPENING? Foreign governments have tried hacking the messaging accounts of high-ranking EU officials, the bloc’s cyber defense unit said in an internal presentation obtained by my POLITICO colleague Sam Clark. The presentation is the first official acknowledgement that EU officials were targeted by cyber attacks through messaging apps and the first reported instance of an EU authority formally linking this to a foreign government.
TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND
LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) and ITV Evening News (6.30 p.m.) lead on five further arrests in the Middlesbrough A66 crash investigation … Channel 4 News (7 p.m.) focuses on the government’s social housing plans.
Simon Marks at Drive (LBC, until 7 p.m.): Home Builders Federation Chief Executive Neil Jefferson (5.05 p.m.) … Tory London Assembly Member Neil Garratt (6.35 p.m.).
Drive with John Pienaar (Times Radio, until 7 p.m.): West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker … Crossbench peers Richard Dannatt, Mark Malloch Brown and Peter Ricketts.
BBC PM (Radio 4, 5 p.m.): University of Sheffield academic Michael Jacobs (5.30 p.m.).
The News Agents (Podcast, drops at 5 p.m.): Historian and author Anthony Seldon.
Dewbs and Co (GB News, 6 p.m.): Reform UK London mayoral candidate Laila Cunningham.
The Evening Edition with Kait Borsay (Times Radio, 7 p.m.): Prison Officers Association National Chair Mark Fairhurst (7.15 p.m.) … unaffiliated peer Claire Fox (9 p.m.).
Jacob Rees-Mogg’s State of the Nation (GB News, 8 p.m.): Reform UK governing board member Gawain Towler.
REVIEWING THE PAPERS TONIGHT: Sky News (10 p.m.): Total Politics Group’s Mark Wallace and journo Jenny Kleeman … Times Radio (10.30 p.m.): Talk’s Peter Cardwell and broadcaster Carolyn Quinn.
TOMORROW’S WORLD
THE TOUR CONTINUES: Andy Burnham is expected to be out and about talking NEETs.
FEELING THE HEAT: Ofgem announces the energy price cap covering October 1 to December 31 at 7 a.m.
NEXT JEN: Reform MP Robert Jenrick is hosting a press conference in London at 11 a.m. to talk about business regulation.
ANY OTHER BUSINESS
MOVING ON: Spinner Robin Chappell is stepping down from the Lib Dems’ comms team this week after 13 years working for the party.
IN MEMORIAM: Commons staffer Dom Casoria will run the Luleå Sea Ice Marathon in the Arctic Circle in February, fundraising for Bipolar UK in memory of his first boyfriend, Liam Love, who died in November. Casoria decided to run the closest marathon to the northern Swedish town where Liam was from and is buried. Full details here.
WHAT I’VE BEEN READING: The Marginal Revolution blog from Canadian-American economist Alex Tabarrok suggesting peers in the U.K. House of Lords could be given votes proportional to bond holdings and real-GDP shares — since bond-holders value a stable market, but might need occasional nudging in favor of consumer prices. Nice to be a theorist, eh.
PACKED LUNCH OR PALACE LUNCH: It’s recess! Make the most of a quiet parliament with a wander around to check out the menus.
ON THIS DAY IN POLITICS: On August 25, 1939, the IRA carried out a Coventry bombing where five people were killed. On the same day in 1944, Paris was liberated from Nazi occupation by the Allies.
WRITING PLAYBOOK TOMORROW MORNING: Sam Blewett.
THANKS TO: My editor Luke McGee, reporter Noah Keate and the POLITICO production team for making it look nice.

Playbook | D.C. Influence | Canada Playbook | POLITICO Forecast | Canberra Playbook | All our POLITICO Pro policy morning newsletters
summary: Ministers are defending social housing funding plans after criticism that Andy Burnham watered down a previous campaign pledge for all new council homes to be for social rent. Meanwhile, Kemi Badenoch is planning a post-recess mini-reshuffle, and Nigel Farage suggested there is a risk that small boat migrants could form an army against Britons. Additionally, the government is reportedly preparing an emergency preparedness campaign encouraging the public to store tinned food and bottled water.
key_points: The government confirmed that 60 percent of the initial £10 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme funding will be allocated for social rents.
Kemi Badenoch is plotting a mini-reshuffle following upcoming parliamentary recess to manage HR logistics and cover a maternity leave.
Nigel Farage claimed there is a risk that aggressive young small boat migrants could form an anti-British force in the future.
The UK government is preparing an emergency campaign advising citizens to store tinned food and bottled water for weather or cyber emergencies.
