title: The Best Bars For A Girls’ Night In London
author: Natasha Harding
content:
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/barsgirlsnightout.gif)
You’ve finally got a night when everyone’s free, the group chat is buzzing, and now the only question is: where to drink? Skip the obvious picks and book somewhere that actually feels like a night out. After you’ve found a cool spot for dinner, these are the bars we keep coming back to when the girls are in town and you want something a bit more interesting than the usual.
Smokey Kudu
Nearest tube: Baker Street
Upstairs above Kudu in Marylebone, Smokey Kudu is an intimate cocktail lounge with a South African twist. Expect classic cocktails, a solid champagne offering, and breathtaking caramel interiors.
Where: 7 Moxon Street, London W1U 4EP
Website: www.kuducollective.com
The Red Room
Nearest tube: Bond Street
Hidden behind a velvet curtain at The Connaught, The Red Room is a plush, intimate hideaway with a wine list to match. Whether you’re looking for a special occasion spot, or a way to elevate your Friday night, this is a spot to know.
Where: The Connaught, Carlos Place, London W1K 2AL
Website: www.maybourne.com
Bar Crispin
Nearest tube: Oxford Circus
Located adjacent to Soho’s Kingly Street, Bar Crispin is a buzzing natural wine bar with a terrace that’s perfect for people-watching. The wine list is eclectic, the plates are shareable, and the tables are almost always full.
Where: 19 Kingly Street, London W1B 5PY
Website: www.crispinlondon.com
Naked & Famous
Nearest tube: Notting Hill Gate
Hidden beneath Zephyr on Portobello Road, Naked & Famous is a retro-inspired cocktail lounge with a moody vibe. Able to house just 35 guests at a time, it’s perfect for a chic yet intimate girls’ night.
Where: 100 Portobello Road, London W11 2QD
Website: www.nakedandfamousbar.com
Sol’s
Nearest tube: Bayswater
A neighbourhood wine bar and deli in Bayswater, Sol is all about great wines and a relaxed atmosphere. This is the kind of place where you turn up for a glass or two, and end up staying until closing.
Where: 25 Leinster Terrace, London W2 3ET
Website: @solslondon
    This is a local gem that’s opened up near me, and it’s already a favourite. It’s got a brilliant choice of wines, the vibe is lively, and it’s clearly a go-to for other cool girl catch ups in the area.
Natasha, Digital Editor
![](https://www.thehandbook.com/cdn-cgi/image/width=300,height=300,fit=cover,q=80,format=webp/https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2024/12/tash-1.jpg) 
The Dreamery
Nearest tube: Essex Road / Haggerston
Part wine bar, part ice-cream parlour, The Dreamery in De Beauvoir Town is as fun as it sounds. Pair a glass of glou-glou with an unexpected ice cream scoop – this is a brilliant option for when you’re after a slightly different kind of girls’ night.
Where: 20a Halliford Street, London N1 3HD
Website: @thedreameryldn
Flute Bar
Nearest tube: Oxford Circus
Set atop Broadwick Soho, Flute is the ultimate retro-inspired cocktail bar. With panoramic views, maximalist interiors, and a cocktail list that changes with the seasons, it’s a fail-safe central option.
Where: 7th Floor, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8HT
Website: www.broadwicksoho.com
Scarfes Bar
Nearest tube: Holborn
Inside the Rosewood Hotel, Scarfes Bar is a jazz-age cocktail lounge with plush sofas, towering bookcases, and live music most nights. Notify the group chat to dress up, order a martini, and feel like you’ve stepped into another era.
Where: Rosewood London, 252 High Holborn, London WC1V 7EN
Website: www.rosewoodhotels.com
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/amie-wine-for-friends-amie-wine-studio-26-81f74fe3-538a-4ecf-9444-6e666761d484-540x-edited.png)
Amie Wine
Tucked away in Eccleston Yards, Amie Wine is a low-key local spot that feels like a secret. Think natural wines, warm lighting, and a relaxed vibe with spot-on interiors.
Where: 13 Eccleston Yards, London SW1W 9AZ
Website: www.drinkamie.com
Upstairs at Hausu
Nearest tube: Peckham Rye
Above the restaurant Hausu in Peckham, Upstairs at Hausu is a dimly lit listening bar with hi-fi sound, vinyl spins, and a full bar. It’s the perfect spot for a night of casual drinks, great tunes, and a little dancing.
Where: 11a Station Way, London SE15 4RX
Website: www.hausu.co.uk
Nipperkin
Nearest tube: Green Park
Nipperkin is a subterranean cocktail bar that feels more like a private living room than a hotel spot. British ingredients meet Japanese precision in the drinks – you’re in for a smorgasbord of unconventional savoury cocktail options. With the vinyl spinning in the background, it’s equal parts cool and intimate.
Where: 20 Berkeley Street, London W1J 8EE
Website: www.nijulondon.com/nipperkin
Zum Barbarossa
Nearest tube: Tottenham Court Road
Located in the basement of a Grade II-listed Georgian townhouse on Dean Street, Zum Barbarossa is Soho’s answer to a Parisian-style speakeasy. Think plush sofas, curved brick ceilings, and a cocktail list that leans into French classics with a playful twist.
Where: 77 Dean Street, London W1D 3SH
Website: www.zumbarbarossa.com/london
Three Sheets
Nearest tube: Dalston Junction or Tottenham Court Road
Three Sheets is the kind of no-fuss cocktail bar that your ‘in the know’ friend already counts among their favourites. The drinks are bang on (whether you’re opting for the famous gateway martini, or the 0% whiskey sour) and the vibe is relaxed enough that you can actually catch up and have a proper chat.
Where: Dalston & Soho
Website: www.threesheets-bar.com
Ellie’s
Nearest tube: Dalston Junction
On Kingsland Road in Dalston, Ellie’s is the kind of neighbourhood bar that feels like home. It’s fuss-free, has affordable drinks (as far as London pricing goes, at least), making it a top pick for a relaxed girls’ night.
Where: 428 Kingsland Road, London E8 4AA
Website: @elliesdalston
summary: This article provides a curated list of recommended bars across London for a girls' night out, featuring a variety of venues ranging from intimate cocktail lounges to natural wine bars. The selections highlight unique atmospheres, specialized drink menus, and ideal locations for socializing with friends. Each featured bar includes its nearest tube station and address information.
key_points: Smokey Kudu in Marylebone offers an intimate cocktail lounge setting with a South African twist.
Bar Crispin in Soho functions as a buzzing natural wine bar with a popular terrace for people-watching.
The Dreamery in De Beauvoir Town uniquely combines a wine bar with an ice-cream parlour.
Scarfes Bar inside the Rosewood Hotel provides a jazz-age lounge experience featuring plush sofas and live music.
Ellie’s on Kingsland Road serves as a fuss-free, affordable neighbourhood bar ideal for a relaxed evening.

title: Brandon To: Sadiq Khan has killed off the last Good Samaritans | Conservative Home
author: Brandon To
content:
Brandon To is a Politics graduate from UCL and a Hong Kong BN(O) immigrant settled in Harrow.
London has a new kind of crime fighter.
He does not wear a uniform. He is not paid by the Metropolitan Police. He has hundreds of thousands of followers on social media and spends his time watching for pickpockets around London.
His name is Diego Galdino, better known as “Pickpocket London”. And, according to Sadiq Khan, he has played no role in reducing crime.
I find that astonishing.
Diego told Metro that he has helped victims, identified pickpockets and passed information to police. He says that he has seen around 25 suspects arrested, including two who were subsequently deported. He has even noticed that offenders recognise him and leave when they see him coming.
Is he a substitute for the police? Of course not. But why should that mean he deserves no credit?
The Mayor’s response was to praise the Metropolitan Police for bringing phone theft down while dismissing the contribution of “vigilantes”. He is right about one thing: nobody should be encouraged to put themselves in danger or take the law into their own hands.
But he has spread a very wrong message.
He’s telling the public to witness a crime happening and do nothing, except… perhaps call the non-emergency 101 line and wait 45 minutes for someone to pick up.
And he’s telling good citizens not to stand up against crime. You will not be rewarded for stopping it. Worse, you may even face consequences.
I’m not exaggerating, we’ve seen it happen before.
Remember Mark Hehir?
The London bus driver who chased down a thief after he stole a passenger’s necklace, recovered the jewellery and returned it to her, only to be dismissed by Metroline after the thief came back and attacked him. The police took no further action against Hehir, and a police review concluded that his use of force was proportionate and necessary. More than 100,000 people subsequently signed a petition supporting him. At the same time, the London Assembly unanimously called for action to ensure transport workers acting in good faith to protect passengers are treated fairly rather than punished.
Yet, our mayor still refused to act on behalf of the one good Londoner.
Khan had so many ways to help, from pressuring Metroline to helping Mark find another job. Instead, he left the matter where it was.
Think about the message that sends.
You see someone being robbed. You help them. And you might lose your job.
So next time a full bus of passengers watches someone being robbed in silence, don’t ask why all we ended up with was a happy robber and 80 police reports. You helped create this culture yourself, Sir Khan.
And that culture has even started influencing big corporates. As I laid out in my previous column, fearing legal consequences, supermarkets have set up policies forbidding staff from physically intervening when shoplifters steal. Employees are expected to stand back, report what happened, and that’s it. Stopping a shoplifter because you actually care about your store? I’m sorry, you’re fired. It doesn’t matter if you’ve worked at the same Morrisons for 29 years, since you were 17.
Put simply, we are told to be “active bystanders”, just not too active. Perhaps that’s why I find the Mayor’s comments so depressing.
Whilst mayors around the world, even Andy Burnham, stand with their people, we have a Mayor of London who refuses to recognise the contribution Londoners are making, not even a tiny bit.
In other cities, stopping a crime might earn you a citizen’s award. In London, all you get is an application form for unemployment benefits.
Now, of course, there are limits. Again, I’m not suggesting that an elderly pensioner should chase an armed robber down an alleyway, or assault somebody simply because they suspect them of stealing. The police exist for a reason.
But there is a huge space between reckless vigilantism and passive indifference. It’s called civic responsibility, and it is disappearing.
There’s another issue I find daunting.
Sadiq Khan sees London from the grand City Hall. Diego sees it from behind a cardboard box near Victoria, watching for thieves.
The Mayor sees a 14 per cent fall in neighbourhood crime on his City Hall vellum. Diego sees the tourist whose phone has just been taken.
Both realities can be true.
But only one of them is standing on the pavement.
That is what worries me. Politicians are increasingly out of touch and hide behind statistics. Don’t get me wrong, numbers do matter. They tell us whether policies are working. But they do not tell us whether people feel confident walking through their neighbourhood, or whether international tourists think of London as a great city or a great joke. There’s another factor that matters too — public perception.
Diego is perhaps one of the most visible examples showing Britain, and the world, that people are still willing to uphold the law in London. Yet, thanks to politicians living in ivory towers, he may soon be gone.
Conservatives should side with Diego instinctively. We pride ourselves on civic responsibility and strong communities. We support people taking responsibility for their communities, and taking pride in the places they call home.
And in this case that means recognising the citizen who spends his evenings helping police catch pickpockets.
Perhaps recognising Diego Galdino was simply too much to ask of Sir Khan. His knighthood must have stripped him of whatever remaining empathy he had for “peasants” like us.
But he should be careful about the message he sends to the hundreds of thousands of Londoners, and to the criminals, who are paying close attention.
Because when people who step forward are dismissed, while those who cause disorder are repeatedly given another chance, eventually the public learns a very simple lesson:
Keep your head down. Don’t get involved. Let someone else deal with it.
That is not a recipe for a safer London.
That is how you kill the last Good Samaritan.
summary: London Mayor Sadiq Khan has dismissed the crime-fighting contributions of social media figure Diego Galdino, known as "Pickpocket London," while praising the Metropolitan Police. The author argues that dismissing citizens who intervene against crime discourages civic responsibility and creates a culture where bystanders do nothing. Citing examples like a dismissed bus driver and strict supermarket policies, the piece warns that penalizing or ignoring helpful citizens ultimately harms public safety.
key_points: Diego Galdino, known as "Pickpocket London," uses social media to track pickpockets, help victims, and pass information to police.
Mayor Sadiq Khan praised the Metropolitan Police for lowering phone theft while dismissing the contributions of vigilantes.
The author compares this to the case of Mark Hehir, a bus driver who was dismissed after stopping a thief and being attacked.
Supermarkets also enforce strict policies preventing staff from intervening against shoplifters due to legal and employment fears.
The author argues that discouraging citizens from taking civic responsibility fosters a culture of passive indifference.

title: Thousands of north London homes without water: 'It's a crazy situation'
author: Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2024/05/08/12/07/Muswell_Hill_Broadway_xk7sub1w.jpeg?trim=172,0,172,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Residents claim that they have been facing disruption since 9am on Monday morning, with several postcodes suffering from low pressure or no water at all. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/7/31/Screenshot-2026-08-25-at-08-56-39.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) In an update at 11am, Thames Water said it was excavating the burst water main and working to remedy the situation. In the meantime, Woodside Avenue will remain closed while teams attend to the burst water pipe. It is not clear when the pipe is expected to be repaired, but an update is expected at around 4pm. ![

Muswell Hill Broadway has a buzzy feel

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2024/05/08/12/07/Muswell_Hill_Broadway_xk7sub1w.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Nigel Rumble, a local resident in the Swiss Cottage area, told the Standard that the majority of the 161 flats in his tower block were without water in an “unprecedented” and “crazy” situation. He explained that the water had been out from around 9:35am on Monday, but briefly returned for around half an hour at 9:30am on Tuesday. “The water was out all day and all last night. People can’t flush their toilets which is one of the most major things. You can go out to the shops and buy drinking water - you can’t do that for a toilet,” he said. He added that Thames Water had not brought over any additional supplies to support residents. “Many of the older community have struggled,” he said. “And I’m thinking of the wider community - young children, mothers, people with disability, elderly people who are less mobile. People do need to drink and if there’s no water it could cause a health concern for the vulnerable.” Mr Rumble also raised concerns that potential thunderstorms on Wednesday “could hinder” the efforts to repair the pipe. Despite the frustration of residents, Mr Rumble said the community is “hankering on” as they wait for water supplies to return. Thames Water has been approached for comment. In a statement on its website, the utility company said: "Our teams remain on site and are continuing work to repair a burst water main on Woodside Avenue. Read More "Teams worked overnight and made several network changes to help restore supplies, significantly reducing the number of customers without water. "Most customers remain in supply, although some may experience lower pressure than usual. During periods of higher demand, some customers may also experience short interruptions to their supply. "We are planning to open a bottled water station this morning to support customers who may have been affected. Details of the location and opening times will be shared as soon as they are confirmed. “We are also arranging bottled water deliveries for customers on our Priority Services Register who may need additional assistance.” The Standard has approached Camden Council and Thames Water for comment.
summary: Thousands of north London homes have experienced water disruptions and low pressure due to a burst water main on Woodside Avenue. Thames Water teams have been working on-site and made overnight network changes to restore supplies, while planning to open a bottled water station. Residents have expressed frustration over the prolonged outage, highlighting difficulties for vulnerable community members.
key_points: A burst water main on Woodside Avenue left thousands of north London homes without water or facing low pressure.
Thames Water stated that teams worked overnight and made network changes to significantly reduce the number of affected customers.
The utility company is planning to open a bottled water station and arrange deliveries for customers on the Priority Services Register.
Local residents reported severe disruptions, including an inability to flush toilets and concerns for vulnerable community members.

title: Step inside the world of Bookish as Gabriel Book’s bookshop comes to London
author: The editorial unit
content:
Step inside the world of Bookish as Gabriel Book’s bookshop comes to London
![Step inside the world of Bookish as Gabriel Book’s bookshop comes to London](https://www.theupcoming.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/UKTV_BookishS2_001489-1280x927.jpg) 
A corner of Gabriel Book’s 1940s London is being recreated in Cecil Court this week, with a free Bookish-inspired bookshop opening ahead of the detective drama’s return to U&alibi.
Your Book’s Bookshop will run on 25th and 26th August, taking inspiration from the antiquarian shop where Mark Gatiss’s bookseller-turned-sleuth conducts his investigations. Visitors will be able to search the shelves for clues and teasers for the forthcoming series, while resident writers will create personalised fictional identities and backstories for guests, typed live as the opening page of an imagined story.
The pop-up coincides with the second series of Bookish, created by and starring Gatiss as Gabriel Book, an antiquarian bookseller who assists the police with mysterious crimes in post-war London.
“Bookish is all about hidden depths – the idea that everyone might be concealing a secret history, hiding in plain sight,” Gatiss said. “Walking through those doors, sitting down at a typewriter and walking away with your own alias and cover story – it’s the closest you’ll get to actually living inside the show.”
The concept is accompanied by research commissioned by U&alibi into the British appetite for reinvention and amateur detective work. Of 2,000 adults surveyed, 44% said they had invented a different version of themselves, while detective was the most popular fictional alter ego respondents would choose. More than half – 55% – also reckoned they would make a good detective, although only 36% went as far as believing they could outsmart the professionals.
For Bookish viewers, the two-day event provides an unusual bridge between the show’s first and second series, recreating one of its central locations just as Gabriel Book prepares to reopen his casebook on screen.
The editorial unit
Your Book’s Bookshop takes place at 22-24 Cecil Court, London, on 25th and 26th August, with free tickets available online. Bookish season two is released on U&alibi on 26th August 2026.

Created to coincide with the second series of the show on U&alibi, the shop features clues for visitors to find and resident writers who will type personalized fictional identities for guests. Commissioned research for the event found that 44% of surveyed adults have invented a different version of themselves, with detective being the top choice for a fictional alter ego.

title: Sadiq Khan issues dead of night flash flood warning as thunderstorms threaten London
author: Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Spectacular thunderstorms hit London causing thousands of lightning strikes and flash floods](https://static.standard.co.uk/2024/07/09/19/ff1f00c92fb69c95f6ef57346eb8588dY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzIwNjM2NTM3-2.6204507.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Sir Sadiq Khan put London on alert for flash floods to hit homes as thunderstorms were forecast to erupt over the city.
The London Mayor urged Londoners to prepare for possible torrential downpours.
“From 3am, London is at risk of severe flash floods,” he posted on X.
“Intense downpours could see up to 50mm of rainfall arrive in the space of just a few hours - almost the total average rainfall for August.”
There is also a chance of “intense” downpour with an expected 20-30mm of rainfall in less than an hour. In some areas, there may even be 40-50mm of rainfall within two to three hours, which could lead to some surface water flooding, the warning said.
![The Met Office has extended its yellow thunderstorm warning to cover most of northern England (Lewis Whyld/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2024/07/09/19/ff1f00c92fb69c95f6ef57346eb8588dY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzIwNjM2NTM3-2.6204507.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Many places will miss the showers, but others could see large hailstones and frequent lightning.
The showers are expected to ease during the evening, with the warning in place between 3am and 10pm.
Yellow flood warnings mean that there is a small chance that businesses and homes could experience flooding.
The Met Office also warns whereflooding or lightning strikes occur, there is a chance of delays and some cancellations to train and bus services.
Spray and sudden flooding could lead to difficult driving conditions and some road closures
There is a slight chance that power cuts could occur and other services to some homes and businesses could be lost
This could lead to cancellations of public transport services and some road closures.
The hard ground after the sustained hot weather is expected to increase the risk of flash flooding.
There is also a small risk of power cuts.
The Met Office is advising that Londoners check if their location is at risk of flash flooding and to consider preparing a flood plan if so.
For those who find themselves outside during thunderstorms, it is advised to find safe enclosed shelter, like a car. But you should not seek shelter under a tree or other structures that might be struck by lightning.
The warning has a very low likelihood of happening, but could have a medium impact on affected areas.
Read More
Parts of the east of England, East Midlands, North West and South West of England could also be affected, as well as parts of Wales and the West Midlands.
The rain comes after London experienced one of its driest summers on record. Millions of people were placed under hosepipe bans as London was declared to be in drought, while green spaces and parks across the capital were scorched by the blistering heat.
London also saw a spate of wildfires break out amid the dry conditions. For many, the rainfall will be a welcome reprieve to the scorching summer.
Thunderstorms frequently happen after periods of hot weather when high temperatures warm up the ground and air. As the warm air rises and condenses, it unsteadies the atmosphere, creating thunderstorm clouds. These clouds produce hail, thunder, and lightning.
summary: London Mayor Sadiq Khan issued a flash flood warning as thunderstorms and torrential downpours were forecast to hit the city starting at 3am. The severe weather threatens homes and businesses with potential surface water flooding, transit disruptions, and power cuts following a period of sustained hot weather and drought. While many areas may miss the worst of the showers, others could experience up to 50mm of rainfall, large hailstones, and frequent lightning.
key_points: London Mayor Sadiq Khan warned residents that severe flash floods could hit the city starting at 3am.
Intense downpours could bring up to 50mm of rainfall in a few hours, risking surface water flooding.
The Met Office warned of potential travel delays, road closures, and a small risk of power cuts.
Hard ground resulting from sustained hot weather and drought conditions increased the risk of flash flooding.

title: Where to watch the August 2026 lunar eclipse in London this week
author: Amy Houghton
content:
[title]
It’s been a fortnight since the partial solar eclipse had London in a chokehold. People flocked to the city’s parks in their thousands, armed with elusive eclipse glasses or colanders, to lay their eyes on a once-in-a-lifetime celestial event. If you want more where that came from, look up to the sky later this week to see the partial lunar eclipse.
It’s no coincidence that the two events are happening in such quick succession. A lunar eclipse always happens roughly two weeks before or after a solar eclipse. It’s not quite as rare as the solar event, but nonetheless is a sight to behold.
When the eclipse reaches its maximum, the moon will appear deep coppery red, caused by sunlight passing through our planet’s atmosphere being scattered and reflected back towards the moon. That’s why the phenomenon is also often referred to as a ‘blood moon’. Here’s everything you need to know if you want to catch the lunar eclipse this week.
What is a lunar eclipse?
A lunar eclipse is when the moon passes through the darkest part of Earth’s shadow (the umbra). It happens around the world two to four times per year but can only be seen from specific places once every year and a half. Total lunar eclipses happen every two-and-a-half years.
This week, we’ll see a partial lunar eclipse in which around 93 percent of the moon will be within the umbra.
RECOMMENDED: The best places in the world to see August’s lunar eclipse.
When is the August lunar eclipse?
The next partial lunar eclipse visible from the UK is on Friday August 28.
What will be the best time to see the lunar eclipse?
You’ll need to set your alarm for this one. The phenomenon will begin at 3.33am and reach its maximum at 5.12am.
![A partial lunar eclipse](https://media.timeout.com/images/106180497/image.webp) 
Where to see the lunar eclipse in London
Most of the major London parks will be shut at the time of the lunar eclipse, so there’s no point heading to the likes of Primrose Hill or Greenwich Park.
However Hampstead Heath is open 24 hours, so you will be able to get a good spot on Parliament Hill. The moon will get lower and lower on the horizon as the eclipse happens, so you should find a high point that has a clear, uninterrupted view to the southwest.
How to watch the lunar eclipse in London
You’ll be glad to know that there’s no need for any special glasses this time. We can look directly at the lunar eclipse without doing any damage to our eyes. It’ll be worth sourcing some binoculars if you want a closer look at the moon’s surface.
What is the weather forecast?
It’s not looking great. At the moment, forecasters say there will be clouds and light rain in the early hours of Friday morning. Watch this space for any last-minute forecast changes.

The event begins at 3:33 am and reaches its maximum at 5:12 am, turning the moon a deep coppery red. London viewers can watch safely without special glasses, and Parliament Hill on Hampstead Heath provides a suitable 24-hour viewing location.
key_points: The partial lunar eclipse takes place on Friday, August 28.
The eclipse begins at 3:33 am and reaches maximum at 5:12 am.

title: Shock as man left seriously injured after city centre brawl
author: Jack Warren
content:
Passersby were left shocked and saddened after a man believed to be homeless was seriously injured in a brawl in Norwich.
Police were called to London Street at 1.16am on Tuesday after reports a fight had broken out.
It is understood that a rough sleeper was attacked by two other men, and when he fought back he was hit over the head with a bag of cans.
  Two cordons remained in place until the afternoon (Image: Supplied)
Officers arrived at the scene and the injured man was taken to hospital.
A cordon was put up around two separate areas in the street, one around a bin outside HSBC and another on Little London Street, where the man is believed to have been sleeping rough.
A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and was taken to Wymondham Police Investigation Centre for questioning.
  Police remained on the scene until the afternoon (Image: Supplied)
Police remained at the scene until around 2.30pm after a forensics team had worked to capture evidence from the scuffle.
Items believed to belong to the man, which were near the cordon, including a sleeping bag, a roll-up mat, and a shopping bag, were taken away.
Onlookers passing through the busy city street were shocked to see the scene.
Blood was seen on the floor outside Sostrene Grene.
  Blood could be seen on the ground behind the cordon (Image: Supplied)
Richard, who lives in Norwich said: “Things like this are happening all the time. Norwich is getting worse and I want to leave.
“I’ve lived in Norwich for seven years. It doesn’t shock me anymore."
  Forensics were on the scene (Image: Supplied)
A man who wished to remain anonymous said: “It’s a shame. Older people are terrified.
“Norwich is a lovely place, but there are so many homeless people now they’ve got cans and bottles you don’t know what they are going to do next."
  Police were called to London Street after reports of a fight (Image: Supplied)
summary: A man believed to be homeless was seriously injured during a brawl in Norwich city centre early Tuesday morning. Police arrived on London Street following reports of a fight and transported the injured man to the hospital. A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm, while forensics and officers secured the scene until the afternoon.
key_points: Police responded to a fight on London Street in Norwich at 1.16am on Tuesday.
A rough sleeper was reportedly attacked by two men and hit over the head with a bag of cans.
A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm.
Police cordoned off areas of the street and remained on the scene until approximately 2.30pm for forensics work.

London has arguably had far too much hot weather this summer. title: This north London gastropub has the best breakfast in the city, according to Time Out
author: Leonie Cooper
content:
[title]
From the classic fry-up to the millennial favourite avocado on toast, we love a good breakfast at Time Out.
You can score sublime morning meals across the city, but there’s one that’s recently taken our fancy and shot straight to the top of the very best brekkies in London list.
The new number one breakfast in London comes courtesy of… The Angel in Highgate. The Angel, which relaunched in 2024 under new management, is now run by the same team as the nearby Red Lion & Sun gastropub, but there’s been a pub on the same site for around 400 years. Though we doubt they were serving vegan sausage baps in 1687.
Our glowing review of their breakfast was written by Ella Doyle, who commented: ‘It’s rare to find a breakfast in London that doesn’t secretly make you think “I could’ve made this at home”. But trust me, none of you are getting anywhere close to this kind of finesse on a hangover.’
She added: ‘The Angel breakfast menu has got it all, from expertly crafted brunch classics – full English, avo toast and the likes – to a wonderfully thick Croque Madame, Thai sausage bap with lime mayo and crispy prawn chilli oil, and a whopping great kipper glistening with parsley butter.’
![Angel Highgate](https://media.timeout.com/images/106307751/image.webp) 
The Angel opens at 8am and breakfasts run, quite brilliantly, until 4pm every day – apart from on Sundays, when they make way for roasts at 11.45am. The breakfast also includes mushrooms on toasted sourdough and Greek yoghurt with blueberries, banana and granola.
Our list of the best breakfasts in London also includes the chic Italian offering at Martino’s in Chelsea, shakshuka saffron buns at Cafe Jikoni in Stratford, the bacon bap at St John Neal’s Yard Wine Bar, and the Irish-inspired weekend breakfast at Cafe Cecilia in Hackney.

title: REVIEW: As You Like It - A giddy celebration of Shakespearean mischief | South West Londoner
author: Newsdesk
content:
In a spirited and visually stunning production at Shakespeare’s Globe in London, comic merriment and elaborate costumes are punctuated by moments of quietly moving reverie. Co-directed by Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine, this performance is a giggling caper of cheek and charm.
As You Like It is a tale that dances with concepts of liberation, transformation and identity. In this production, the game of disguise is played long before its figures embark on their tournaments of gender. Greeting their audience in decadent gowns that flirt with the late 17th-18th centuries, the costumes reflect the pageantry of court.
The grandeur of Duke Frederick’s court – reminiscent of Louis XVI’s Versailles – contrasts dramatically with the simplicity of its backdrop: a series of interlocking, stark white canvases. The resulting dichotomy suggests that these characters are already living in an eternal dress-up game of pretence.
Shakespeare at his most playful
Lola Shalam shines as Rosalind throughout this performance. Girlishly excitable, her arch humour and blissful love for Orlando compliments her character’s lyrical charm. Josephine’s Orlando is a man of the people; his conversational delivery and estuary accent elicit a down-to-earth sympathy, casting the character as a working-class hero. The pair’s instant attraction to each other results in a slapstick of giddy awkwardness, amplified by Rosalind’s transformation into Ganymede.
The comedy of this play cannot be understated. Shakespeare’s humour is often forgotten in the shade of his melancholic tragedies. But, Shakespeare is undeniably funny, and this is sublimely enacted by each cast member. Jonnie Broadbent is a jocular delight as the amorous Touchstone, his lacy ruff and lusty jollity seducing his audience. Gracie Oddie-James is similarly endearing, excellently portraying the role of Celia with aristocratic pomp.
The audience’s occasional singalong participation to Katie Richardson’s folksy music is similarly amusing, and avoids feeling trite. In this play, the jest and witticisms of the verse illuminates its subversive subjects – from same-sex passion between Orlando and Ganymede to the spectrum of class culture within the forest.
![A pair face each other dressed in Shakespearean garb on the stage of Shakespeare's Globe.](https://www.swlondoner.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Charlie-Josephine-as-Orlando-and-Lola-Shalam-as-Rosalind-in-As-You-Like-It-at-Shakespeares-Globe-c.-Marc-Brenner-1024x683.jpg)
A forest alive with possibility
Amidst its humorous frolics, the players also offer moments of touching reflection. Katherine Pearce as Jacques is serenely affecting in her “All the world’s a stage” soliloquy. Similarly, Colm Gormley extends a poignant rationale for his simple life: “I earn that I eat, get that / I wear, owe no man hate, envy no man’s happiness.”
The set design by Paul Wills offers Shakespeare’s Forest of Arden a touch of magic, turning it into a character itself. Gradually painted upon the austere blank canvases by scenic artist Emily Carne, it eventually blooms with the developing love stories themselves, its role evolves with our characters.
![Members of the court stand in their finery on the stage of Shapeare's Globe theatre.](https://www.swlondoner.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-company-in-As-You-Like-It-at-Shakespeares-Globe-c.-Marc-Brenner-1024x683.jpg)
This production succeeds because it embraces As You Like It in all its contradictions. Riotously comic, yet unexpectedly tender, it is steeped in Shakespearean artifice. Holmes and Josephine have created a rendition both playful and poignant, giving its audience a fresh take on an enduring drama.
As You Like It runs until 25 August. For more details, click here.
Featured image credit: Marc Brenner
summary: Shakespeare's Globe in London is hosting a visually stunning and spirited production of As You Like It, co-directed by Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine. The play blends riotous comedy, elaborate court costumes, and interactive folksy music with moments of touching, quiet reflection. Running until August 25, the production successfully highlights the play's themes of liberation, transformation, and identity through strong performances and dynamic set design.
key_points: Co-directed by Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine, the production features decadent late 17th-to-18th-century court costumes set against stark white canvases.
Lola Shalam stars as an excitable Rosalind alongside Charlie Josephine as a working-class hero version of Orlando.
The cast includes standout comedic and dramatic performances, such as Jonnie Broadbent as Touchstone and Katherine Pearce delivering Jaques' soliloquy.
The set design by Paul Wills features blank canvases that gradually bloom with painted elements to reflect the evolving stories in the Forest of Arden.
The production runs until August 25 and includes audience singalongs to Katie Richardson's folksy music.

title: London stationery shop adored by celebrities overrun with e-bikes: 'I've had enough'

![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after poorly parked cycles force blind man into busy road](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/25/8/19/Our-shop-at-21-Tower-Street-was-created-to-be-a-modern-fantasy-of-an-old-fashioned-French-shop.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![STYLE](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_style_embed_desktop.png)
![Gracie Abrams has achieved her second UK number one album (Ian West/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/24/18/1dd38cdadd2140582e396a30b33c9692Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg0OTg0MDc4-2.83578971.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The 41-year-old said that the large number of e-bikes on the pavement has been proving a “nightmare”, claiming that she has seen a sharp rise in anti-social behaviour and drug dealing in the area.
Speaking to The Telegraph, she said: “It affects deliveries, it can block fire exits.
She has claimed that neither she nor neighbouring businesses were consulted on the parking bay, and has accused the local authority of failing to address the situation.
![Camden Council offices](https://static.standard.co.uk/2023/07/30/10/Camden%20Council.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
“The council give us no help. They laugh at us. I feel humiliated.”
In June, Camden Council approved a new five-year procurement strategy for its dockless bike hire schemes.
Councillor James Slater said the local authority will continue to encourage the use of e-bikes throughout the borough, citing their growing popularity.
However, he stressed that it will “take a no-tolerance approach to e-bikes that are blocking pavements and left stranded in car parking bays”, explaining that more than 2,000 have been impounded.
Some boroughs, including Westminster, have launched crackdowns on e-bikes in light of the scale of the problems they are causing.
In Bromley, Lime bikes have been banned throughout the borough after a blind man had to walk into a dual carriageway with his guide dogs as the e-bikes were blocking the pavement. The company has since changed its app to stop the hiring of its bikes in the borough, The Standard reports.
![Poorly parked Lime bikes in west London (Lucy North/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/03/18/09/bbbb3fde6a311787023c6c6cbb142fdbY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzczOTEwMjcy-2.81298368.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Responding to Jeuvell’s claims, Camden Council stressed that it remains committed to supporting high streets and local shops, especially when “businesses across the country are facing very challenging times”.
Read More
“We want to assure Ms Jeuvell that we take reports of anti-social behaviour very seriously and, in line with our £1m investment this year to expand community safety patrols in Camden, we are taking action alongside the police to target this area.”
It said it is aware of concerns regarding the bay outside her store and will be reviewing its location, with the intention of consulting on it shortly.
A Lime spokesperson said the bay is being treated as a “priority area”, with parking patrollers tidying up the bikes four times a day. It said those who do not park compliantly will be fined, warned or even banned from using the service.
“Given the growing demand for e-bikes, there is a clear need for more designated parking locations, especially in areas where people use them to access local businesses daily.
“Lime is committed to working with Camden Council to deliver more parking that works for everyone and is responsibly managed.”
summary: A London business owner has expressed frustration over poorly parked e-bikes blocking pavements, fire exits, and deliveries outside her shop. The issue has prompted wider scrutiny of dockless bike schemes across London, with some boroughs implementing bans or crackdowns following safety incidents. In response, Camden Council stated it is reviewing the parking bay location and addressing community safety concerns, while Lime noted it is increasing patrollers and enforcement in the area.
key_points: A shop owner reported that large numbers of e-bikes are blocking pavements, fire exits, and deliveries while contributing to local anti-social behaviour.
Camden Council stated it will review the parking bay outside the store and consult on its location shortly.
Lime is treating the area as a priority, utilizing parking patrollers four times a day and penalizing non-compliant users.
Other London boroughs, such as Bromley, have banned Lime bikes following severe pedestrian safety incidents like blocking blind individuals.

title: London bus strike begins again after drivers reject deal offer
author: Rachael Burford; Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![London bus strike chaos: Over 1,500 drivers strike over heatwave working conditions](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/37/IMG_20260814_091450-(1).jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75>)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
More than 1,500 drivers resumed industrial action on Tuesday over sweltering conditions in their cabs during the recent heatwaves.
The latest strike began at 4am on Tuesday and is due to continue until 4.30am on Friday.
Drivers have argued that temperatures in their cabs can reach a sweltering 40C, putting them at risk of fatigue and heat exhaustion, heat stroke and dehydration.
Union Unite said most buses operated by Arriva North London have air cooling systems, rather than air conditioning, which only managed to reduce temperatures by around two or three degrees during the recent series of heatwaves.
![Bus drivers on strike in Stratford](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/07/IMG_20260814_091603-(1).jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
“Arriva can fully afford to make meaningful changes our members can accept. Until that happens, strike action will continue and our members at Arriva North London will continue to have the full backing of Unite.”
Drivers at the Barking, Edmonton, Enfield, Grays, Palmers Green, Stamford Hill, Tottenham and Wood Green garages are taking part in the latest round of strikes having previously walked out on Friday, August 14, and Saturday, August 15.
Unite regional officer Steven Stockwell said: “There is still time for Arriva to stop this disruptive action, but it relies on it coming back to the table with a deal our members believe will solve the serious problems with conditions once and for all.”
Read More
The remaining walkout dates are:
- August: 25 to 28
- September: 4 to 5, 7 to 8, 18 to 19, and 21 to 22
- October: 2 to 3, 5 to 6, 16 to 17, and 19 to 20
Arriva has said the wellbeing of its staff and customers is its “top priority”, adding it has added extra welfare checks and cooling breaks during hot weather and is collaborating with Transport for London to roll out upgraded air conditioning on newer fleet buses.
summary: More than 1,500 Arriva North London bus drivers resumed a strike on Tuesday after rejecting a pay and conditions deal, following disputes over sweltering cab temperatures reaching up to 40C during recent heatwaves. The union Unite stated that current air cooling systems are inadequate, while Arriva maintained that staff wellbeing is a top priority and highlighted ongoing efforts to introduce upgraded air conditioning. Further strike dates are scheduled through October if a resolution is not reached.
key_points: Over 1,500 drivers resumed industrial action after rejecting a deal offer.
The strike began at 4am on Tuesday and is scheduled to run until 4.30am on Friday.
Drivers are protesting dangerous heat conditions in cabs that can reach up to 40C.
The union Unite argues that Arriva's current cooling systems only reduce temperatures by two to three degrees.
Arriva stated it has implemented extra welfare checks and is working with Transport for London to upgrade air conditioning.

title: What does it mean when a London Underground station is in two zones?
author: Amy Houghton
content:
[title]
Tube maps can be confusing. You’ve got some Underground lines that run straight, others that go round in a circle, there are dozens of different branches and, perhaps most confusing of all, there are stops that are somehow in two zones at the same time.
Earl’s Court, Notting Hill Gate, Hampstead, Stratford – they are all dual-zone Underground stations. TfL’s zones dictate how much you pay for your tube journey, so how on earth does it work when you get on or off at a station that is in both zone 1 and zone 2? Are you better off alighting at a single-zone station? We’ve got all the answers below.
RECOMMENDED: What are London’s pink Oyster card readers and when should you use them?
What is a dual-zone Underground station?
It’s a station that straddles two London fare zones.
How are passengers charged at dual-zone stations?
If you get on or off at a dual-zone station, TfL will charge you for the cheapest option based on where you tapped in or out.
![Stratford station, London](https://media.timeout.com/images/106439641/image.webp) 
Does traveling through a dual-zone station save you money?
Yes it does! And you don’t even need to think about it – TfL will automatically charge the lower fare.
For example, if you travel to Earl’s Court (zone 1/2) from zone three, you’ll be charged the zone 2 price of £2.50 (peak) or £2.30 (off-peak). But if you travel there from central London, you’ll pay the zone 1 to zone 1 price of £2.70 to £2.80 instead of the more expensive zone 1 to zone 2 fare of £3.60 or £3.10.
Which London Underground stations are in two zones?
Zone 1/2
- Earl's Court
- Vauxhall
- Notting Hill Gate
- Elephant & Castle
- Kennington
Zone 2/3
- Turnham Green
- Manor House
- North Acton
- Bromley-by-Bow
- East Putney
- North Greenwich
- Willesden Green
- Willesden Junction
- Hampstead
- Archway
- Clapham South
- Stratford
- West Ham
- Canning Town
![Kew Gardens station, London](https://media.timeout.com/images/106439640/image.webp) 
Zone 3/4
- Bounds Green
- Leytonstone
- East Ham
- Kew Gardens
- Hendon Central
- South Wimbledon

summary: Some London Underground stations straddle two fare zones, such as Zone 1 and Zone 2. Transport for London (TfL) uses these dual-zone stations to automatically charge passengers the cheapest possible fare based on their journey. Traveling through or using these stations can save riders money without requiring any extra effort.
key_points: Dual-zone stations are London Underground stops that sit across two different fare zones.
TfL automatically charges passengers the lower fare option when using a dual-zone station.
Examples of dual-zone stations include Earl's Court, Stratford, and Kew Gardens.
Using a dual-zone station can lower travel costs depending on the direction of your journey.

title: 33 strategic partners chosen in first £10bn wave of SAHP cash
author: Grainne Cuffe
content:
You are viewing 1 of your 1 free articles
The government has allocated £9.58bn to 33 strategic partners outside of London, in the first wave of funding under the Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP).
In an announcement yesterday (Monday 24 August), prime minister Andy Burnham and housing secretary Angela Rayner revealed that strategic partners include housing associations and councils, and the funding is expected to support the delivery of 73,600 new social and affordable homes across England over the next 10 years.
The government said the announcement “marks a major step” in the ambition to get councils building at scale again.
However, it has not yet revealed the names of each strategic partner. Inside Housing expects more information in the next few days.
Nearly two-thirds of the homes are expected to be for social rent. More than £2bn of the funding is expected to be spent in mayoral areas outside of London.
Greater Manchester is set to see the most funding out of the established mayoral strategic authorities (EMSAs), with an estimated spend of £529m to support the delivery of around 4,400 homes .
The West Midlands will see an estimated £409m for around 3,200 homes; the North East will receive £445m for around 3,400 homes; £441m will go to West Yorkshire for around 4,000 homes; the Liverpool City Region will see £380m for around 3,100 homes; and £249m will go to South Yorkshire for around 2,200 homes.
London will get £6bn of funding through the SAHP – although the Greater London Authority has yet to allocate the cash – and councils are expected to deliver more than half of the homes funded.
More than £16bn remains to be allocated outside of London.
As part of the government’s wider devolution agenda, EMSAs will set the strategic direction for the programme in their areas, including four new authorities: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midland, West of England, and York and North Yorkshire.
The government said that more funding is expected to flow directly to mayoral authorities as the SAHP develops, building on Mr Burnham’s pledge to move power and decision-making out of Whitehall.
Funding will prioritise social rent homes and council housebuilding, it said.
Mr Burnham said the funding will go to the places where families are waiting the longest for a home. “Councils built this country out of a housing crisis once before. Backed properly, and trusted to get on with it, they will do it again,” he said.
The government said housing associations and other providers “will continue to play a vital role in delivering the social and affordable homes the country needs”.
Kate Henderson, chief executive of the National Housing Federation (NHF), said: “It is hugely welcome to see this much-anticipated funding confirmed, something we have been calling for to kick-start construction on tens of thousands of desperately needed new social homes.
“This is a major vote of confidence in not-for-profit housing associations and in the vital and distinct role they play in this country, as organisations that work for the long-term benefit of their communities.
“Housing associations have risen to the challenge of delivering the governments ambitions.”
In July, the NHF and major sector bodies called on Mr Burnham to confirm the bids to the SAHP or risk delays to housebuilding.
Gavin Smart, chief executive at the Chartered Institute of Housing, said: “We welcome the strong focus on homes for social rent and the ambition for council housebuilding, and the recognition of the vital role that councils, housing associations and other providers will play in delivering the next generation of genuinely affordable homes.
“If delivered at pace, this investment has the potential to reduce homelessness, ease pressure on temporary accommodation and help more people access a safe, secure and affordable home.”
Amy Rees, chief executive at Homes England, said: “By working with councils, mayors, housing associations and local partners, we can support the return of council housebuilding at scale, increase the supply of social rent homes and create thriving places that people are proud to call home.”
London mayor Lord Khan said: “I want to work with this new government to deliver a step change in how many council homes we can deliver across the capital.
“Thousands of Londoners will benefit from this new wave of new social and affordable homes, which will help people out of temporary accommodation and provide good, affordable homes to live in for the long-term, as we build a fairer, better London for everyone.”
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also announced that it is investing a further £46m of ‘Capacity to Build’ funding over the next three years to strengthen councils’ skills, expertise and capacity to build more homes.
The SAHP announcement comes after it emerged that Mr Burnham is set to offer regional mayors the power to overrule local councils on planning decisions.

Announced by prime minister Andy Burnham and housing secretary Angela Rayner, the funding aims to support the delivery of 73,600 new social and affordable homes across England over the next decade. Nearly two-thirds of these homes are expected to be for social rent, with specific regional allocations outlined for mayoral strategic authorities.

title: Calls to ban London delivery drivers with L plates
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![Deliveroo and Just Eat takeaway delivery cycle couriers on a main road, near a pedestrian crossing with traffic lights. The Deliveroo driver is on the right. There is a car to the right of the Deliveroo driver and a TfL bus can be seen ahead. There are pedestrians in the distance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/594/cpsprodpb/9c33/live/aabbb200-9f9f-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
London Assembly has called for the government to ban the use of provisional licences for commercial work, including food delivery driving
- Published
Motorcyclists without a full driving licence could be banned from working as delivery drivers in London.
Last month the London Assembly passed a motion calling on the government to prohibit the use of provisional licences for commercial work, to improve road safety.
Currently moped drivers can become fast food delivery drivers once they have obtained their Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) certificate, which remains valid for two years and can be renewed repeatedly without any requirement to progress to a full driving test.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) had consulted on reforms to the CBT and it was analysing the responses.
A CBT certificate allows a rider to use a moped with an engine size of up to 125cc, as long as they use learner plates.
Thomas Turrell, Conservative London Assembly member who proposed the motion, said the CBT "wasn't built for indefinite use" and described the practice as a "menace to the road".
"The CBT was built as a way for people to learn the roads and build up that knowledge," he told the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan has previously called for a reform of the CBT.
In 2022, the Labour mayor told the London Assembly he "firmly" believed the current CBT was "not fit for purpose" and was "not an appropriate level of qualification, particularly for those driving for work".
He added that Transport for London could not mandate couriers to ride on a full licence, and that these powers lie at a national level.
![A man in an off-white polo shirt and grey jeans standing in front of London City Airport entrance. He has dark brown hair, a beard and is wearing glasses. Behind him the entrance reads "Welcome to London City Airport".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/941e/live/85874110-9fa5-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Thomas Turrell said the purpose of the CBT was not for "indefinite use"
Earlier this year ministers launched a consultation on changes to moped and motorcycle training, which could involve CBT certificate reform.
Rebecca Paul, the MP for Reigate, tried to amend the Crime and Policing Act, passed in April, to ban learner moped drivers from undertaking commercial activity using the roads. However, it was unsuccessful.
Louie French, the MP for Old Bexley and Sidcup, said: "The Labour government has lost control of delivery drivers abusing the L plate system.
"The government must urgently grip this situation to ensure that all delivery drivers are working here legally and are not endangering other road users."
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "As part of our road safety strategy, the DVSA consulted on reforms to moped and motorcycle training and testing, including whether there should be a time limit on CBT certification.
"We are now analysing the responses, with the aim of improving safety and modernising motorcycling."
Turrell said the biggest barrier to reform could be "pushback" from major employers such as Just Eat, Deliveroo and Uber.
A Just Eat spokesperson said: "The safety of all road users is extremely important to Just Eat."
"We actively support stronger regulation and robust enforcement to tackle modified e-bikes and requiring moped riders to have a full licence.
"We remain committed to working with authorities and our industry peers to ensure the roads are safe for all users."
Deliveroo and Uber Eats have been contacted for comment.

summary: The London Assembly has passed a motion calling on the government to ban delivery drivers from using provisional licences and L plates for commercial work. Currently, moped riders can work indefinitely with a Compulsory Basic Training certificate rather than a full driving licence. Proponents of the ban argue that the CBT is not designed for indefinite commercial use and poses a road safety risk.
key_points: The London Assembly passed a motion urging the government to prohibit provisional licences for commercial delivery work.
Moped riders can currently work using only a CBT certificate, which allows them to ride with L plates and can be renewed repeatedly without a full driving test.
Mayor Sadiq Khan and Conservative Assembly Member Thomas Turrell have both criticized the CBT system as inadequate for professional drivers.
The Department for Transport stated it is analyzing responses from a recent consultation on moped and motorcycle training reforms.
Just Eat expressed support for stronger regulation and requiring moped riders to hold a full licence.

title: London in drought: 'We need to change how we think about water'
author: Tom Edwards
content:
![Two people walk through a park which is very yellow](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1280/cpsprodpb/6f84/live/1c3da380-9d42-11f1-a137-179a8d1c790b.png)
London is one of many regions in the country in drought
- Published
Hyde Park looks more like the Serengeti and the green belt has turned yellow. But with London now seeing the occasional shower, does that mean we are no longer in drought? And if not, the big question is how long will the drought last?
The capital is particularly susceptible to drought as there is a very large population, in an area that is actually very dry. Experts call it "water stressed."
The myth is London is a rainy city, yet the capital gets less rain than many other cities in Europe.
According to the Met Office the Thames Valley, London and the north Kent coast normally receive less than 650mm (26in) of rain every year. By comparison, Rome gets up to 900mm (35in).
![An aerial view of homes and gardens in London, showing the lawns as yellow from lack of water.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1504/cpsprodpb/79a5/live/27629310-9d42-11f1-a137-179a8d1c790b.png)
Most gardens in the capital are parched and dry
SES Water covers parts of Surrey, Kent and south London and at the moment it is one of the few water companies that doesn't have a hosepipe ban.
Daniel Kennedy, the firm's water services director, says it is impossible to predict when the drought will end.
"We do model our position with where we think things might go, but a lot of it is determined by the hot weather and the prolonged dry period that we've had."
He says water companies "are looking forward to when the rain does come because it does ease the position somewhat. But until it happens, it's really difficult to say how long it'll go on for.
"We would want a sustained period of rain... so we can replenish our groundwater stocks and our reservoirs, to enable us to have water in supply in our reserves for next year."
![Two women walk infront of two deckchairs. The ground is yellow and parched.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a7b3/live/15feab90-9d42-11f1-a137-179a8d1c790b.jpg)
Hyde Park in central London
Liz Stephens is a professor in climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading.
She thinks it could take months to get back to normal, noting that previous hosepipe bans in parts of the South East were only lifted "towards the end of January, early February", while "the Thames Water hosepipe ban lifted towards the end of November".
"It really does depend on the amount of rainfall that we get. If we see a dry autumn and winter, and we don't see that recharge of groundwater, the rise in reservoir levels, potentially we could be looking at similar restrictions next summer as well," she says.
There is even a possibility this drought might not come to an end this year, according to Stephens.
"If we don't get the amount of rain that's needed, then there will be a lot of concern about the water supply going into next spring and summer as well. We probably would then expect further restrictions.
"The 1976 drought came after a period of low winter rainfall as well. And in that situation that summer there were the standpipes on the streets for water supply," she says.
Most of the capital's water comes from chalk aquifers under the ground. These take much longer to recharge than reservoirs.
Stephens also points out that while water companies may have been preparing for a prolonged drought, they are now facing other issues as well.
"They might not have been able to anticipate the type of demands that we're now seeing in the South East, not just from the increase in population, but also the very recent increase in data centres and the demand that they're putting on water as well."
![A satellite image of Regent's Park showing it as yellow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/886/cpsprodpb/915b/live/0fe4c7d0-9d42-11f1-a137-179a8d1c790b.jpg)
Regent's Park in central London
Reservoir levels are currently at about 70%, which is lower than usual at this time of year.
Martin Padley, water director at Thames Water, which does have a hosepipe ban, says the company is grateful to everyone for reducing their water use, but given the current situation "we're asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.
"Small changes, such as taking shorter showers, turning off taps and avoiding non-essential water use outdoors, all help reduce pressure on our network while our teams continue working around the clock to find and fix leaks."
Long-term water scarcity is becoming more of an issue in London and the South East.
No major reservoirs have been completed in England since 1992. But a growing population and developments like new data centres are putting intense pressure on our water supplies.
Also, climate change is bringing hotter, drier summers that increase the risk of drought.
The government's solution is to build nine new reservoirs by 2050, potentially providing 670 million litres of extra water daily.
But some experts say we're thinking about water all wrong.
Hannah Cloke, professor of hydrology at the School of Archaeology, Geography and Environmental Science at the University of Reading, believes "we need a complete overhaul of the way we use water".
"We need to plug leaks, cut down on waste and use water more than once in our homes and buildings before sloshing it down the drain. We need to catch more water wherever it falls â not just in the river basins that are linked to big reservoirs," she says.
"An unprecedented climate calls for unprecedented solutions," adds Cloke.
"These could include the widespread roll out of sustainable drainage solutions that mimic nature and capture rainwater where it falls, on roofs or ditches filled with plants, rather than letting it rush straight down the drains into the rivers."
![Two people walking through a parched park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/1f48/live/5f951d40-9d6d-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Greenwich Park in south-east London
And one of the big unknowns long term is data centres.
Stephens says they're making an enormous difference.
"Thames Water had been trying to predict demand over the next 10 years... They've estimated that about 30% of that increased demand is coming from the growth of data centres.
"And I think they've already admitted that they're underestimating the demand that's happened so far from those data centres. It's an incredible amount of water that these centres use."
A huge new reservoir is planned to be built in Oxfordshire, called the White Horse Reservoir, to improve water supply.
However, Stephens says that while it will cover "a very large area of land, actually, by the time it's built, it might already be out of date.
"The extra volume that it's going to supply is roughly equivalent to that sort of upper estimate of the demand from data centres. So these really are crazy amounts of water that these data centres can use."
![There is a very barren and parched square with people walking across it.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/08ab/live/76f96c10-9d78-11f1-8bc3-150f4c5f088b.jpg)
Parliament Square in central London
Kennedy, from SES Water, says we will have to use water wisely throughout the year, especially with a changing climate.
This includes the likes of having shorter showers, turning the tap off when cleaning your teeth and making sure washing machines and dishwashers are only run when they are fully loaded, he says.
"If we can use water wisely all year round, it will obviously help us with our stocks in the times of the year when we really need it.
"The world is changing and we've had five heatwaves already this summer. So people are starting to understand that water is a precious commodity," he says.
![A yellow park with no grass](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/7aa0/live/de1a06c0-9d78-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Danson Park in Bexley, south-east London
At the moment, about 20% of water is lost through leaks. Thames Water says it is investing a record amount Â£21bn in fixing them. Critics say that is too little, too late.
Thames Water has also estimated that it could face a daily shortfall of over one billion litres of water by 2050. The funding needed for improvements and new water systems will be significant.
Its proposals include the new reservoir in Oxfordshire and a water recycling project in west London at Teddington. Both have faced opposition.
To match the demand, Thames Water is also striving to reduce daily water use to 110 litres per person by 2050, with current water use in the area at about 140 litres per person.
In other words, all of us will have to use less water.
In the face of a hotter climate, the mayor of London has created a heat plan, called Heat Ready London, external, which also highlights behaviour change as crucial.
It says: "Alongside infrastructure upgrades, changes in behaviours and system operation are essential to reduce pressure on water supplies.
"To enhance long-term water security, investment should be scaled up through a portfolio-based and integrated water management approach, recognising that no single intervention can address future challenges in isolation.
"A balanced portfolio of measures â including smart meters, active leakage reduction, water-efficiency initiatives, water recycling and reuse, rainwater harvesting, and targeted new supply schemes â should be implemented in a co-ordinated manner to deliver greater resilience and adaptability across the entire water system."
Experts say the whole water system needs a rethink to make it fit for the future.
Certainly, with a warming climate this won't be the last hosepipe ban in London and the South East.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: London and the South East are facing severe drought conditions and lower-than-usual reservoir levels, driven by a dry climate and growing water demand. Experts warn that without a sustained period of autumn and winter rainfall to replenish groundwater and reservoirs, water restrictions could persist into next year. Addressing the crisis will require a complete overhaul of how water is used, including plugging leaks, reducing waste, and adapting to the pressures of a warming climate and rising population.
key_points: London is considered 'water stressed' and typically receives less annual rainfall than many other European cities like Rome.
Reservoir levels are currently sitting at about 70%, which is lower than usual for this time of year.
Experts highlight that the rapid growth of data centres is putting an unprecedented and largely underestimated strain on local water supplies.
The government plans to build nine new reservoirs by 2050, and water companies are aiming to reduce per-person consumption alongside fixing leaks.
Hydrology experts argue that London needs a complete rethink of water management, advocating for rainwater harvesting, sustainable drainage solutions, and year-round water conservation.

title: Freedom Pass online applications to pause until mid-September
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Freedom Pass online applications to pause until mid-September
Londoners who need to apply for or replace a Freedom Pass for use on public transport are being advised to do so soon, as the scheme’s online portal is about to close for more than two weeks for an upgrade.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/freedom-pass.jpg)
The Freedom Pass online portal will be unavailable from 5pm on Monday 31st August until 9am on Tuesday 15th September, while work is carried out to upgrade the service.
During the closure, it won’t be possible to apply online for a new Freedom Pass, request a replacement pass or update personal details through the website. Existing Freedom Passes will continue to work as normal throughout the shutdown, and there are no changes to who is eligible for the scheme.
London Councils, which manages the Freedom Pass scheme, says the upgraded website should make it quicker and easier to apply online and track applications, while improving the service’s reliability and security.
Anyone who needs to apply for a pass or make changes is being encouraged to do so before the website closes on 31st August.
People who cannot apply before then can wait until the online service reopens on 15th September, or submit a paper application during the closure. Paper applications received while the website is unavailable will be prioritised once processing resumes.
There is also a change for Londoners approaching the age when they become eligible for an Older Person’s Freedom Pass.
Previously, people with a 60+ Oyster card could have their details transferred automatically when moving onto a Freedom Pass. That will no longer happen, and people reaching Freedom Pass age will now need to make a separate application.
London Councils says the change is due to updated data-sharing arrangements with Transport for London (TfL) and does not affect eligibility for the Freedom Pass scheme.
The Freedom Pass provides free travel on most public transport in London for eligible older and disabled Londoners, and the Freedom Pass website provides further details on applications and moving from a 60+ Oyster card.
summary: The online portal for London's Freedom Pass will be temporarily unavailable from August 31 until September 15 for system upgrades. During this shutdown, online applications, replacements, and profile updates will be paused, though existing passes will continue to function normally. Additionally, updated data-sharing arrangements mean that Londoners turning eligible for an Older Person's Freedom Pass will now need to apply separately rather than having their details automatically transferred from a 60+ Oyster card.
key_points: The Freedom Pass online portal closes for upgrades at 5pm on Monday 31st August and reopens at 9am on Tuesday 15th September.
Existing Freedom Passes will continue to work normally during the website shutdown.
Paper applications can still be submitted during the closure and will be prioritised once processing resumes.
Londoners reaching the age for an Older Person's Freedom Pass must now submit a separate application instead of relying on an automatic transfer from a 60+ Oyster card.

title: Goodman founders to open first London pub
author: Jungmin Seo
content:
The Albatross will serve live native lobster, Norwegian king crab and £6 pints of Guinness
George Bukhov-Weinstein and Ilya Demichev of Wild Group have announced plans to open their first pub next month in London’s Bank.
The Albatross will open on 7 September at 8-10 Old Jewry, the former Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and is situated close to the group’s sister sites, Goodman City and Wild Izakaya.
The menu specialises in British seafood, featuring dishes such as live native lobster and Norwegian king crab. Bistro classics, such as veal and chicken schnitzel, will also be available.
Head chef Chris Piorkowski, who previously worked at Goodman, leads the kitchen. The pub is supported by landlord Chris Dunlop, who formerly ran the Spotted Pig in New York, alongside landlady Alice Tayler, who worked with Tom Kerridge for nearly a decade.
The Albatross will offer over 15 beers on tap chosen by Shane McHugh, head of beverage across Goodman restaurants. Pints of Guinness and Pilsner are priced at £6, while cocktails cost £12.
The Albatross spans two floors and seats 200, with maximum capacity for 400 people standing. It also includes a private dining room for 14 people.
Wild Group’s Crispin Sugden said: "Pubs are, for me, the most important institution of Great Britain and the world possibly. I bloody love pubs.
“When we asked ourselves what was missing in the city pub scene, it kept coming back to the same thing - somewhere British-led, with proper food, a different selection of draft that wasn’t found on every font, great cocktails, wine and a bit of fun.”
Bukhov-Weinstein and Demichev founded Goodman in 2008, which at its peak operated three restaurants across London (now just two in Mayfair and the City of London following the closure of its Canary Wharf outpost).
The pair were also involved in the launch of Burger & Lobster group in 2011, but they announced a formal split of the business in early 2025.
In 2014, the team launched steak and crab restaurant Beast in London’s Mayfair.
Wild Group currently operates over 10 restaurants across London, including Wild, Belvedere, Pinna, Chelsea Grill and Pinna, and are due to open a new grill concept in Kensington Church Street later this year.
Bukhov-Weinstein and Demichev are also the co-owners of the Michelin-starred Lita in London’s Marylebone, which was launched in early 2024.

summary: Goodman founders George Bukhov-Weinstein and Ilya Demichev are set to open their first London pub, The Albatross, in Bank on September 7. The two-floor venue will specialize in British seafood and bistro classics, offer over 15 beers on tap, and seat up to 200 guests. Headed by chef Chris Piorkowski, the pub adds to Wild Group's portfolio of over 10 London restaurants.
key_points: The Albatross opens on 7 September at 8-10 Old Jewry in London’s Bank.
The menu features British seafood, including live native lobster and Norwegian king crab, alongside bistro classics.
The pub spans two floors, seats 200 people, and includes a private dining room for 14.
Beers on tap include £6 pints of Guinness and Pilsner, with cocktails priced at £12.
Founders George Bukhov-Weinstein and Ilya Demichev are known for launching Goodman and Burger & Lobster.
