title: John Vane: Hammersmith memories
author: John Vane
content:
I went to Hammersmith to learn about lesbians, to cross the Thames and to construct in my mind’s eye a pop star domestic scene that unfolded there four decades ago.
The pop star was the late Ian Dury, vivid, exceptional, unique and originally from Harrow, not Essex, as his lore suggests. One day, a radio producer and presenter went to interview him in his flat in Hammersmith, which had a brilliant view of Hammersmith Bridge. The flat was brilliant too – open, arty and spacious in an Edwardian mansion block. It’s stayed in the family.
Someone else who went there to see him has recalled an Axminster carpet. Our radio duo were struck by what looked like a silk boxer’s robe hanging on clothes rail and by the unscheduled arrival of a member of The Blockheads, Dury’s band.
He shall remain nameless, given that he’s still alive and, for all I know, might not wish to be identified in this re-telling of a long-ago tale. Whatever, the causal aplomb with which he assembled, ignited and puffed his way through a spliff that rivalled the size and the sizzle of the Olympic torch was as impressive as it was unexpected.
This hazy scene ran through my mind as I made my way across the Grade II* bridge, which has been stricken for a good ten years and feels that way, all forlorn with barriers and temporary lanes, its once regal green paintwork on the fade. There were a few fellow pedestrians. The odd cyclist trundled by. Below, a thin thread of river seemed exhausted by the effort required to flow. Aquatic birds pecked at its exposed flanks. The sun blazed, as has been its habit recently.
The psychology of my traverse was kind of trippy. Once half way across Joseph Bazalgette’s grand design, opened in 1887 by the ill-starred Prince Albert Victor, every footstep conveyed a sense of leaving the city behind. And suddenly, I was in Barnes in the London Borough of Richmond upon Thames, with a lady evangelist standing outside a church to my left and a huge expanse of school playing field to my right.
Welcome to the countryside. It had been only a short walk from the heart of Hammersmith, with its growling flyover and gyratory and it complex pedestrian challenges. Striking out from the Tube station, I passed what was once called the Hammersmith Odeon, where Dury and company played strings of sold out nights in the late 1970s and 1980s. Then it was along Queen Caroline Street, with its famous postwar housing estate, and to the Riverside Studios (clue in name).
Which brings us to the lesbians. The Riverside has been running its annual Bitesize Festival, and I had a ticket to see a play called Custard Tarts, “an hour-long inquisition into sexuality, lesbian coding and archetypes”. It was shrewd and funny and also rather nostalgic if you’re old enough to remember the heyday of Ian Dury. Read all about it here.
John Vane’s London novel, a political satire called Frightgeist, can be bought from this very website.

summary: The author takes a nostalgic journey through Hammersmith, reflecting on memories of the late pop star Ian Dury and his former flat near Hammersmith Bridge. Crossing the Thames into Barnes, the author passes historical landmarks like the former Hammersmith Odeon before attending a play titled Custard Tarts at the Riverside Studios. The narrative blends personal musings on London's geography with cultural references from the 1970s and 1980s.

title: UNDER THE INFLUENCE – A NEW MUSICAL – LONDON TRANSFER ANNOUNCED

content:
⭐ UNDER THE INFLUENCE – A NEW MUSICAL – LONDON TRANSFER ANNOUNCED ⭐
The London transfer of original musical comedy, UNDER THE INFLUENCE, by The Gilbert Twins and Shona Maule, has been announced.
Following its critically acclaimed run at this year’s Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the musical will transfer to London’s King’s Head Theatre, this September.
After becoming a viral sensation, identical twins Carine and Frances land in couples therapy as the world’s most co-dependent non‑couple. The session erupts into a hilarious musical intervention and a reckoning that threatens to collapse their lifelong duet.
Best known as @thegilberttwins to their 3M+ followers online, Carine and Frances return to their musical theatre roots with their original score co-written by Shona Maule. This new musical comedy is based on their own real experience of doing couples therapy together. Loud, ridiculous, and unexpectedly heartfelt, this musical explores the chaos of sisterhood, online pressure, and the search for your own voice.
Starring Carine Gilbert, Frances Gilbert and Shona Maule.
UNDER THE INFLUENCE is directed by Georgie Rankcom, with book and lyrics by Carine Gilbert and Frances Gilbert, lyrics, composition & musical direction by Shona Maule, lighting design by Tom Turner, associate direction by Michelle Payn and produced by Speakerphone Productions.
UNDER THE INFLUENCE will play the King’s Head Theatre, London, running from 8th – 26th September 2026, with tickets on sale now.

title: House prices fall in London commuter belt as buyers alerted to new 'opportunities'
author: Holly Bishop
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Can Andy Burnham save London’s housing market?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/12/11/26/GettyImages-159296715.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![Homes & Property](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_hnp_embed_desktop.png)
Rightmove looked at asking prices for homes in commuter locations around six cities - London, Manchester, Glasgow, Birmingham, Bristol and Cardiff.
Looking at annual changes in average asking prices in July, researchers found that n the capital, prices have decreased annually by 3.1% (£646,451).
![The housing market remains subdued, the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors said (Anthony Devlin/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/13/00/957ed317992b8f25659225d74db735a0Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg2NjE2MzM5-2.24335204.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
However, there was one exception to the rule. In Broxbourne, Hertfordshire, house prices have soared by 8.7%, with the average property costing £654,263.
Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said that the price drop would be welcome news to hopeful London commuter belt buyers.
“Some of the more expensive commuter hotspots are seeing prices ease, which could create opportunities for buyers who may previously have been priced out,” she explained.
![EMBARGOED TO 0001 FRIDAY JANUARY 10 File photo dated 03/03/23 of people using a ticket machine at Waterloo train station in London. More than two million train tickets will be discounted during a promotion starting next week, the Department for Transport (DfT) has announced. Cheaper Advance and Off-Peak tickets will be available to buy in the rail sale between January 14 and 20. Issue date: Friday January 10, 2025.](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/01/24/9/44/PA-78649429.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Commuter belt locations can provide numerous benefits for those looking to be close to work whilst also having access to local amenities and green spaces, estate agents have said.
Ian Harris, National Association of Estate Agents Propertymark president, said: “Since the pandemic, we’ve seen an initial reformatting of what many people want and need from the location they choose to live in.
“Initially, we saw many people embrace the concept of working from home and enjoying a lifestyle away from the traditional city commute.
“However, this is now a trend that is starting to swing back, with many people looking for a hybrid location that offers easy commuter access to key cities, while also providing a desirable mix of out-of-city amenities.”
![UK house prices returned to muted growth in July, but the market remains soft (PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/31/09/8b47086a643ed9b83f0d57bf4ac0bc64Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg1NTcxMTYy-2.25284737.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)

Here are the top 15 commuter hotspots with the nearby city, the average asking price in each location and the annual percentages in asking price growth, according to Rightmove:

In contrast to London, affordable commuter locations around Glasgow and Manchester have resulted in a growth in asking prices.
Average asking prices were up by 2.9% annually in Glasgow (£191,530), 1.8% in Manchester (£261,212) and 1.4% in Cardiff (£285,596).
Falkirk in Stirlingshire had the highest price growth in the research, at 13.5%, with an average asking price of £183,596.
Babcock said Rightmove’s data “highlights two very different stories playing out across some of Britain’s commuter markets”.
“In the more affordable locations around Glasgow and Manchester, asking prices are rising strongly as buyers look for value within reach of major cities.”
Rightmove’s research looked at commuter areas surrounding the six cities only, not every commuter location in Britain.
summary: Recent Rightmove research on asking prices in commuter locations around six major British cities reveals falling prices in several expensive areas, such as London, while more affordable commuter spots around cities like Glasgow and Manchester experience strong growth. Property experts note that easing prices in expensive hotspots can create new opportunities for buyers who were previously priced out. Meanwhile, estate agents observe a shifting trend where buyers increasingly seek hybrid locations offering both easy commuter access and desirable out-of-city amenities.
key_points: Rightmove analyzed asking prices in commuter locations surrounding London, Manchester, Glasgow, Birmingham, Bristol, and Cardiff.
In London, annual average asking prices decreased by 3.1%, with Maidenhead seeing a 3.9% drop.
Affordable commuter locations around Glasgow and Manchester have seen notable price growth, led by Falkirk with a 13.5% increase.
Property experts state that easing prices in higher-end commuter hotspots offer new opportunities for previously priced-out buyers.
Estate agents report a growing demand for hybrid locations that combine commuter access with local amenities and green spaces.

title: Professor Green's fast food restaurant Proper Good is coming to London
author: Gavin Hanly
content:
Professor Green has always been a bit of a foodie (we've seen his comments pop up on our reels for years) and cemented that by opening PG Proper Good in Glasgow earlier this year. Now he's following that with a second opening in London, right in the middle of Soho.
He's taking over a space on Soho Street (one that hasn't been a restaurant before) for the second Proper Good, something that he brought to life with the same team that launched Sides by The Sidemen. Assuming you haven't tried it in Glasgow, it's a fast food restaurant where you build your own meal. Those meals are either loaded salad, rice or potato puffs, or a South Korean-inspired UFO (a brioche hot roll). From there, you add flavours like salmon, chicken, pot roast beef, beans, dips and more.
Alongside all that, they have electrolyte-heavy drinks and frozen fruit desserts. For a fast food restaurant, it's definitely offering something new, and the Glasgow original seems to be very highly rated. Will it create queues like recent fast food fro-yo openings have? We'll have to wait and see.
More about PG Proper Food
Where is it? 3 Soho St, London W1D 3QF
When does it open? Mid September
Find out more: Visit their website or follow them on Instagram @pgfastfooduk
Subscribe to be the first to get the news from Hot Dinners
summary: Rapper and foodie Professor Green is opening his second fast food restaurant, Proper Good, in London's Soho this September. Following the success of his first location in Glasgow, the new venue will take over a space on Soho Street. The restaurant was developed in partnership with the team behind Sides by The Sidemen.
key_points: Proper Good's second location is opening on Soho Street in London.
The restaurant is scheduled to open in mid-September.
The menu features build-your-own meals including loaded salads, rice, potato puffs, and South Korean-inspired UFO brioche hot rolls.
Offerings also include electrolyte-heavy drinks and frozen fruit desserts.

title: Boy, 5, died after jumping from ‘compromised’ window in 15th-floor flat, coroner says
author: Jordan Reynolds
content:
A five-year-old boy died after jumping from a 15th-floor tower block window that was "compromised", a coroner said.
Aalim Ahmed was killed instantly in the fall from a tilt-and-turn kitchen window at a residential property in Plaistow, east London.
His distraught father, Makail Ahmed, rushed down from the top-floor temporary social housing flat and found his body shortly before 6am on May 16 2024.
Describing the death as "preventable", Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, blamed Newham Council, stating she had reported safety concerns about the home on multiple occasions.
Conflicting evidence regarding the condition of the window fittings was presented during the inquest into the young boy’s death.
An engineer dispatched by Newham Council to inspect and review overhauling the windows and handles told the court they were fully functional when he visited on December 17 2023.
However, the court heard that Ms Osman had submitted a series of complaints over several months, including fears that the windows opened too far and that she lacked a key.
Assistant coroner Ian Wade, sitting at East London Coroner’s Court, said the windows “were not used appropriately”.
He delivered a narrative conclusion on Monday, in which he said: “Aalim was an active five-year-old boy who suffered from a diagnosed condition called autism, such as to render him incapable of making reliable judgments about his personal safety and abilities.
“In the early hours of May 16 2024… he awoke and went from his bedroom to the kitchen, he climbed onto a chair and then onto the windowsill of an insecure double turn and tilt window.
“He opened the window and in a naive belief that he could fly or alternatively could come to no harm he leapt from the open window… he died at the scene.”
![Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/18/c19e4b574583f0a9bc48bf240fc7e71fY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3Njc3NzY2-2.76191858.jpg)
Mr Wade said he did not find a basis for issuing a report to prevent future deaths, adding: “I find there was no compelling reason why a landlord should’ve considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate.”
He said: “It wasn’t the fact that it was the 15th floor that was significant, what was significant was that the windows had become compromised.”
The court previously heard a young child’s voice is twice heard counting down “three, two, one” followed a few seconds later by “a loud clang” was captured on grainy audio, which was taken from CCTV outside the apartment block.
Detective Constable Joe Linton, who carried out a review of CCTV footage outside Jacobs House, previously said “it is most likely from the footage available” that Aalim had “jumped out” of the flat at the building in New City Road “of his own accord without the presence of a third party”.
A post-mortem examination found Aalim died from “multiple injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height”.
Ms Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put her young family in the flat, which needed repairs, saying Aalim was autistic with “no sense of danger”.
All the windows were closed before the family, which also included her toddler son and a newborn girl, went to bed.
Ms Osman denied any suggestion she may have “forced” the window open to cope in hot weather.
Aalim could have been climbing to get a biscuit from a cupboard but the windows had “faulty” restrictors and her ongoing complaints to get them fixed led only to a series of workmen who did not sort the problem, she said.
Window engineer Charlie Mann said the windows were “all working”, including the handles and restrictors, when he tested them in December 2023.
A restrictor is a safety device which is meant to allow the window to open only 50-100mm.
Having spoken to the mother, who said her son had autism, he decided the restrictors should be changed to a lockable version rather than one that can be worked by a button.
He ordered nine restrictors and contractors came to fix them in January 2024.
Charlie Mann’s father, James Mann, who is managing director of ABC Ltd the firm where the window engineer works, watched videos of police operating the window from which Aalim fell.
He said the window appeared to be going into “dual mode”, which he said could be caused by “misalignment, misuse or force”.
This is a fault which meant the window tilted and turned open at the same time, despite the handle being in only the tilt position.
In the video, the court saw that the restrictor did not engage every time the police officer tested the window.
He said that “there needs to be an adjustment, something is not quite right” but he added he needed to see more of the window to have a clearer idea of the problem.
Tom Monk, who worked for ABC Ltd, told the court he went to the flat in January 2024 to fit the new restrictors and spent one to two hours there.
He said he may have been there twice, a couple of days later and fitted a new hinge on a casement window.
Detective Inspector Jamie Humm, who investigated the incident, said there was “no evidence or suspicion he (Aalim) had been forced”.
“The flat was well furnished and it was clearly a loving environment for a child,” he noted.
He added that soon after arriving at the scene he was satisfied “there was no evidence of a crime, not that I thought there would be”.
John Gray, cabinet member for housing, Newham Council, said: “This was a tragic accident which resulted in the heartbreaking death of a young five-year-old child.
“Our thoughts continue to be with Aalim’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.
“We are grateful to the coroner Ian Wade KC for his thorough and fair hearing of the facts of this case, which have at times been very difficult to hear and revisit.”
summary: Five-year-old Aalim Ahmed died from multiple injuries after falling from a 15th-floor temporary social housing flat window in east London on May 16, 2024. An inquest heard that the autistic boy climbed onto a chair and the windowsill before jumping from the compromised tilt-and-turn window, believing he could fly. While the boy's mother blamed Newham Council and reported previous safety concerns regarding faulty windows, the coroner concluded the death was a tragic accident and did not issue a report to prevent future deaths.
key_points: Aalim Ahmed, a five-year-old autistic boy, died instantly after falling from a 15th-floor window in Plaistow, east London.
Assistant coroner Ian Wade delivered a narrative conclusion stating the child climbed onto the windowsill of an insecure window and jumped.
The boy's mother, Sahra Osman, had previously submitted complaints to Newham Council stating the windows opened too far and lacked proper security.
Conflicting evidence was presented at the inquest regarding the condition of the window fittings and whether the restrictors were fully functional.
Investigators found no evidence of third-party involvement or foul play, treating the incident as a tragic accident.

title: Man 'stabbed partner 70 times in her London home then turned knife on her daughter'
author: Emily Pennink
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/15/54/Samantha-Turner.jpeg?trim=71,0,600,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Alan Dore, 48, is accused of killing grandmother Samantha Turner, 52, in her own home in Shepherd’s Bush, west London, on August 18.
Ms Turner’s 32-year-old daughter Keeley Turner was stabbed twice when she tried to intervene, it is alleged.
Prosecutor Philip McGhee said the allegations in the case involved a “murderous attack” and a knife in a “domestic setting”.
Keeley Turner had been upstairs at the family home in Askew Road when she heard her mother scream and went downstairs, the court heard.
When she tried to stop the defendant, he stabbed her first to the abdomen and then to her back, Mr McGhee said.
She called 999 at 8.19am to report that her mother had been stabbed, saying: “Hurry up man, he’s going to kill her.”
Her mother was found with multiple stab wounds and lying in a pool of blood on the kitchen floor.
She was pronounced dead at the scene at 8.54am.
Dore, who had been in a relationship with Samantha Turner for about a year and lived nearby, was arrested in a bedroom of the property.
Mr McGhee told the court that a post-mortem examination identified around 70 sharp force injuries to her body which were allegedly inflicted with “severe force”.
Read More
Keeley Turner remains in hospital although her injuries are not thought to be life-threatening.
Dore appeared in court by video-link from Wandsworth prison and spoke to confirm his identity.
Dore, also of Askew Road, was remanded into custody.
summary: Alan Dore is accused of murdering his partner, 52-year-old Samantha Turner, at her west London home on August 18. A post-mortem examination found she sustained around 70 sharp force injuries inflicted with severe force. Her 32-year-old daughter, Keeley Turner, was stabbed twice in the abdomen and back when she attempted to intervene.
key_points: Alan Dore, 48, has been accused of the murder of Samantha Turner in Shepherd's Bush, west London.
A post-mortem examination revealed approximately 70 sharp force injuries on the victim's body.
The victim's daughter, Keeley Turner, was stabbed twice while trying to stop the attack and called 999.
Keeley Turner's injuries are not considered life-threatening and she remains in the hospital.
Dore appeared in court via video-link and was remanded into custody.

title: Lime pulls bikes from London borough after blind man's 'very frightening' road ordeal
author: Nicholas Cecil; Luke Reevey
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after poorly parked cycles force blind man into busy road](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/9/29/Beal.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Jason Beal, 53, stressed that his Labrador Retriever guide dog Caine baulks at leading him into the road in south east London.
So, unable to see traffic as it goes by, he has to listen out and “very nervously” take Caine into the carriageway with him.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/22/Beal1.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Assistive technology manager Mr Beal and his wife Jessica, 45, who is also blind, raised the dangers they were facing with their local MP Liam Conlon.
Lime had been operating in Bromley without a contract with the council which has told it to remove its bikes immediately.
Speaking to The Standard, Mr Beal said: “There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement.
“Then I’ve got to stop, Kent House Road is quite a busy road.
“He (Caine) will refuse to go into a road at any time.
“So, I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road.
“That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”
He added: “Alternatively, there have been times when we have been walking up to the station and there have been loads of bikes parked up against where the tactile pavement is and I’ve had to go into the edge of the road there.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/13/30/lime1.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Marketing audience manager Mrs Beal, 45, who walks using a white cane, told how she has injured herself colliding with e-bikes: “You never know when they are going to crop up and if you are going to hit one, or are they going to fall on you.
“So, it’s quite scary just walking around.”
The couple recognise that “bikes are a great way for people to get around” but stressed it “feels unfair” that they were being left in their way in “difficult places for us”.
Mrs Beal described as “fantastic news” that Lime was removing its bikes from their neighbourhood.
“It does feel like a victory although obviously we want people to continue riding bikes and walking,” she added.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/08/blindman.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Conlon, Labour MP for Beckenham and Penge, told of his “real anger” over the ordeal faced by the Beals.
Read More
“We cannot allow new barriers to be created for disabled residents who already face challenges getting around,” he said.
“As a disabled person myself, who was unable to walk for four years as a teenager, I understand these issues first-hand.
“It is something I take seriously, and something I will not accept.”
He added: “I’m delighted that Lime have announced they are withdrawing their bikes from Penge – and would like to thank them for their cooperation, and for their apology.”
It is understood that the Lime app allowed bikes to be hired in the Penge area last week but by Monday morning this was no longer possible.
In a letter to Mr Conlon, Lime stressed the benefits of the e-bikes but also that it is “critical” that their use “works for both riders and the communities in which they operate”.
The company added: “We would therefore like to apologise to Jessica and Jason for the issues they have faced due to rider parking in Penge.
“To address the specific issue in Penge...we have made a change to the Lime app to prevent Lime bikes from being used beyond the Lewisham boundary until we can agree an approach that supports the roll-out of an effective local scheme, with appropriate parking locations.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/24/11/26/Liam2.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Lime had been operating its bikes in Bromley on a “non-contractual” basis.
It emphasised that the “build-up of bikes” at the border with Lewisham showed a “considerable demand” for rental bikes in Bromley.
It is keen to work with the council and Mr Conlon on a scheme that “works for your constituents, ensuring both appropriate parking solutions for residents to access the service and the removal of bikes parked irresponsibly”.
Councillor Simon Fawthrop, Bromley council’s executive councillor for transport and highways, said, “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough, with their map allowing hiring use in Penge in the last few weeks.
“We welcome it appears to have changed now.
“This remains a serious matter and needs to permanently stop and ultimately if it does not, we will take action to remove the Lime bikes and then charge Lime for these costs.”
summary: Lime has withdrawn its e-bikes from the London borough of Bromley following complaints from a blind couple who were forced into busy roads by poorly parked cycles. Jason and Jessica Beal raised the issue with local MP Liam Conlon after experiencing dangerous obstructions on pavements and tactile paving. In response, Lime apologized and updated its app to prevent bikes from being used beyond the Lewisham boundary until an agreed local scheme with proper parking is established.
key_points: Poorly parked Lime bikes forced a blind man with a guide dog and his blind wife into a busy road in south east London.
Lime was operating in Bromley without a contract or council consent, prompting the council to demand the bikes be removed.
Local MP Liam Conlon intervened on behalf of the couple, expressing anger over the barriers faced by disabled residents.
Lime apologized to the couple and updated its app to stop bike usage beyond the Lewisham boundary.

title: A Tiny Forest is growing on an old railway site in Hammersmith
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
A Tiny Forest is growing on an old railway site in Hammersmith
A patch of unused land at a London Underground control centre is being transformed into a miniature woodland, with 600 native trees planted with the help of local schoolchildren and volunteers.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Tiny-Forest.jpg)
Transport for London’s (TfL) first “Tiny Forest” has been created at its Hammersmith Service Control Centre, where the densely planted woodland occupies an area roughly the size of a tennis court. The Tiny Forest concept is designed to pack a large number of native trees into a relatively small area, creating new habitats for wildlife while increasing biodiversity and providing more greenery in urban areas.
The project started in March and is being developed by TfL with Earthwatch Europe, Hammersmith & Fulham Council and local communities. The council funded it, with support from the Forestry Commission.
The Hammersmith woodland recently had its first maintenance session, when volunteers were joined by 60 pupils from nearby Flora Gardens School. As well as learning how to look after the young trees, the pupils were given a tour of the Hammersmith Service Control Centre to find out how parts of London’s transport network are managed and learn about careers in transport and engineering.
TfL says the woodland should require progressively less attention as it becomes established, and after around three years is expected to need relatively little maintenance. The dense woodland should also provide shade and cooling during hot weather, capture carbon as the trees grow and provide additional habitat for wildlife.
Simon Feldman, a service controller and lead of the Tiny Forest project at TfL’s Hammersmith Service Control Centre, said: “We’re delighted to see TfL’s first Tiny Forest continuing to thrive with the support of local volunteers and our partner organisations.”
He added that as well as creating new habitats for wildlife, the project showed what could be possible elsewhere across TfL’s estate to create a “strong green heartbeat for London”.
The forest forms part of TfL’s wider Green Infrastructure and Biodiversity Plan, which looks at how land alongside and around the transport network can be used to protect and expand habitats and connect existing green spaces.
It also adds to a growing collection of Tiny Forests in Hammersmith & Fulham. The council says there are now seven across the borough, including sites at Eelbrook Common, Normand Park, Frank Banfield Park, Hammersmith Park, Wormholt Park, Norland North Open Space and Trussley Road.
Councillor Nicole Trehy, Hammersmith & Fulham Council’s Cabinet Member for Climate Emergency and Travel, said the forests are “home to hundreds of species and are helping to clean our air and cool our streets”.
There’s a bit of history to the Trussley Road site where the Tiny Forest was planted, as it’s land that used to be part of the short-lived Kensington and Richmond line, with a loop from Hammersmith to the mainline railway next to Shepherds Bush.
Although this is TfL’s first Tiny Forest, if the Hammersmith experiment proves successful, they have plenty of patches of otherwise unused land where similarly compact woodlands could potentially take root.
summary: Transport for London (TfL) has planted its first "Tiny Forest" at the Hammersmith Service Control Centre, utilizing a tennis-court-sized patch of unused land. Developed in partnership with Earthwatch Europe, Hammersmith & Fulham Council, and local volunteers, the project features 600 native trees designed to boost urban biodiversity, capture carbon, and provide cooling. Local schoolchildren helped maintain the young woodland while also learning about careers in transport and engineering. The site historically formed part of the short-lived Kensington and Richmond railway line.
key_points: TfL created its first Tiny Forest at the Hammersmith Service Control Centre, spanning an area the size of a tennis court.
The project features 600 native trees planted with the help of Earthwatch Europe, Hammersmith & Fulham Council, and local volunteers.
Students from Flora Gardens School participated in maintenance and toured the control centre to learn about transport careers.
The densely planted woodland aims to increase biodiversity, capture carbon, and cool urban streets.
The forest is located on historical land that was once part of the short-lived Kensington and Richmond railway line.

title: Iran war helped send London contractor under, administrators say
author: Rockwool
content:
Curo Construction collapsed in June owing unsecured creditors more than £21m
A company set up at the end of 2013 went into administration after jobs stalled and inflation ramped up with the Iran war proving the final straw for its survival.
Curo Construction specialised in the London refurbishment and fit out sector but had plans to move into the industrial sector with jobs including data centres.
The firm, which at one stage had 140 staff, had moved into a new office in the City and was targeting revenue to £200m.
![curo](https://d3sux4fmh2nu8u.cloudfront.net/Pictures/480xAny/2/1/1/2036211_curo_683858_crop.jpg)
But in its last set of accounts, the company saw income fall a third to £108m in the year to September 2024 with pre-tax profit slumping 65% to £1.1m. Management accounts for the first five months of 2026 show revenue was just £29m.
A report by administrators Antony Batty, which was appointed in June, said: “Throughout 2025 and early 2026 Curo Construction won numerous projects that were either delayed or in some instances postponed indefinitely.
“Overheads were heavily cut in 2025 and early 2026 however ongoing delayed starts to projects, increased material inflation and then the start of the Iran war led to losses that could not be sustained or managed whilst in the current economic client with projects delayed or withdrawn.”
Administrators said they have not yet received a report outlining the company’s estimated financial position – known as a statement of affairs – from its directors and so had provided an estimate at the time of their appointment on 17 June.
“The reason for the delay is that two critical employees who had familiarity and access to the accounting system are now fully employed elsewhere and [our] agent is seeking to enlist their assistance in this regards,” it added.
But the administrators have estimated unsecured creditors are owed £21.2m, with trade creditors owed £19.6m of this amount. Unsecured creditors have been told not to expect any money back. HMRC has said it is owed £6m.
All 135 employees were made redundant in May and are owed £861,000 in wages and holiday pay, the report says.
The report also said that insolvency expert Ashwells had asked former employees to help it provide login details to access a software system “which contains key records relating to retentions, contracts and other project information necessary to progress recoveries”.
It added: “To date, Ashwells has not been provided with the login credentials required to access the platform. Steps are now being taken to obtain these details from one of the former employees to enable access to the system.”
summary: London-based contractor Curo Construction collapsed into administration in June owing unsecured creditors more than £21m after experiencing stalled jobs, surging inflation, and the impact of the Iran war. The firm's income and profits had declined sharply in the period leading up to its failure, resulting in the redundancy of all 135 employees in May. Administrators are currently working to access company software systems and obtain a formal statement of affairs from directors.
key_points: Curo Construction entered administration in June, leaving unsecured creditors owed an estimated £21.2m.
The collapse was driven by stalled or delayed projects, rising inflation, and the Iran war.
All 135 staff members were made redundant in May and are owed £861,000 in wages and holiday pay.
HMRC is among the creditors, stating it is owed £6m.
Administrators have faced delays in compiling the statement of affairs and accessing accounting software because former key employees have taken other jobs.

title: Strikes are taking place on 42 London bus routes this week
author: Ed Cunningham
content:
[title]
London bus strikes involving 1,500 drivers and impacting more than 40 routes are taking place this week. Drivers working for Arriva London North voted to reject a deal over working conditions and are set to walk out on dozens of dates across August, September and October.
Have you been struggling with London’s stifling heat this summer? Think of the bus drivers. During periods of hot weather in-cab temperatures can soar beyond 40C. The current dispute is in response to those working conditions, and the first strike was on August 14.
The striking drivers are part of the Unite union. They’re based at eight bus garages and work on routes across north, east and central London, as well as Essex. The walk-outs were set to impact more than 40 routes – including not just normal London buses but also night buses, school services and Superloops. Last week’s strikes were postponed while union members voted on a deal, which they’ve now rejected.
Worried that your local bus route could be hit by strikes? Here’s what you need to know about the industrial action.
When are London bus drivers going on strike?
The following walk-outs are planned:
- August 25 (4am) to August 28 (4.30am)
- September 4 (4am) to September 5 (4.30am)
- September 7 (4am) to September 8 (4.30am)
- September 18 (4am) to September 19 (4.30am)
- September 21 (4am) to September 22 (4.30am)
- October 2 (4am) to October 3 (4.30am)
- October 5 (4am) to October 6 (4.30am)
- October 16 (4am) to October 17 (4.30am)
- October 19 (4am) to October 20 (4.30am)
Which bus routes will be affected by strikes?
The following services are set to be impacted by walk-outs.

TfL warns that ‘little or no service is expected on affected routes’ on strike dates.
![London bus with passenger](https://media.timeout.com/images/106229136/image.webp) 
Why are bus drivers going on strike?
Unite said that the dispute was due to Arriva North having ‘failed to act on driver complaints about poor working conditions in hot weather’.
Unite says that current air-cooling systems only manage to reduce in-cab temperatures by ‘around two or three degrees’, arguing that hot weather is both dangerous for drivers – causing heat exhaustion, heat stroke and dehydration – and exacerbates fatigue.
Which London bus garages are affected by the strikes?
Arriva North drivers at the following garages were walking out:
- Barking
- Edmonton
- Enfield
- Grays
- Palmers Green
- Stamford Hill
- Tottenham
- Wood Green
What’s been said about the bus strikes?
Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: ‘Time and time again drivers have complained to Arriva North London about working in dangerous conditions but the company has failed to act which is completely unacceptable.
‘A profitable company such as Arriva could easily invest in improving conditions for its drivers and protecting the general public but is instead prioritising greed. We will back our members all the way in this dispute.’
TfL said: ‘We are working together on a range of measures to further improve working conditions, health and wellbeing.
‘We are committed to ensuring that all staff have a fair work schedule, with safe vehicles and access to the facilities they need to carry out their roles effectively.
‘We would like to reassure colleagues again that any reports from drivers are always fully investigated and our operators should never take action against people raising concerns about welfare.’

summary: Approximately 1,500 Arriva London North bus drivers represented by the Unite union are holding strikes across August, September, and October. The industrial action impacts 42 routes, including normal buses, night services, school services, and Superloops, affecting eight bus garages. Drivers rejected a recent deal because they are protesting poor working conditions and dangerously high in-cab temperatures during hot weather.
key_points: Around 1,500 drivers are participating in walkouts across 42 London bus routes.
The strikes are organized by the Unite union following the rejection of a deal over working conditions.
Drivers are protesting dangerous in-cab temperatures exceeding 40C during hot weather and inadequate air-cooling systems.
The industrial action affects eight bus garages across north, east, and central London, as well as Essex.
Walkouts are scheduled on multiple dates across August, September, and October.

title: Every London Spot Kendall Jenner & Jacob Elordi Visited This Weekend
author: Natasha Harding
content:
![](https://files.thehandbook.com/uploads/2026/08/kendall-jenner-jacob-elordi-cipriani-1.jpg)
A week after Taylor Swift was seen leaving Mayfair establishment Annabel’s, Kendall Jenner and Jacob Elordi were spotted departing multiple beloved London venues. Scroll through to see the full list of additions to the celebrity-approved restaurants in the capital.
The River Cafe
Kicking off the list is perhaps the most well-known celebrity haunt, The River Cafe. Located in Hammersmith, the Michelin-starred destination has been frequented by everyone from David Beckham and Sir Elton John to Gwyneth Paltrow and Kim Kardashian.
Famed for its high-end, seasonal Italian menu, favourite items to order include the wood-roasted sea bass, fresh handmade pastas and, of course, the chocolate nemesis cake for dessert.
where: Thames Wharf, Rainville Rd, London W6 9HA
website: www.rivercafe.co.uk
China Tang
Over on Park Lane, Kendall and Jacob were spotted exiting The Dorchester on Saturday night, where they reportedly enjoyed dinner at authentic Cantonese restaurant China Tang.
When you’re there, make sure to check out the signature Peking duck along with two notable additions from the dim sum menu: the Iberico cha siu pork siu long bao and har gau.
where: 53 Park Ln, London W1K 1QA
website: www.chinatanglondon.co.uk
Soho House
It’s believed that, after dinner at China Tang, Kendall and Jacob visited private members’ club Soho House, where they stayed until the early hours of the morning.
where: multiple locations
website: www.sohohouse.com
Cipriani

title: Rail service changes in east London and Essex due to dried-out clay
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Rail service changes in east London and Essex due to dried-out clay
There are going to be changes to Greater Anglia and c2c train services from tomorrow (Tues 25th Aug) as the railway deals with the side effects of the recent heatwaves.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/Uneven-track-on-the-c2c-route-caused-by-dried-out-soil-measures-are-in-place-to-keep-services-running-safely-smoothly-and-reliably.jpg)
Because of sustained heat and low rainfall, the clay under long stretches of the railway in Essex has dried out and shrunk, causing track quality issues. To keep everyone moving safely and reliably, speed restrictions and temporary timetable amendments are being applied to give passengers more certainty about services and reduce the risk of short-notice disruption.
Timetable changes will come into effect on the c2c route on Tuesday 25 August and on the Greater Anglia line between Southend Victoria and London on Tuesday 1st September.
GBR Anglia says that some journeys will take 2–8 minutes longer than usual, with slightly adjusted departure and arrival times.
While speed restrictions are currently not affecting Elizabeth line services, customers are advised to check for the most up-to-date travel information before starting their journey.
Engineers are closely monitoring track conditions across the region, and further speed restrictions may be needed in the coming weeks to keep services running smoothly. GBR Anglia says it will advise of any additional service alterations in advance.
Speed restrictions will remain in place until ground conditions recover, which will require a prolonged period of rain.
To minimise the effects of dried-out soil on Anglia this summer, extra engineering work will continue, with Network Rail using machines called tampers to help create a solid foundation so that trains can run smoothly. Engineers are also laying new ballast (the stones underneath the rails and sleepers) to help raise the track level.
Last year, railway engineers used tampers to treat around 100km of track affected by dried-out soil on Anglia. Ahead of this summer season, thousands of tonnes of ballast were dropped to help keep the track as smooth as possible, with 49,000 tonnes expected to be dropped during 2026 in total.
Martin Beable, Chief Operating Officer for GBR Anglia, said: “We’re taking action to keep everyone moving safely and reliably while minimising the impact on passengers. Our teams are working together across Anglia to keep running the best possible service despite the significant challenges we’re facing because of this exceptionally hot and dry weather.
“We never want our customers to experience disruption, but safety will always be our priority. Thank you for bearing with us, and please do check before you travel, particularly if you’re used to getting the same time train every day.”
summary: Recent heatwaves and low rainfall have dried out and shrunk the clay beneath railways in east London and Essex, leading to track quality issues. To maintain safety, Greater Anglia and c2c are introducing speed restrictions and temporary timetable changes starting August 25 and September 1. Journeys may take two to eight minutes longer, and restrictions will remain in place until prolonged rainfall allows ground conditions to recover.
key_points: Sustained heat and low rainfall caused clay beneath the railway in Essex to dry out and shrink.
Speed restrictions and temporary timetables begin on August 25 for c2c and September 1 for the Greater Anglia line.
Affected journeys will take two to eight minutes longer with adjusted departure and arrival times.
Network Rail is using tampers and laying new ballast to help stabilize the tracks.
Speed restrictions will remain in place until a prolonged period of rain allows the ground to recover.

title: Stop damaging London mobile phone signal, Sadiq Khan tells developers
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Why doesn't my 5G work in central London? Expert explains](https://static.standard.co.uk/2022/02/08/23/10971db0f8e2e585e8ac49939d565319Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNjQ0NDQ3MjE0-2.49899390.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Mobile phone operators are struggling to maintain signal coverage due to the number of “notices to quit” (NTQs) which have risen in recent years, forcing them to remove antennas as developments take place. Finding an alternative site can take on average two-and-a-half years, possibly up to seven. Faced with this growing problem, Sir Sadiq has laid out requirements on developers in the draft London Plan. “His draft London Plan treats mobile connectivity as essential infrastructure and requires it to be considered from the outset of new developments. “It also protects existing infrastructure and supports action by boroughs and operators to tackle mobile not-spots and strengthen network resilience.” The draft London plan warns of “unintended consequences” of new housing, offices and other schemes. It states: “This is a particular issue with digital infrastructure, for instance, where development may result in ‘notices to quit’ that have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities.” It then stresses: “Provision for continuity of service means there is an expectation that notices to quit should not be issued without other arrangements being put in place to ensure service continuity during construction and beyond, in dialogue with affected providers.” Read More Gareth Elliott, director of policy and communications at Mobile UK, said: “The Greater London Authority has already led the charge, writing into the London Plan draft guidance an expectation that NTQs should not be issued without alternative arrangements in place to maintain service continuity. “Ministers must now follow through nationally to turn these principles into practical policy.” He added: “Mobile connectivity underpins London’s economic dynamism. “By bringing developers, local planning authorities, and mobile operators together early, we can turn network disruption into a win-win for urban regeneration.” ![

Workers are already making their way into offices in the city

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/09/09/5/37/IMG_3290.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The Government has taken a first step in response to the problem. The recent National Planning Policy Framework says that in considering proposals for expansion or upgrading of electronic telecommunications networks “substantial weight” should be given to the benefits of maintaining or improving network coverage, capacity, reliability and resilience. A Government spokesperson said: "We recognise that maintaining mobile coverage during redevelopment can present challenges where telecoms infrastructure needs to be relocated.
summary: London Mayor Sadiq Khan has introduced new requirements in the draft London Plan to protect mobile phone signal and infrastructure from being disrupted by developers. The rules mandate that developers consider digital connectivity from the outset and ensure alternative arrangements are made before issuing notices to quit that force the removal of antennas. This initiative aims to address the erosion of London's mobile connectivity caused by redevelopment projects and lengthy delays in finding alternative sites.
key_points: Developers are increasingly issuing 'notices to quit' that force mobile operators to remove antennas and damage signal coverage.
Finding alternative sites for mobile infrastructure can take between two-and-a-half and seven years on average.
The draft London Plan treats mobile connectivity as essential infrastructure and requires it to be considered at the start of new developments.
The policy expects that notices to quit should not be issued without alternative arrangements to ensure service continuity.
The Government's National Planning Policy Framework now gives substantial weight to maintaining and improving telecommunications networks.

title: Ethnic minority victims make up 9 out of 10 unsolved murders in London, report shows
author: Shaun Wilson
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Met Police say knives used in three London murders within 24 hours](https://static.standard.co.uk/2023/09/27/12/POLICE%20Croydon%20%2012432766.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Black people represented 83 per cent (36 incidents) of unsolved shootings as well as 73 per cent (39 incidents) of unsolved stabbings.
Read More
The analysis was carried out by Action on Armed Violence, which also discovered fatal shootings were more likely to go unsolved than stabbings, while the average age of homicide victims in the capital is 36.
However, for unsolved cases, the average victim’s age falls down to just 28.
Iain Overton, of Action on Armed Violence, stated: "Our data suggest that London’s unsolved murders are not evenly distributed. Instead, they are concentrated among young Black men and in cases involving firearm violence.
"While there are many reasons for why such murder investigations are especially difficult, the result must seem often clear to the victims’ families: those communities most affected by deadly violence are often the least likely to see those responsible brought to justice.
"This in itself risks deepening existing mistrust and creating the perception of unequal protection under the law. And that can’t be a good thing.”
Despite the gloomy figures, the Met has a comparatively positive record in solving murders, with nine out of 10 killings resulting in a conviction. Meanwhile, the force reported 97 homicides in London last year, its lowest in a decade and a significant drop from 153 in 2019.
The Met’s head of homicide, commander Paul Brogden, said: “We know serious violence disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly young black men, who have the lowest trust in policing. This means sadly victims or witnesses are less likely to come forward and trust us.
“As this report outlines, that is an added complexity following shootings or stabbings on the streets, where identifying suspects requires more detailed investigative work, particularly when compared to domestic murders.
“While we use every tool at our disposal such as CCTV and forensics, often it’s witness evidence which can prove vital in securing convictions.”
summary: A report by Action on Armed Violence reveals that ethnic minority victims account for nine out of ten unsolved murders in London, with young Black men and firearm violence cases disproportionately represented. The analysis highlights that unsolved cases feature younger victims and are harder to resolve due to lower trust and witness cooperation in affected communities. Despite these challenges, the Metropolitan Police note that they maintain a high overall murder clearance rate and that London homicides have decreased to their lowest in a decade.
key_points: Ethnic minority victims make up 9 out of 10 unsolved murders in London.
Black people represented 83 percent of unsolved shootings and 73 percent of unsolved stabbings.
The average age of victims in unsolved cases drops to 28, compared to an overall average of 36.
The Metropolitan Police reported 97 homicides last year, marking its lowest total in a decade.
Police cite lower trust and reluctance of witnesses to come forward as key complexities in solving these crimes.

title: London faces five days of rain and thundery showers as bank holiday washout looms
author: Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Spectacular thunderstorms hit London causing thousands of lightning strikes in June](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/01M0FGM7PFKA584505TS8Y08EH.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Rain is set to move in from Wednesday, according to BBC Weathers, with light showers and drizzle scattered through the day and highs of 26C. A bout of thundery showers is forecast at around 3am on Thursday morning, rumbling on until around 7am. The showers are forecast to continue across the morning until around 11am, with highs of around 24C. The relatively dry afternoon will see sunny spells and light winds, though the reprieve from the rain will be short-lived. Thursday night will bring another shower at around 9pm, before the rain returns at 2am on Friday morning. Rain is forecast to pepper the capital from the early hours of Friday until 1am on Saturday. The downpour will turn to drizzle between 4pm and 8pm, but it will still be a very wet end to the working week. Saturday is set to be much drier throughout the morning, but Londoners will see a drizzly spell between 3pm and 6pm, before another spate of showers hits the capital at 7pm. ![

People shelter under umbrellas from the rain in Whitehall, central London. Picture date: Thursday August 20, 2026.

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/13/01M0FGM7PFKA584505TS8Y08EH.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Sunday looks to be the wettest day of the weekend with a 66% chance of rain forecast at 10am, showering down on the capital until 4pm. There will be some sunny spells during the late afternoon. In its 10-day outlook, the forecaster is also anticipating more rain to fall on bank holiday Monday. Light showers are expected in London between 7am and 10am, and again between 2pm and 3pm. ![The show must go on: rain won't damped the party mood](https://static.standard.co.uk/s3fs-public/thumbnails/image/2016/08/22/18/notting-hill-carnival-2015.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The spate of rain showers will provide some much needed reprieve for Londoners. There was no meaningful rain in London in July, with forecasters measuring zero rain in parts of north London and just 1mm in areas south of the river. Read More This summer has seen record wildfires in England and Wales, totalling more than 1,000, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC). In a weather update on its website, the Met Office wrote: “A relatively unsettled start to this period, as showers or longer spells of rain are possible across many parts of the UK, along with some strong winds. “Some heavy bursts and thunderstorms are likely at times. It will likely remain changeable into early September, with rainfall amounts probably above average for the time of year and the potential for some more strong winds at times. “However, some drier, more settled interludes could develop at times. Temperatures are likely to be near average, although some short-lived warm or hot spells are possible, especially in the south.”
summary: London is facing a five-day forecast of rain and thundery showers starting Wednesday, potentially disrupting the bank holiday weekend. The upcoming wet weather follows a very dry July that saw virtually no rain in parts of the city and record wildfires across England and Wales. The Met Office anticipates an unsettled and changeable start to the period with above-average rainfall across the UK into early September.
key_points: Rain is set to move into London starting Wednesday, with thundery showers forecast for early Thursday morning.
Sunday is projected to be the wettest day of the weekend, with rain continuing into bank holiday Monday.
The incoming rain follows a July with zero recorded rainfall in parts of north London and only 1mm south of the river.
England and Wales have experienced record wildfires this summer, totaling more than 1,000 according to the NFCC.

title: Taiwanese restaurant Din Tai Fung has revealed its fifth London location
author: India Lawrence
content:
[title]
If you know your dumplings, chances are you’ll be familiar with the cult phenomenon that is Din Tai Fung. The Taiwanese chain founded in 1958 by a Chinese immigrant is famous for its xiao long bao (Shanghainese soup dumplings). These days it’s a global outfit with 170 sites around the world, including four – soon to be five – in London.
Din Tai Fung has revealed the location of its fifth London location. Soup dumplings, wontons and fried rice are thought to be coming to King’s Cross, as Din Tai Fung is reportedly in talks to open at the former site of Babel Beerhouse on Lewis Cubitt Walk. The beerhouse next to Lightroom closed in May before being snapped up by the dumpling chain.
The chain’s famous xiao long bao are traditionally made with a rich pork filling encased in a delicate wrapper that’s hand-folded at least 18 times. They also come stuffed with crab, chicken and truffle. It’s not unusual to see long queues outside the restaurants as people flock to try the famous dumplings.
Currently, you can visit Din Tai Fung restaurants in Canary Wharf, Covent Garden, Selfridges and Centre Point by Tottenham Court Road station. The opening date for Din Tai Fung King’s Cross hasn’t been revealed yet, and exact details of the restaurant are also still under wraps. When it arrives it will be in good company, joining the likes of Dishoom, Lina Stores and Barrafina in Coal Drops Yard.
Did you hear that cult vegan sandwich spot Coven of Wiches has moved to a new location?
Plus: Caravan’s biggest restaurant yet is opening on the South Bank.
