Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: Taiwanese dumpling chain Din Tai Fung is reportedly planning to open its fifth London location in King's Cross. The new restaurant is slated for the former site of Babel Beerhouse on Lewis Cubitt Walk. An official opening date and exact restaurant details have not yet been announced.
key_points: Din Tai Fung is known globally for its signature xiao long bao and other dishes like wontons and fried rice.
The chain is reportedly in talks to take over the former Babel Beerhouse site at Lewis Cubitt Walk in King's Cross.
Din Tai Fung currently operates four London locations in Canary Wharf, Covent Garden, Selfridges, and Centre Point.
The new King's Cross location will join other notable dining spots in the area such as Dishoom, Lina Stores, and Barrafina.

title: CASTING ANNOUNCED FOR NEW ADAPTATION OF WOYZECK'S 'FRANZ AND MARIE' DEBUTING AT CHARING CROSS THEATRE - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
Featuring some of London’s hottest musical theatre talent, Brenock O’Connor and Jade Oswald lead a 14-strong actor-muso company in this haunting new musical. Inspired by Georg Büchner’s Woyzeck, this now classic fable has a feminist twist, placing Marie alongside Franz Woyzeck at the heart of the narrative.
Set in the twisted and war-torn world of late 19th Century Europe, a platoon of young soldiers have been stationed in an isolated outpost for months, awaiting further orders. Franz Woyzeck, a man haunted by nightmares since his return from the front, has agreed to medical experimentations by the army doctor in order to supplement his meagre income to support.his girlfriend Marie, and their baby, the pressures take their toll with disastrous consequences.
The full casting comprises:
Brenock O’Connor (Channel 4; Game of Thrones; Alex Rider, Amazon TV; Derry Girls,) as Woyzeck and Jade Oswald (Little Women, UK Tour and Salisbury Playhouse; Treason The Musical Concert, Theatre Royal Rury Lane, Stephen Sondheim’s Old Friends, Sondheim Theatre) as Marie are joined by Steve Simmonds (Assassins, Watermill Theatre and Nottingham Playhouse; The Secret Garden, Theatre Royal York) as ‘Sergeant Ursid’; Paula James (Equus, Menier Chocolate Factory and Theatre Royal Bath; Our Man In Havana, Watermill Theatre; The Comedy of Errors, RSC) as ‘Zella’; Richard Emerson Gould (Alternations, The National Theatre; Twelfth Night, Shakespeare in the Squares; Hamlet, Salisbury Playhouse) as ‘Doctor Simian’; Matthew Heywood (Little Shop of Horrors, UK Tour; Zorro, Charing Cross Theatre; Alice in Wonderland, Marylebone Theatre) as ‘Drum Major Varg’; Max Alexander-Taylor (Jesus Christ Superstar, Watermill Theatre; Cable Street, Marylebone Theatre, 59E59 New York and Southwark Playhouse; The Lion, Southwark Playhouse US Tour and Korea/Japan,) as ‘André Schmitt’; Mark Meadows (The Tempest, RSC; The Secret Life of Bees, Almeida Theatre; Flowers For Mrs Harris, Sheffield Theatres and Chichester Theatre) as ‘Captain Peccary’; Eve Polycarpou (From Here to Eternity, Charing Cross Theatre; Sunset at Villa Thalia, The National Theatre; In The Heights, Southwark Playhouse and Kings Cross Theatre) as ‘Vashti’; Elaine Hua Jones (Places I Never Think About, The Cockpit; Wishmas: A Fantastical Christmas Adventure, Secret Cinema) as ‘Kat’; Antony Lam (Miraculous, The King’s Head; The Smeds and the Smoos, Lyric Theatre and UK Tour), Anna-Marie Piazza (War Horse, National Theatre and UK Tour; Day of the Living, RSC; Wicker Husband, The Other Palace), Emily Panes (The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, Ambassadors Theatre; Malory Towers, UK Tour; Mozart: Her Story, Theatre Royal Drury Lane) and Tom Aubrey, making his professional stage debut, completing the ensemble.
This raw, soul-rattling Indie Folk score was originally commissioned by award-winning Korean musical theatre company Acom and created by Chris Broderick and Rob Shepherd, key members of cult Medway band The Singing Loins. Their adaptation of Woyzeck was staged at the LG Arts Center in Seoul in 2014 and has now been reimagined as Franz & Marie for its 2026 production at Charing Cross Theatre.
With book and lyrics by Chris Broderick and music by Rob Shepherd and Chris Broderick, Franz & Marie is newly adapted by Teresa Howard, with additional music, arrangements and orchestrations by Steven Edis.
Franz & Marie is directed by Michael Oakley, with choreography by Ben Wright.
summary: Brenock O'Connor and Jade Oswald will star in the new musical adaptation 'Franz and Marie' at the Charing Cross Theatre. Inspired by Georg Büchner’s Woyzeck, the production features a feminist twist that places Marie alongside Franz at the narrative's heart. Set in late 19th-century Europe, the story follows a haunted soldier who undergoes medical experiments to support his family, leading to disastrous consequences. The 14-strong actor-muso company is rounded out by a full cast announced for the 2026 production.
key_points: Brenock O'Connor and Jade Oswald lead the 14-strong actor-muso company as Franz and Marie.
The new musical is inspired by Georg Büchner’s Woyzeck and features a feminist twist.
The production is set in a war-torn late 19th-century European outpost.
The score is an indie folk creation by Chris Broderick and Rob Shepherd, originally commissioned in Korea and reimagined for the Charing Cross Theatre in 2026.

title: Keeping London's canal boats afloat during summer drought
author: Leyla Hayes
content:
![A narrowboat on a canal approaches a lock, while a person stands beside the lock gates. Trees and vegetation line the waterway in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/6785/live/cef795b0-9d76-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Lock closures on the Grand Union canal have helped maintain water levels downstream
- Published
Drought conditions in the capital mean that London's waterways are being more actively managed to maintain water levels.
In west London on the Grand Union Canal, the gates of six locks known as the Hanwell Flight have been locked up at night with their paddles shut to prevent misuse that impacts the canal downstream.
Colin Beesley, waterway operative at Canal and River Trust, described the situation as "unprecedented", adding: "It's been one of the driest summers we've ever seen and of course there's been virtually no rain.
"Because this drought has been extending for so long, we've made the decision to lock this flight of locks overnight."
Additionally, all of the lock gates have been "ashed up", a traditional method of sealing gaps between planks in lock gates with coal dust to hold water in.
![Colin Beesley standing at a lock in west London.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0f3b/live/82be42b0-9e08-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Colin Beesley said the situation facing the waterways was "unprecedented"
The action on the Hanwell Flight has helped maintain water levels at the "Long Pound", a 27 mile (43.4km) lock-free stretch which encompasses the Grand Union Main Line, Paddington Arm and Regent's Canal all the way to Camden.
In east London, closures are also helping to manage the water levels.
Charlotte Wood, head of operations at the Canal and River Trust, explained that they have closed the Hertford Union Canal, a 1.2 mile (2km) long stretch of water that acts as a short-cut from the Regent's Canal to the River Lee, avoiding the River Thames.
Wood said the "non-critical" route near Victoria Park was closed so that water coming in from west London from the Hanwell Flight area and beyond went into central London.
"We're keeping the Regent's Canal open for as long as possible for our boats to move and to keep afloat," she added.
![Aerial view of a canal and lock flight running through a green open space, with buildings and housing visible in the distance.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/cd9c/live/c4dff240-9d88-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
A series of locks on the Grand Union Canal are shut at night to manage water levels
In Hanwell, boats are still allowed to travel through the canal during the day, but for boaters like Paul Findlay, the drought has made things much more challenging.
"It's kind of the new normal really," he said. "You have to get used to it in the summer months.
"It needs careful management by both the boaters and the people looking after the canals.
"If we work together we can help keep it as good as it can be."
![Paul Findlay in a navy and white striped top and a navy cap.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/44c7/live/fb49f0d0-9e08-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Boater Paul Findlay said people needed to work together under the drought conditions
Nicholas Jones, area operations manager at the Canal and River Trust, said they were using an app to monitor water levels, and were also keeping a close eye on the weather, adding that he was "deeply desperate" for rain to return to the capital.
"We get hopeful whenever it starts to speckle slightly, but it generally never arrives," he said.
This stretch of the Grand Union Canal has been open since 1794 - all the locks need now is more water to fill them.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Drought conditions in London have prompted the Canal and River Trust to actively manage water levels across the city's waterways. Measures include locking the Hanwell Flight gates at night, sealing lock gates with coal dust, and closing the Hertford Union Canal to preserve water for central London. These actions aim to keep boats afloat during an unprecedentedly dry summer.
key_points: The Hanwell Flight of six locks on the Grand Union Canal is locked overnight with paddles shut to prevent water misuse.
Lock gates are being "ashed up" with coal dust to seal gaps and retain water.
The Hertford Union Canal has been closed to direct water toward central London and keep the Regent's Canal open.
The Canal and River Trust is monitoring water levels and weather conditions using an app while waiting for rain.

title: Somerset woman 'saved' by thyroid cancer trial rides for hospital
author: Rachel Candlin
content:
![Julie smiling to the camera on a country lane with green fields, trees and cow parsley in the background. She is wearing a striped blue and mauve cycling jacket and is leaning against her black bike with a helmet in her hand.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/569/cpsprodpb/8877/live/9751d7d0-9d6f-11f1-bdcc-8926c4a74c43.png)
Julie Rose is cycling from her home town of Bridgwater to The Royal Marsden hospital
- Published
A woman, who said her life was saved by a new treatment for a rare cancer, has set herself the challenge of a long-distance cycle ride.
Julie Rose, 49, from Bridgwater, Somerset, was referred to The Royal Marsden Hospital after being diagnosed in 2020 with medullary thyroid cancer.
She was accepted onto a clinical trial, and within six months her tumours had shrunk by 60%.
She started the 186-mile ride in her home town on Friday and hopes to complete the challenge by arriving at the London hospital later.
Rose first started to notice symptoms while training for a half-marathon in March 2020.
"I started to get backache when I was running, but I'd had a hip replacement a few years previously and thought the pain was just wear and tear," she said.
Rose said her "world just stopped" when, a few months later, she found a lump in her neck and was told she had cancer.
"I have three children and a partner, and there were lots of tears â it was all very traumatic," she told BBC Somerset.
More from Somerset
Rose joined the clinical trial after the cancer had spread to her adrenal glands and liver.
"There were only about nine or 10 places in the UK," she said.
"I thought I had nothing to lose. It was either an old drug that made me poorly, or this new one that I was reading about.
"So, I took the gamble and got the new drug - that was May 2021, and I'm still on that medication now."
![Julie is standing outside a cafe holding her bicycle against a large plant pot. There are lots of picnic tables and parasols behind her on the tarmacked ground. She is wearing a pastel-coloured, patterned cycle shirt and is smiling to camera](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/64a0/live/16713d50-9d5f-11f1-a979-27696fc3a013.jpg)
Rose has returned to cycling after treatment
Rose, who has twice taken part in the London to Paris Cycle, said she was inspired to create her own unique challenge, supported by medical staff who had cared for her.
"I have good news at every scan, and some of my tumours have completely disappeared, so I wanted to make this [ride] personal," she said.
"I feel really well with this drug, and my body doesn't actually feel poorly. And the work they do at The Royal Marsden is just so important to raise money for."
The hospital has led research into advanced thyroid cancers, including ongoing clinical trials into different aspects of the disease.
Antonia Dalmahoy, the hospital charity's managing director, said: "Julie's incredible fundraising effort will contribute towards vital work at The Royal Marsden aimed at diagnosing cancer earlier and developing better, more personalised treatments for patients across the UK and the world."
summary: Julie Rose, a 49-year-old woman from Somerset, is undertaking an 186-mile cycle ride from her hometown to The Royal Marsden hospital to raise money. Rose was diagnosed with rare medullary thyroid cancer in 2020, but joined a clinical trial at the hospital in 2021 that successfully shrunk her tumours. Inspired by her ongoing successful treatment and positive scans, she decided to raise funds for the medical staff who cared for her.
key_points: Julie Rose was diagnosed with medullary thyroid cancer in 2020 after initially experiencing backache while training for a half-marathon.
She joined a clinical trial at The Royal Marsden hospital in May 2021, which resulted in her tumours shrinking by 60% within six months.
Rose is cycling 186 miles from Bridgwater to the London hospital to raise money for its vital research and treatment work.
Some of Rose's tumours have completely disappeared, and she continues to take the trial medication.

title: Camden Fringe 2026: If By Starlight – Museum of Comedy, London - The Reviews Hub
author: The Reviews Hub
content:
Writer and Director: Aissa Martell
If By Starlight follows Janelle (Kat de Leiros) and Jacob (Adrian Pel), two romantics who meet at a bar after separate tragic first dates and spend the rest of the piece explaining themselves to each other and to the audience, at jarring length. Janelle’s romantic hopes are pinned on a proclivity for astrology; a supposed Mercury retrograde or some sort of alignment of stars being evidence to Janelle that the proverbial tide will change on tonight’s date.
The show is littered with monologues feigning depth, with ornate vocabulary attempting to mask nonsensical metaphors, failing to logically follow from the preceding text – at one point, whilst referencing Janelle’s pet birds: ‘exotic lovebirds often outlive their humans, it must be a sign that this relationship will be good’. What?
Janelle’s opening story about her childhood crush, who she went off after he ate a bogey, resurfaces 11 times as a comparison for practically everything that follows, to the effect of: ‘at least he didn’t eat a bogey’, or ‘at least he’s not a snot-devouring monster’; the joke dies of exhaustion on its second beat. Jacob meanwhile nurses an attachment to vodka martinis that he insists is not a fetish, another weak ‘bit’ drained to death.
Two chairs and a table make up the entire set, and little is done with it to inspire anything meaningful. A mid-show detour sees Jacob disappear and argue with an unseen cat, vying for a laugh that never arrives. Pel’s cockney accent is a little contrived and, at times, the performance as a whole feels under-rehearsed.
Delivery on both sides stays flat long enough to suggest that the company and the writing have more soul-searching yet to do if If By Starlight has a future.
Reviewed on 22 August 2026
Camden Fringe 2026 runs until 30 August
summary: "If By Starlight," a play written and directed by Aissa Martell for the Camden Fringe 2026 at the Museum of Comedy, follows two romantics who meet after disastrous first dates. The production is criticized for its lengthy monologues, nonsensical metaphors, repetitive jokes, and under-rehearsed performances. Overall, the reviewers suggest the show requires significant soul-searching if it has any future.
key_points: The play features characters Janelle and Jacob, played by Kat de Leiros and Adrian Pel.
The script relies heavily on forced monologues and confusing metaphors, such as a weak running joke about a childhood crush eating a bogey.
The minimalist set consists of only two chairs and a table.
Performances by both actors were described as flat and under-rehearsed.

title: Ethnic minority victims make up 9 out of 10 unsolved murders in London, report shows
author: Shaun Wilson
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Met Police say knives used in three London murders within 24 hours](https://static.standard.co.uk/2023/09/27/12/POLICE%20Croydon%20%2012432766.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Ethnic minorities made up over 90 per cent of unsolved murders in London over a four-year period, according to new research.
An examination of unsolved homicides in the capital from 2019 to 2023 shows ethnic minorities represented 61 per cent of reported victims, as well as nearly 93 per cent of all unsolved murder victims.
Black people represented 83 per cent (36 incidents) of unsolved shootings as well as 73 per cent (39 incidents) of unsolved stabbings.
Read More
The analysis was carried out by Action on Armed Violence, which also discovered fatal shootings were more likely to go unsolved than stabbings, while the average age of homicide victims in the capital is 36.
However, for unsolved cases, the average victim’s age falls down to just 28.
Iain Overton, of Action on Armed Violence, stated: "Our data suggest that London’s unsolved murders are not evenly distributed. Instead, they are concentrated among young Black men and in cases involving firearm violence.
"While there are many reasons for why such murder investigations are especially difficult, the result must seem often clear to the victims’ families: those communities most affected by deadly violence are often the least likely to see those responsible brought to justice.
"This in itself risks deepening existing mistrust and creating the perception of unequal protection under the law. And that can’t be a good thing.”
The Met Police has argued the disparity in victims could be due to black people having less trust in the police than the rest of the population.
Despite the gloomy figures, the Met has a comparatively positive record in solving murders, with nine out of 10 killings resulting in a conviction. Meanwhile, the force reported 97 homicides in London last year, its lowest in a decade and a significant drop from 153 in 2019.
The Met’s head of homicide, commander Paul Brogden, said: “We know serious violence disproportionately affects certain communities, particularly young black men, who have the lowest trust in policing. This means sadly victims or witnesses are less likely to come forward and trust us.
“As this report outlines, that is an added complexity following shootings or stabbings on the streets, where identifying suspects requires more detailed investigative work, particularly when compared to domestic murders.
“While we use every tool at our disposal such as CCTV and forensics, often it’s witness evidence which can prove vital in securing convictions.”
summary: A recent report by Action on Armed Violence reveals that ethnic minorities accounted for nearly 93 percent of unsolved murders in London between 2019 and 2023. The data shows that young Black men and cases involving firearms are disproportionately represented among these unsolved homicides. While the Metropolitan Police maintain a high overall conviction rate and recorded a ten-year low in homicides last year, officials noted that lower trust in policing among affected communities creates investigative challenges.
key_points: Ethnic minorities made up over 90 percent of unsolved murders in London from 2019 to 2023.
Black people accounted for 83 percent of unsolved shootings and 73 percent of unsolved stabbings.
The average age of victims in unsolved cases drops to 28, compared to an overall average of 36.
Fatal shootings were found to be more likely to go unsolved than stabbings.
The Metropolitan Police attribute some investigative difficulties to lower trust in policing, which reduces witness cooperation.

title: London Assembly member calls for ban L Plate motorcyclist deliveries on London’s roads
author: Mark Brown
content:
Conservative Thomas Turrell described the motorcyclists as a “menace to the road” reports Kumail Jaffer, Local Democracy Reporter
![The City Hall building in Royal Docks with a cable car in the background](https://i0.wp.com/barnetpost.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/City-Hall-4.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1)
Motorcyclists without a full licence must be banned from operating in London, ministers have been told.
Currently, individuals are allowed to ride mopeds on a provisional licence following completion of a Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) course. The qualification, which usually takes a single day to obtain, is valid for two years and can be renewed repeatedly without any requirement to progress to a full driving test.
Last month the London Assembly passed a motion calling on the Government to prohibit the use of provisional licences for commercial work, including food delivery driving, to improve safety for all road users.
The same motion, proposed by Conservative Assembly Member Thomas Turrell, also demanded an expiry cap on the CBT certification so that riders are incentivised to progress to a full licence.
“The CBT was built as a way for people to learn the roads and build up that knowledge,” he told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).
“Because you can’t learn on a bike the same way you’re learning a car, because with a car [you are] with an instructor who will have his own set of pedals.
“It wasn’t built for indefinite use. You’ve got people who are now working into delivery drivers, commercially working on the roads. This is not a qualification to drive on the road. We’ve got to end that practice.
“It is clear these are a menace to the road – if I’m in Bromley Town Centre, and I’m going home, I will see multiple offences on the way home, L plate motorbikes mounting the pavement, for example.
“This is dangerous behaviour from people who think they are ready to drive on the road because they’ve done their CBT.
“But they just aren’t, and that’s the real problem in this, that they’re not ready to drive on the road because this is their basic qualification, and there is no incentive to get that full licence.”
Turrell said the issue was one he and Sir Sadiq Khan were “quite aligned on”, and that he hoped ministers “have the stomach” to take this problem on.
In 2022, the Mayor of London told assembly members that he “firmly believes” that the current CBT is “not fit for purpose and is not an appropriate level of qualification, particularly for those driving for work”.
He claimed TfL has no powers to regulate private companies, meaning the authority could not mandate couriers to ride on a full licence. These powers lie at a national level.
Earlier this year ministers launched a consultation on changes to moped and motorcycle training, which could involve CBT certificate reform.
Rebecca Paul, the MP for Reigate, attempted to table an amendment to the Crime and Policing Act, which was passed in April, to ban learner moped drivers from undertaking commercial activity using the roads. However, it was unsuccessful.
Louie French, the MP for Old Bexley and Sidcup, told the LDRS: “The Labour Government has lost control of delivery drivers abusing the L plate system.
“High streets and roads across the country are now littered with men using mopeds to deliver food.
“The Government must urgently grip this situation to ensure that all delivery drivers are working here legally and are not endangering other road users.”
Turrell said the biggest barrier to reform may be “pushback” from major employers such as Just Eat, Deliveroo and Uber.
“It’ll be interesting to see whether the government do have the stomach to take this on,” he added.
“They’ve been consulting on it, so I couldn’t say whether or not they’re dragging their feet or reluctant for sure, but I think it will be telling over the coming months to find out whether this is something that they want to get their teeth stuck into.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “As part of our road safety strategy, the DVSA consulted on reforms to moped and motorcycle training and testing, including whether there should be a time limit on CBT certification. We are now analysing the responses, with the aim of improving safety and modernising motorcycling.”
A Just Eat spokesperson said: “The safety of all road users is extremely important to Just Eat.
“Last year we were the first food delivery platform to partner with the leading road safety charity Brake, and we provide regular guidance on safety and responsible behaviour.
“We actively support stronger regulation and robust enforcement to tackle modified e-bikes and requiring moped riders to have a full licence. We remain committed to working with authorities and our industry peers to ensure the roads are safe for all users.”
Deliveroo and Uber Eats were contacted for comment.

Proposed by Conservative Assembly Member Thomas Turrell, the motion also demands an expiry cap on Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) certificates to encourage riders to get full licences. Supporters argue that indefinite CBT usage leads to dangerous road behavior, while the Department for Transport stated it is analyzing responses to a recent consultation on moped training reforms.

title: Barbican Conservatory to give away 2,000 free plant cuttings
author: Ruth Comerford
content:
![Artist impression of the new Barbican Conservatory  issued by City of London Corporation, showing a modern staircase, plants and people gathered on wide paths.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a7d9/live/77d96330-9bb4-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
The venue is preparing for its multi-million pound restoration
- Published
The Barbican Conservatory is offering free plant cuttings to the public, ahead of its three-year closure for restoration in January.
More than 2,000 plant cuttings will be available to people who have booked online on Wednesday, with two more opportunities to collect plants scheduled later in the year.
The Grade II listed arts venue is to undergo a Â£231m overhaul, including the development of a climate-controlled habitat to support plant health.
Barbican chief operating officer Dr Philippa Simpson said the conservatory restoration was focused on "creating a healthier home for plants and enabling more people to enjoy the environment and the activities it will host".
Opened in 1984, the multi-storey glasshouse is home to 800 species of plant.
Monstera, ficus, and purple-and-green tradescantia are among the cuttings that will be shared with the public, in collaboration with Wayward Plants Reuse Centre.
The first plant adoption event is being held on Wednesday. Two more events are planned for 13 September and 2 December and must be booked in advance via the Barbican website.
Each event will include information about about the Conservatory's architectural history and the development of its plant collection.
Under the redevelopment plans, there will be a new lift and staircase in the conservatory to allow public access to raised balconies. It will also be relandscaped to encourage optimal plant-growing conditions, and the building will be made fully accessible.
The Barbican's distinctive brutalist foyers and lakeside terrace will also be developed to protect the heritage of the building.
![People sit in by an indoor leafy pond in an artist's impression of the Barbican conservatory.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b4fc/live/ba27b8e0-9bb4-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
A number of accessibility issues will be addressed in the revamp
The Conservatory currently opens several times a month, but from 2030 it will be open on a daily basis. Entry will continue to be free.
Simpson said the restoration was focused on "creating a healthier home for plants and enabling more people to enjoy the environment and the activities it will host".
"Each cutting is the beginning of something new, and as thousands of plants start putting down roots across London, we'll be laying the foundations for a greener, more resilient and more welcoming Conservatory than ever before," she added.

summary: The Barbican Conservatory is giving away more than 2,000 free plant cuttings ahead of its upcoming three-year closure for a multi-million pound restoration starting in January. The Grade II listed venue will undergo a £231m overhaul to improve plant health, accessibility, and architectural features, including the addition of a climate-controlled habitat. The first plant adoption event takes place on Wednesday, with two additional events scheduled for later in the year.
key_points: The Barbican Conservatory is offering over 2,000 free plant cuttings to the public prior to its closure in January.
The venue is set to undergo a £231m restoration to create a climate-controlled habitat and improve accessibility.
Plant adoption events require online booking in advance, with dates scheduled for Wednesday, 13 September, and 2 December.
Following the completion of the revamp, the conservatory is planned to open on a daily basis from 2030 while maintaining free entry.

title: ACORN members challenge Government's cost of living promise with action against Greystar in London - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
ACORN members in London took action against Greystar yesterday (20/08/26), a multi-billion pound build to rent developer, demanding they freeze their rents and give their tenants collective bargaining power, as part of a coordinated national Day of Action over the cost of living.
Members demonstrated outside of Greystar’s offices in Finsbury Square, demanding to meet with and put our demands to their UK Director Thomasin Renshaw. Renshaw refused to meet with us, and instead Greystar put the building into lockdown. Greystar have been contributing to and profiting from the housing crisis across the UK, using AI to inflate the rents in its over 50,000 properties.
This action was one of nine taking place across England and Wales as part of ACORN’s national Day of Action on the cost of living. Across the country, members are taking on energy companies, water companies, bailiffs and landlords, who ACORN says are profiting while ordinary people struggle to afford the basics.
ACORN says that if the Government is serious about being a “cost of living government”, it must take on those profiting from essential needs and bring down the cost of the basics.
The union is calling for a cap on rents, the writing off of unaffordable energy and water debt built up during the cost of living crisis and the replacement of council tax with a fairer proportional property tax.
Callum Waterhouse, Comms Officer at ACORN Islington, said:
“We took the fight to Greystar today and showed them that we won’t stand for them profiteering from the housing crisis while so many people suffer. They showed that they would rather cower in their offices than come out and speak to us, but they should know ACORN aren’t going anywhere.”
summary: ACORN members in London demonstrated outside Greystar's offices on August 20, demanding rent freezes and collective bargaining power as part of a national Day of Action on the cost of living. Greystar refused to meet with the protesters and placed their building into lockdown. The nationwide protests targeted entities accused of profiting from the housing and cost of living crises, with ACORN calling on the government to cap rents, write off essential utility debt, and replace council tax with a proportional property tax.
key_points: ACORN members protested outside Greystar's London offices demanding rent freezes and collective bargaining.
Greystar refused to meet with the demonstrators and put their building into lockdown.
The demonstration was part of a coordinated national Day of Action across England and Wales addressing the cost of living crisis.
ACORN is urging the government to cap rents, write off utility debt, and replace council tax with a fairer property tax.

title: TV Dr, Amir Khan, calls on the Government to end postcode healthcare inequality - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
TV star Dr Amir Khan has called on the Government to end postcode lottery healthcare inequality across the UK.
The media medic and author has described life expectancy disparities as a “national crisis” after it emerged those living in affluent places like Marylebone and Berkhamsted are living up to 18 years longer than those in generally poorer areas like Blackpool and Glasgow.
Having been raised himself in a working-class inner-city area of Bradford, he argued “health (care) starts long before someone walks into a GP surgery.”
The TV doctor, who has teamed with Health Equals [https://healthequals.org.uk/shelf-life/], a campaigning coalition group aiming to improve health equality opportunities across the UK, added: “I don’t just see the impact of health inequalities in my work as a GP, I’ve lived them too.
“Today, I see these same challenges affecting many of my patients. I see people living in damp homes, struggling with financial insecurity or juggling multiple jobs, and I see the impact that can have on their health.”
To raise awareness of the group’s work he unveiled a “traffic-stopping” ‘Shelf Life’ installation in Old Spitalfields Market in East London yesterday [Tuesday August 18].
The activation featured oversized supermarket-style packaging displaying reduced ‘expiry dates’ based on life expectancy figures from different parts of the country, highlighting how some people are effectively losing years off their life.
He said: “We’re very good at treating illness, it is shaped by things like our homes, jobs, education and local environment. Your postcode shouldn’t determine your shelf life. But right now, in the UK, it does.
“That’s why these figures should be considered a national crisis, and why we need governments to commit to meaningful action to tackle the root causes of poor health and health inequalities.”
The life expectancy figures in the activation comes from analysis of an ONS report on ‘health state life expectancy estimates’ for those born in England between 2019 and 2023.
They were calculated from criteria including housing quality, air pollution, financial pressures and local living conditions – all believed to significantly influence how long someone lives.
With life spans in more affluent areas life Marylebone and Berkhamsted estimated to be up to 88 years of age – 18 years more than they are in areas like Glasgow and Grimsby, where 70 is the average.
In a poll of 2,000 adults, also commissioned by Health Equals, it emerged almost all appear to share Dr Khan’s concerns – 95 per cent agreed the difference in life expectancy across the UK is a problem.
With education (65 per cent), access to transport (57 per cent) and access to affordable healthy food (92 per cent) among the most significant factors influencing lifespan, according to respondents.
Actor and TV presenter, Will Mellor, who is also supporting the campaign, added: “It’s shocking to think that there’s an 18-year gap in life expectancy between some communities across the UK.
“Having grown up on a council estate in Stockport, that’s difficult to get my head around.
“Two people from different parts of the UK can be working hard, doing their best, and yet one could still live so many years fewer than the other.
“What really struck me about this campaign is seeing the data broken down to such a local level. It stops being just a set of statistics and becomes about the places we live, work and raise our families.
“I’d encourage everyone to check their own postcode on the Health Equals website because the results are genuinely eye-opening.
“When you see the difference between communities that can be just a few miles apart, the issue becomes impossible to ignore.”
Of those who took part in the study by OnePoll.com, only 21 per cent think that the government is doing enough to help reduce inequalities in health between people in different postcodes in the UK.
Paul McDonald, director of Health Equals, which is calling on our new Prime Minister to change the law to make it a legal duty to create better health in every postal area, added: “Your postcode shouldn’t determine your shelf life, but in the UK, it does.
“Let’s not forget that behind these figures are real people with families, loved ones, jobs, hobbies, and their lives are being cut short because of things out of their control – this should be considered a national crisis.
“This isn’t just bad luck or down to individual choices, it’s because too many people don’t have access to the basics that help us stay healthy.
“And these inequalities don’t just affect individuals, they hold back families, jobs and our economy, and put pressure on services like the NHS.
“Our health should be a national priority, and change is possible. We are calling for a change in the law to make improving health and tackling inequalities a legal duty for this and future governments.
“If Andy Burnham is serious about creating good growth in every British postcode, this will be one of his first priorities in Number 10.”
summary: TV doctor Amir Khan has urged the UK Government to address postcode healthcare inequality, which he described as a national crisis. Teaming up with the Health Equals coalition, he highlighted that residents in affluent areas can live up to 18 years longer than those in poorer regions. The campaign calls for government action and a change in the law to make reducing health inequalities a legal duty.
key_points: An 18-year life expectancy gap exists between affluent areas like Marylebone and poorer regions like Blackpool, Glasgow, and Grimsby.
Dr Amir Khan and Health Equals unveiled an installation in East London featuring oversized supermarket packaging with reduced expiry dates based on life expectancy data.
A poll of 2,000 adults showed that 95 percent view the difference in life expectancy as a problem, while only 21 percent believe the government is doing enough.
Health Equals is calling on the government to make improving health and tackling regional inequalities a legal duty.

title: Learn about Luke Thompson's stage work ahead of 'The Lives of Others' | London Theatre
author: Julia Rank
content:
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/4AlBqkwft15CAxtJCXYydb/1cfae49741c46d42dc02080bc60517f8/the_lives_of_others_1200_LT.jpg?h=200&fm=webp&q=90)
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/4AlBqkwft15CAxtJCXYydb/1cfae49741c46d42dc02080bc60517f8/the_lives_of_others_1200_LT.jpg?h=550&fm=webp&q=90)
Learn about Luke Thompson's stage work ahead of 'The Lives of Others'
The Bridgerton star and Olivier nominee stars opposite Keira Knightley in Robert Icke's stage adaptation of The Lives of Others this autumn.
Summary
- Luke Thompson made his professional debut at Shakespeare's Globe in 2013
- He has worked with Robert Icke on Oresteia and Hamlet
- He was nominated for an Olivier Award for A Little Life
- Thompson stars in The Lives of Others opposite Keira Knightley this autumn
![Julia Rank](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/2g43hngoF3VTSOpS4ulTL3/1e21bed173775dce4996de773a4f4370/julia_rank-200.jpg?w=32&h=32)
Born in Southampton in 1988, Luke Thompson was raised mostly in France. He studied English and Drama at the University of Bristol prior to training at RADA. He made his professional stage debut in 2013.
To date, Thompson is best known for his role as Benedict Bridgerton, the aristocratic Regency-era dynasty’s artistic second son, in the hit Netflix romantic costume drama Bridgerton. He had his opportunity to take the lead in the most recent season earlier this year as the Prince Charming to Yerin Ha’s Cinderella-esque Sophie.
This autumn, Thompson returns to the West End in Robert Icke’s The Lives of Others alongside Keira Knightley and Stephen Dillane. Read on to learn more about his impressive theatre credits to date.
Book The Lives of Others tickets on LondonTheatre.co.uk.
A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Blue Stockings
In 2013, Thompson made his professional theatre debut with two shows at Shakespeare’s Globe. He played young lover Lysander in A Midsummer Night’s Dream directed by Dominic Dromgoole, then the venue’s artistic director, which also featured the Globe’s current artistic director Michelle Terry as Titania. The production was filmed for posterity and Thompson was nominated as Best Newcomer in the Evening Standard Theatre Awards and for an Ian Charleson Award.
Thompson also appeared in Blue Stockings by Jessica Swale (Paddington The Musical), about the female students of Girton College, Cambridge who fought for the right to be awarded degrees in 1897. He played Will, the protagonist Tess’s (Ellie Piercy) potential love interest.
Julius Caesar
Thompson returned to the Globe the following year as Mark Antony in Julius Caesar, again directed by Dominic Dromgoole. LondonTheatre.co.uk’s reviewer was mightily impressed with his performance: “Luke Thompson's clear, fresh delivery is a constant delight, particularly his sensitively modern phrasing of Shakespeare, allowing the most familiar of Mark Antony's fine speeches to strike us anew (and gaining a great, and appropriate, roar of laughter at his mendacious ‘I am no orator’).”
Tiger Country
Later in the year, Thompson appeared in Nina Raine’s A&E-set play Tiger Country at Hampstead Theatre. Thompson played James, a junior doctor. The cast also featured Indira Varma as an ambitious registrar.
Oresteia
In 2015, Thompson first worked with director Robert Icke on Aeschylus’ Oresteia, which was part of Icke’s Greeks Season at the Almeida Theatre. LondonTheatre.co.uk’s reviewer admired “The naturalism in both Luke Thompson and Angus Wright's portrayals of Orestes and Agamemnon” and called it “one of the finest pieces of theatre I've ever seen”.
Hamlet
Thompson and Icke worked together again in 2017, when Thompson played Laertes to Andrew Scott’s Hamlet in a production that was set in a modern surveillance state. LondonTheatre.co.uk’s reviewer singled Thompson out for praise: “There's an excitement in Luke Thompson's Laertes that refreshes the stage and commands a new energy as the tragedy bounds towards its conclusion. His relationship with Ophelia reads as one of the most believable on stage.”
King Lear
When Jonathan Munby’s staging of King Lear was first performed at Chichester Festival Theatre, Thompson’s future Bridgerton brother Jonathan Bailey played Edgar. Thompson took over the role for its West End transfer in 2019. The production showcased a “superlative” performance from Ian McKellen in the title role.
![A Little Life - LT - 1200](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/342eABz2AU0CIyjtEmmIVd/9ccec98337f0c32e4d88b3c95d63fdfc/image.jpg)
A Little Life
After achieving mainstream fame with Bridgerton in 2020, Thompson returned to the stage in 2023 in Ivo Van Hove’s four-hour-long stage adaptation of Hanya Yanagihara’s harrowing novel A Little Life. James Norton, Omari Douglas, Elliot Cowan, and Thompson played four friends in New York City with numerous traumas. According to LondonTheatre.co.uk’s reviewer: “Luke Thompson plays the beating heart of the piece: Jude’s best friend and confidant Willem. Thompson must usher the character from apathetic party boy to deeply intellectual and empathetic partner, and he is present and rooted in the show’s message of love throughout.” He received an Olivier nomination for Best Supporting Actor in a Play.
Love’s Labour’s Lost
In 2024, Thompson made his Royal Shakespeare Company debut as the witty Berowne in Shakespeare’s early comedy Love’s Labour Lost. The production was directed by Emily Burns (soon to direct Hay Fever in the West End), who reimagined the kingdom of Navarre as a luxury wellness resort in Hawaii.
The Lives of Others
This autumn, Thompson reunites with Robert Icke for the world premiere of the stage adaptation of German filmmaker Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s film The Lives of Others. Set in East Berlin in 1984, Thompson plays playwright Georg Dreyman, who is spied on by Stasi officer Gerd Wiesler (Stephen Dillane). Keira Knightley plays his girlfriend and leading lady Christa-Maria Sieland. It’s sure to be one of the biggest challenges of Thompson’s career to date, with another truly complex character to embody.

title: Man, 34, arrested on suspicion of murder after west London house fire leaves one woman dead and another critical | LBC
author: Jacob Paul
content:
Man, 34, arrested on suspicion of murder after west London house fire leaves one woman dead and another critical
Eight people were injured in the blaze in Hounslow, west London.
A 34-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a woman died and a further eight people were taken to hospital following a house fire in west London.
Listen to this article
Officers were called to reports of a fire at a property on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 1.14am on Wednesday.
A 48-year-old woman died in hospital and another woman, 40, remains in a life-threatening condition, the Metropolitan Police said.
Six men and one woman who were taken to hospital have since been discharged with minor injuries, the force added.
The man was arrested by Kent Police on Sunday while he was travelling to France by train, and remains in custody.
Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, who is leading the investigation, said: âOur thoughts remain first and foremost with the victimâs family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured.
âOur investigation is continuing at pace and we have arrested one man in connection with the incident.
Read more: Murder investigation launched after human remains found after wildfire
Read more: Murder inquiry launched after woman dies and eight others injured in fire
âDetectives are continuing to build a full picture of the circumstances surrounding the incident and are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry.
âWe continue to ask any witnesses or anyone with information about the incident to please contact us as soon as possible.â
Images from the scene showed a light-coloured terraced house that was blackened on the outside, with window panes peeling and part of the upstairs eaves apparently melted.
The door appeared badly affected and the fire damage reaches the neighbouring house.
Anyone with information or footage that may assist the investigation is urged to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 359/19Aug, or reach out anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or online at crimestoppers-uk.org.
summary: A 34-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following a house fire in Hounslow, west London, that resulted in the death of a 48-year-old woman. Another woman remains in critical condition, while seven other people were treated for minor injuries and discharged. The suspect was apprehended by Kent Police on Sunday while traveling to France by train and remains in custody as the investigation continues.
key_points: A 34-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder by Kent Police while traveling to France.
A 48-year-old woman died in the hospital following the house fire on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow.
A second woman, aged 40, remains in a life-threatening condition.
Six men and one woman suffered minor injuries and have been discharged from the hospital.
Police are appealing for witnesses and anyone with information or footage to contact them.

title: Camden Fringe 2026: Renée Rossi: God Bomb – Hens & Chickens, London - The Reviews Hub
author: The Reviews Hub
content:
Renée Rossi’s explosive satire God Bomb questions the credentials of many Catholic saints. Taking pot shots at Mother Teresa, this one-woman show tackling some of the most difficult religious questions can, at its best, produce clever and biting jokes that question the very pillars of Father, Son or Holy Spirit. At other times, falling short of the mark, the sketches can be confusing or over-the-top and force an agenda rather than making a nuanced point about the big guy upstairs.
With an armoury of sketches, quips and original forms of roleplay, Rossi’s comical ammunition works with various effects. Sometimes it’s a blast and other times, well, it’s more of a tiny crackle.
It all kicks off when she stands in front of a panel and interviews for the role of one of God’s representatives on earth as a saint. Recycling and abortion rights are what she wants to become patrons of, and Rossi, weaving them into the piece like a musical motif, makes sure she returns to these points continuously when she’s confronted with many of God’s officials.
The audience then enjoys other short and snappy scenes where she auditions for the Nativity, plays Mary as a modern Italian-American and works with the first manuscript of the Bible as a publisher. Make sure to watch out for the incredibly light audience participation that’s missing from the show’s marketing as well.
Rossi certainly gives every biblical or religious character her all and has endless energy, matched with a great stage presence. A director is missing, however, throughout the performance. Rossi brings a box of many different tricks as a writer, but as the work nears its end, the characters blend too much into each other. Adam is too similar to Eve. The snake slithering through the Garden of Eden is not that much unlike Jesus rocking his body around an office to escape having to sleep with nuns, and one saint is often indistinguishable from the other.
She’s not afraid to be inventive with each part of the stage: an apple hangs from the exit door, halos poke out from the back stage, and Rossi will freely come up into the seating area for the audience. It’s a brave, in-your-face kind of theatre that she creates.
Overall, Rossi’s world premiere has a lot of potential for its first showing. Her work is original in form and subject matter and is occasionally laugh-out-loud funny. Yet, there’s work still to be done on each component. But with a touch here and there, it will make for a treat for any theatre-goer.
Runs until 23 August 2026
Camden Fringe 2026 runs until 30 August
summary: Renée Rossi's one-woman satire "God Bomb" at the Camden Fringe 2026 questions Catholic saints and religious pillars through a series of comedic sketches and roleplay. The world premiere features inventive staging and high energy, though some sketches feel forced and characters begin to blend together due to a lack of direction. Overall, the show demonstrates strong potential with clever, biting humor while still needing refinement.
key_points: Renée Rossi stars in the one-woman satirical show "God Bomb" at the Camden Fringe 2026.
The premise involves Rossi interviewing to become a saint and seeking patronage over recycling and abortion rights.
The performance features varied sketches, light audience participation, and inventive use of the stage space.
Reviewers noted a lack of a director, causing characters to blend together toward the end of the show.
The production runs until August 23, 2026, as part of the Camden Fringe.

title: Sourdough Sophia announces new bakery opening in Covent Garden - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
On Wednesday 29th July, Sourdough Sophia – the award-winning London based micro bakery – will open its seventh site in Neal’s Yard, Covent Garden. To celebrate, Sourdough Sophia will be giving away FREE goody bags to the first 200 customers on opening day.
Founded by husband-and-wife duo Sophia and Jesse in their North London dining room during lockdown, Sourdough Sophia has quickly expanded and built a loyal following for its high-quality sourdough bread and artisanal pastries, with other sites in Highgate, Hampstead, Crouch End, Essex Road, Primrose Hill and Bermondsey.
Now, Sourdough Sophia brings the delicious baked goods that they are known for to one of London’s most vibrant and central destinations, Covent Garden – 16 Neal’s Yard, WC2H 9DP. To celebrate the opening of the new location, Sourdough Sophia is offering FREE goody bags worth over £30 to the first 200 customers through the door on opening day. The surprises don’t stop at the treats inside the bag – those who claim a goody bag will be in with a chance to win one of five golden tickets, allowing each of them one free cruffin per week, for a year!
The new location will serve up the same decadent and fresh baked goods that Sourdough Sophia is known for, from its wide range of bread varieties to the classic and innovative pastries – including the Passion Fruit Bow and the Strawberry Cruffins. Covent Garden will also sell the brand’s range of savoury items, such as the Smoked Salmon Bun and Courgette Danish – perfect for those looking for a delicious bakery item for lunch.
Exclusive to the Covent Garden location will be the Ice Cream Cruffin Cup – soft, buttery, pillowy interior with a flaky and sugared exterior acting as the perfect cup for a scoop of creamy and thick, soft serve ice cream.
Alongside the bakes, the Covent Garden site will continue to serve a speciality coffee and drinks menu, from hot teas to chilled options, including the Iced Ube Latte with Cold Foam – perfect for summer days strolling in the city.
Following the expansion of the Crouch End site, the opening of the Covent Garden store proves Sourdough Sophia’s commitment to growing the brand’s presence and community across London, continuing to be one of the capital’s stand-out bakeries.
Walk don’t run to Sourdough Sophia in Covent Garden on July 29th to claim free goodies.
summary: Award-winning micro bakery Sourdough Sophia is opening its seventh location in Neal's Yard, Covent Garden, on Wednesday, July 29th. Founded by husband-and-wife duo Sophia and Jesse, the new shop will offer their signature breads, artisanal pastries, savoury items, and exclusive menu additions like the Ice Cream Cruffin Cup. To celebrate the launch, the first 200 customers will receive free goody bags worth over £30, with five bags containing golden tickets for a free cruffin every week for a year.

The first 200 customers on opening day will receive free goody bags valued at over £30.
Five of the opening day goody bags will include golden tickets for one free cruffin per week for a year.
