title: Londoners face Government home inspections as part of mansion tax enforcement
author: Rachael Burford
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Homeowners who refuse would be committing a criminal offence and could be fined.
Inspectors will gather information on the size and style of a house, as well as the number of floors, bedrooms and bathrooms.
Properties could be visited multiple times to ensure valuation data is up to date.
The Tories branded the scheme “sinister”, but the Government argued that the Valuation Office has “extensive experience in valuing domestic property”.
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced in her Budget last year that properties worth more than £2 million face an annual charge of between £2,500 and £7,500 from 2028.
London homeowners are expected to be hardest hit by the mansion tax, known officially as the high-value council tax surcharge.
Estimates show that households in just four boroughs - Kensington and Chelsea, Wandsworth, Richmond upon Thames and Westminster - will pay £270 million a year, half of what the Government predicts the tax will raise nationally.
Treasury minister Dan Tomlinson confirmed that homeowners faced the Valuation Office contacting them to “arrange a visit”.
The Government said property visits would take place by prior agreement with the owner.
A spokesman added: “The public understands that we are addressing a longstanding unfairness, where a Band D home in Darlington pays more in council tax than a £10m mansion in Mayfair.
Read More
“The Valuation Office has extensive experience valuing domestic property, and will use a wide range of evidence to determine bandings.”
But shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said: “This is sinister. Not content with ramping up taxes on hardworking families Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner will send tax inspectors to snoop around people’s homes.
“This is a massive expansion of state snooping and an invasion of privacy.
“Hard-working families and pensioners face the prospect of HMRC tax inspectors snooping around their gardens and inside their homes, to justify hiking taxes on them.
“Even homes which are below the new tax thresholds face these intrusive checks, with the threat of criminal prosecutions and fines if people refuse.”
Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride added: “We may have changed Prime Minister, but it’s the same old story with Labour: how can we raise taxes to pay for more benefits? Now they have chosen a sinister assault on civil liberties as their latest method.
“Burnham and Rayner are sending their council tax police to people’s homes so they can drag them into paying their new family homes tax.
“This is a tax on aspiration, on working hard and investing well, and Labour will stop at nothing to make as many people as possible liable for it.”
The leaders of Richmond, Westminster, Kensington and Chelsea and Wandsworth councils last week wrote to new Chancellor John Healey to warn that their residents will be “disproportionately affected” by the proposals compared to other areas of the UK.
They argued that it will hit pensioners who have lived in their homes for decades the hardest.
“A home is the centre of family life, not an untapped tax stream”, the leaders of the four boroughs wrote in a letter Mr Healey.
“Our residents have often lived in the same home for decades.
“They have raised families there, built communities and lasting connections, and in many cases have seen the value of their homes rise even as their incomes have stayed flat or fallen. It is simply wrong to assume that everyone living in these homes is wealthy.
“Many are not, and under this proposal, some will be forced to sell the family home simply to meet the tax.”
summary: London homeowners face government property inspections by the Valuation Office as part of the enforcement for a new high-value council tax surcharge on homes worth over £2 million, announced by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves. Refusing the inspections will be a criminal offence subject to fines. While the Government defends the measure as addressing longstanding unfairness, Conservative critics and local council leaders have condemned the plan as an invasion of privacy that will disproportionately and unfairly impact Londoners and pensioners.
key_points: Properties worth more than £2 million face an annual charge between £2,500 and £7,500 starting in 2028.
Refusing home inspections by the Valuation Office will be a criminal offence punishable by fines.
Households in just four London boroughs are expected to pay half of the tax's national revenue.
Conservative politicians criticized the inspections as a sinister invasion of privacy and an expansion of state snooping.
Council leaders warned that the tax will hit pensioners hard who have lived in their homes for decades and seen values rise while incomes remained flat.

title: Meet the brothers giving away houses for the price of a raffle ticket
author: Meghann Murdock
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Have London house prices really become more affordable?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/10/49/Daniel-Will-and-Jay-Twenefour.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![Homes & Property](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_hnp_embed_desktop.png)
Unable to find a buyer for his home in Mitcham, Daniel Twenefour was on the brink of bankruptcy six years ago. Sale after sale fell through as Covid restrictions came into force and the housing market ground to a juddering halt with no real indication as to when it might be back up and running.
The property, which Twenefour had bought and renovated using savings and a bridging loan, was near a tram stop which deterred lenders from offering mortgages to interested buyers. The bank demanded the return of Twenefour’s £370,000 loan and was threatening to seize his personal assets.
He describes the time as an “absolute nightmare”, which left him searching for ways to clear his debt, even if it meant losing his deposit and the cost of renovations. “I was desperate. I just wanted to get the loan off my back,” he says. Twenefour decided to try to raffle the house at £2 a ticket. Providing he sold 200,000 tickets, he would have enough to clear his loan and pass on the house to a new owner with the stamp duty and legal fees paid.
“I just wanted to get the loan off my back”
Ticket sales were slow to start with. Londoners are dubious of anything that sounds too good to be true, but eventually Twenefour was able to raise enough money to give the house away as planned and fully cover his costs as well. It was a move borne out of desperation, but one that has sparked a new career as the creator of property prize company Tramway Path.
Drawing on his background in tech project management and property, Twenefour, 35, launched the house giveaway company with the help of his brothers Jay, 41, and Will, 40, who both still work full-time in their respective industries.
![Daniel, Will and Jay Twenefour poses together](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/10/49/Daniel-Will-and-Jay-Twenefour.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Property raffles are often linked to glossy trophy homes with flash amenities that cost a fortune to run — nice on paper but hardly affordable for the many ticket buyers hoping a lucky punt might get them a foothold on the housing ladder when their own earning power falls short. Questions have also been raised about how many homes are actually handed over to winners, rather than a percentage of ticket sales being offered as a cash prize — usually after hefty marketing costs have been deducted.
Twenefour says that the Tramway Path model is different in that winners can choose whether to accept the property or choose a guaranteed cash prize to buy something more suitable for them. In their current draw, the choice is between a three-bedroom home in Bexleyheath valued at £650,000 or £500,000 towards an alternative property, an amount which Twenefour says does not depend on ticket sales. “They need to be able to choose the place they believe they can call home,” says Twenefour. “We’re not expecting a winner from Manchester to uproot their entire lives and move down to London.”
Properties are selected by area, proximity to local transport links and condition — usually recently renovated or mid renovation. They have a minimum of two bedrooms and, ideally, come with parking. The purchase is under way at the time of the draw so winners can decide to take ownership of the featured property or choose somewhere more suitable.
What to look our for
- As prize competitions are not regulated by the Gambling Commission, it can’t provide advice on whether a competition is safe to enter but advises caution.
- A property raffle must either be a competition requiring some skill on the part of the entrant — often by way of answering a question correctly at the point of buying tickets — or competitions can be classed as a free draw provided that some of the entries are free. The free route must be no more expensive to achieve (i.e. via post or a paid text number) and no less convenient than the paid entry route.
- Make sure stamp duty, any additional tax and legal fees are paid for by the seller.
The brothers have given away 20 homes so far, with 13 winners now living in London. The rest are spread across Essex, Kent, Wales, Cumbria and Bristol. The road hasn’t been without its twists and turns, and occasionally the brothers have had to use their own money to make up the shortfall between ticket sales and the property price or promised cash prize. The cash prize needs to be put towards the purchase of a home, says Twenefour, but if a winner chooses a property which costs less than the prize amount then they are transferred the remaining balance.
The aim is to raise enough through ticket sales to pay themselves, their team and their marketing costs, which Twenefour says can be as much as half the value of the home they’re giving away. Previous winners have included one Londoner who has just started searching for their own home to buy with the cash prize; another Londoner who moved into their raffle home in Surrey and was featured on Channel 4’s My £2 Dream Home; and a software developer apprentice who bought a two-bedroom garden flat on the same street as his parents’ home in Elephant and Castle.
The current draw, for a three-bedroom house in Bexleyheath valued at £650,000 or £500,000 cash towards the cost of another home ends on September 14. Tickets start at £10 for 10. The winner is chosen using random.org, a platform which selects a ticket number at random, in the presence of an independent solicitor and livestreamed on social channels.
![Bexleyheath  home in the  current draw](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/10/31/Bexleyheath-home-in-the-current-draw.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Ongoing uncertainty in the housing market has dampened sales momentum and it’s easy to see why sellers and first-time buyers may turn to raffles. But while the idea of getting on the property ladder for less than a round of drinks holds obvious appeal, the reality is that property raffles are a gamble at very low odds. A bit of fun, best approached with caution and a hefty dose of realism.
summary: Faced with bankruptcy and unable to sell his Mitcham home due to pandemic restrictions and lender issues, Daniel Twenefour successfully raffled the property for £2 a ticket. This experience led him and his brothers to launch the property prize company Tramway Path, which has since given away 20 homes. Winners can choose between taking the featured property or a guaranteed cash prize to buy a home more suitable for them.
key_points: Daniel Twenefour created the first property raffle out of desperation to clear a £370,000 loan after failing to find a buyer for his Mitcham home.
He and his brothers, Jay and Will, subsequently launched the property prize company Tramway Path, giving away 20 homes so far.
Unlike many property raffles, Tramway Path winners can choose between the physical property or a guaranteed cash prize to buy an alternative home.
Prize competitions are not regulated by the Gambling Commission, and experts advise participants to approach them with caution.

title: London bus strikes to resume next week after drivers reject deal offer
author: Rachael Burford
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![London bus strike chaos: Over 1,500 drivers strike over heatwave working conditions](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/37/IMG_20260814_091450-(1).jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75>)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
More than 1,500 drivers will resume industrial action on Tuesday, August 25 over sweltering conditions in their cabs during the recent heatwaves.
Drivers have argued that temperatures in their cabs can reach a sweltering 40C, putting them at risk of fatigue and heat exhaustion, heat stroke and dehydration.
Union Unite said most buses operated by Arriva North London have air cooling systems, rather than air conditioning, which only managed to reduce temperatures by around two or three degrees during the recent series of heatwaves.
![Bus drivers on strike in Stratford](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/07/IMG_20260814_091603-(1).jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
“Arriva can fully afford to make meaningful changes our members can accept. Until that happens, strike action will continue and our members at Arriva North London will continue to have the full backing of Unite.”
Drivers at the Barking, Edmonton, Enfield, Grays, Palmers Green, Stamford Hill, Tottenham and Wood Green garages are set to take part in the latest round of strikes having previously walked out on Friday, August 14, and Saturday, August 15.
The last industrial action led to delays and cancellations for more than 40 bus routes in the capital.
Unite regional officer Steven Stockwell said: “There is still time for Arriva to stop this disruptive action, but it relies on it coming back to the table with a deal our members believe will solve the serious problems with conditions once and for all.”
The remaining walkout dates are:
• August: 25 to 28
• September: 4 to 5, 7 to 8, 18 to 19, and 21 to 22
• October: 2 to 3, 5 to 6, 16 to 17, and 19 to 20
Arriva has said the wellbeing of its staff and customers is its “top priority”, adding it has added extra welfare checks and cooling breaks during hot weather and is collaborating with Transport for London to roll out upgraded air conditioning on newer fleet buses.
summary: More than 1,500 Arriva North London bus drivers will resume strikes on Tuesday, August 25, after rejecting a recent pay and conditions offer. The union Unite stated that drivers face dangerously hot cab temperatures reaching up to 40C during heatwaves, as current air cooling systems are inadequate. The industrial action is set to span multiple dates through August, September, and October, following previous walkouts that disrupted over 40 bus routes.
key_points: Over 1,500 drivers at Arriva North London are resuming strikes starting August 25.
The industrial action is driven by safety concerns over cab temperatures reaching up to 40C during heatwaves.
Unite union reports that current air cooling systems only reduce temperatures by two or three degrees.
Previous strikes caused delays and cancellations across more than 40 London bus routes.
Arriva stated it has implemented extra welfare checks, cooling breaks, and is collaborating to roll out upgraded air conditioning on newer buses.

title: Soaring number of fires at recycling centres blamed on vape batteries
author: Shaun Wilson
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![UK: Major Fire Breaks Out at Bermondsey Recycling Centre.](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/09/8/48/recycling-fire.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Over ten fires are breaking out at recycling centres across the UK each week due to lithium batteries from devices such as vapes being carelessly disposed of, according to new research.
The figures follow major fires at recycling centres in London last week, including 100 firefighters called out to a mass blaze in Deptford, south east London, the cause of which has yet to be revealed, as well as another fire in Ilford attributed to lithium ion batteries.
Industry insiders estimate the rate of the battery fires is costing the UK economy around £1 billion a year, with concerns that workers’ lives are being put at risk.
Of these, over a third (541) of fires were directly linked to lithium ion batteries, with a further 216 battery fires in bin lorries.
The ESA admitted these figures could be underestimates, as most fires at recycling centres leave no trace of the cause. An ESA spokesman said: “We know 40% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries, but we think the actual number is more like 70%.”
As a safety measure, the ESA is proposing new rules for a £5 deposit on the purchase of all vapes, giving users an incentive to return old devices to shops for safe disposal.
Patrick Brighty, the head of recycling policy at the ESA, said: “Battery fires are reaching epidemic proportions across Britain’s recycling and waste industry, placing workers at risk and threatening vital infrastructure upon which we all rely every day.
“It only takes a single battery hidden in household rubbish or recycling to cause a huge fire and decimate a facility. The total cost of battery fires now exceeds £1bn a year, with huge knock-on implications for insurance costs.
Read More
“Vapes are among the biggest culprits because they’re cheap, abundant and typically have a short use-life. ESA and others across our industry are calling on the government to implement a mandatory deposit scheme for vapes to incentivise users to return them safely back to the point of purchase so they can be recycled properly and away from other waste.”
Following the Ilford fire, the London Fire Brigade stated: “We’ve seen a growing number of fires at waste disposal sites that are believed to have been caused by a lithium battery.
“Fires that we attend at sites like recycling centres and scrap yards can be very time consuming for our firefighters and often require a high level of resources to put the fire out. We’ve also seen the detrimental environmental and societal impact these fires can have on local communities.”
Dr Francesco Restuccia, a fire expert at King’s College London, described the increase in fires at recycling centres as "exponential" and stated that the public are now using lithium batteries in a huge variety of everyday objects such as smartphones, children’s toys, toothbrushes and vapes, with many of these carelessly thrown away.
Dr Restucccia stated that when a lithium battery is crushed, it causes "a lot of internal short circuits" in the battery, sending its temperatures soaring until it reaches ignition point.
summary: Over ten fires are breaking out at UK recycling centres each week as a result of lithium batteries from items like vapes being improperly discarded. These fires cost the UK economy an estimated £1 billion annually and endanger workers' lives and infrastructure. In response, the Environmental Services Association (ESA) is proposing a mandatory £5 deposit on vapes to encourage safe returns and proper recycling.
key_points: Over 40% to an estimated 70% of fires at recycling centres are caused by batteries.
Lithium battery fires cost the UK economy approximately £1 billion every year.
The ESA has proposed a £5 deposit on vapes to incentivise safe returns to shops.
Crushing discarded lithium batteries causes internal short circuits that lead to ignition.

title: Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie returns to London - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie, the internationally celebrated musical built around the songs and writings of American folk icon Woody Guthrie. After returning to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, nearly two decades after its Fringe debut, the biographical musical transfers to the Underbelly Boulevard for an exclusive run, packed with live performances of Guthrie’s songs woven together with stories drawn from his life. The uplifting production captures the highs, hardships and restless spirit that shaped one of America’s most influential folk musicians.
David M. Lutken, who reprises the role of Guthrie for this production, devised Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie with original director Nick Corley and original cast members Darcie Deaville, Helen Jean Russell and Andy Tierstein, drawing from Guthrie’s autobiographical works including ‘Bound for Glory’ and ‘American Folk Song’, letters, diary entries and excerpts from Guthrie’s 1930s-40s newspaper column ‘Woody Sez’ to create a music-led portrait of one of America’s defining folk voices. Intertwined with more than two dozen of Guthrie’s songs, these personal writings illuminate the people, places and experiences that shaped his travelling years: from the Dust Bowl and the Great Depression through to Union halls, radio broadcasts, his wartime service with the Merchant Marines in North Africa, Sicily and the UK, his life in New York, and his tragic demise from Huntington’s Disease in 1967.
Performed by a cast of four actor-musicians, David M. Lutken, David Finch, Nyssa Grant, and Raquel Chavez playing more than twenty instuments between them, Wood Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie combines live music and storytelling with the raucous and heartfelt intimacy of a folk music session. Instruments pass between performers throughout as the cast move between narration, character and song, collectively evoking the communities and travelling culture that shaped Guthrie’s world. The show becomes a moving and exhilarating shared musical experience, balancing moments of humour, spontaneity and joy with the hardship, restlessness, tragedy and hope that informed both his life and writing.
Originally developed in the early 2000s, the show premiered at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in 2007 and returned in 2009, before touring internationally with more than 80 productions worldwide. Previous runs include a West End engagement at the Arts Theatre and an Off-Broadway production at the Irish Repertory Theatre in New York in 2017, as well as productions across the United States, Europe, China and the Middle East.
The production has maintained a longstanding relationship with Woody Guthrie Publications, with Lutken having worked closely with Woody’s family for decades. Created and performed with the support of the Guthrie estate, Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthriecontinues to introduce new audiences to his timeless songs while preserving the communal spirit and live musicianship at the heart of American folk tradition.
Rooted in American folk history, Guthrie’s music resonates with contemporary audiences. His songs remain a cornerstone of American folk music and the artists he inspired: Pete Seeger, The Kingston Trio, Lonnie Donegan, Bob Dylan, Bruce Springsteen and beyond – from Ani DiFranco, Billy Bragg, Tom Morello and the Dropkick Murphys to current artists Slaid Cleaves, Jonatha Brooke, Dar Williams and Jessie Welles.
For newer generations of listeners, his relevance lies in his ability to articulate feelings of instability, frustration and disillusionment so familiar in today’s political and economic climate, without abandoning his foundation of humour, optimism and communal resilience.
Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie places audiences alongside Guthrie as songs and storytelling unfold in real time, creating a musical portrait of an artist whose work continues to find new audiences decades later around the world.
summary: The biographical musical "Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie" is transferring to London's Underbelly Boulevard for an exclusive run following its return to the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. Devised by David M. Lutken along with original creators, the production features a cast of four actor-musicians performing over two dozen songs and sharing stories drawn from Guthrie's life and writings. Created with the support of the Guthrie estate, the internationally toured show captures the highs, hardships, and restless spirit of the influential American folk icon.
key_points: The biographical musical "Woody Sez: The Life & Music of Woody Guthrie" is coming to London's Underbelly Boulevard for an exclusive run.
The show is devised by David M. Lutken with original director Nick Corley and original cast members, drawing from Guthrie's autobiographical works, letters, diaries, and columns.
A cast of four actor-musicians plays more than 20 instruments to perform over two dozen of Guthrie's songs and blend them with storytelling.
First premiering at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in 2007, the production has since had more than 80 runs worldwide, including West End and Off-Broadway engagements.
The production is created and performed with the support of Woody Guthrie Publications and the Guthrie estate.

title: TfL underestimating fare evasion by 10 per cent due to data collection limitations
author: Mark Brown
content:
Up to £211million of potential income may be being lost reports Kumail Jaffer, Local Democracy reporter
![A London Underground sign](https://i0.wp.com/barnetpost.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/London-Underground-credit-TfL.jpg?resize=700%2C469&ssl=1)
Fare evasion could be costing Transport for London (TfL) up to £21million more than officially reported, it has emerged.
Officials have revealed that they incorporate a 10 per cent reduction on the estimated value of the amount lost to evaders due to the “limitations of available data”.
TfL say they lose £190million annually to those who choose not to pay for their journeys on the network – a rate of around 3.5 per cent. Transport chiefs say they hope to bring the rate down to 1.5 per cent by the end of 2031.
However, they have now admitted that the amount lost could be as high as £211million per year – far higher than the £168million in estimated extra revenue raised from fare rises on buses and Tubes earlier this year.
The admission, made for the first time in a disclosure to the Tube Alerter website and shared with the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS), is due to officials not wanting to “overstate the estimated level of revenue loss”.
This means that the publicly stated figure of £190million “represents an evidence-based assessment that takes these limitations into account.”
TfL say the adjustment is made due to staff deriving their estimates from intelligence-led activity at some locations where fare evasion is more likely to occur, and therefore “may not be fully representative of the network as a whole”.
“The estimated value of fare evasion incorporates a 10 per cent reduction to reflect the medium confidence level associated with the overall assumptions,” an internal TfL review concluded.
“This recognises the limitations of the available data and the absence of a system that automatically matches passenger journeys with payments made.”
Newer style technology, such as modern gateline infrastructure which is currently being tested in New York, will be able to more accurately track those passing through the barriers without paying, TfL predicts.
The internal confidence assessment and supporting assumptions have never been published separately, officials confirmed, as they said publication of such “detailed information…could compromise TfL’s ability to prevent, detect and respond to fare evasion, ultimately impacting the protection of public revenue”.
Thomas Turrell, the transport spokesman for the City Hall Conservatives, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS): “Sadiq Khan has lost control of fare evasion.
“Instead of showing leadership and gripping the issue, he has trapped TfL in a doom loop where underestimating data leads them to not take the issue seriously, causing more underestimation.
“It is wrong, it must stop, and Londoners’ confidence must be restored that the Mayor is serious about tackling this crime that fare-paying commuters are expected to pick up the £200m bill for.”
Festus Akinbusoye, a former Police and Crime Commissioner who sits on Westminster City Council, added: “This is unfair for millions of Londoners who work hard and play by the rules.
“Instead of tackling fare evasion – which has doubled on the London Underground – TfL and the Mayor have been too busy fudging statistics to downplay the problem.”
A TfL spokesperson said: “Robust analysis of fare evasion on London’s transport network is a vital tool in tackling it, and the estimated total cost of fare evasion is just one of many figures we produce to measure the scale of the issue.
“All figures produced are estimates that are calculated according to TfL’s best interpretation of the data, in line with industry standards.
“The estimated cost of £190m represents an evidence-based assessment that takes limitations of the data used into account.”

Officials apply a 10 per cent reduction to their estimates due to data collection limitations and a lack of automatic journey-matching systems. Critics, including opposition politicians, have condemned the discrepancy and accused leadership of downplaying the scale of the issue.
key_points: TfL officially estimates an annual loss of £190 million due to fare evasion.
Actual losses could be as high as £211 million because a 10 per cent reduction is applied to account for data limitations.
Estimates rely on intelligence-led activity in specific locations rather than network-wide automatic journey matching.
TfL aims to reduce the fare evasion rate from roughly 3.5 per cent down to 1.5 per cent by the end of 2031.
Politicians and critics have criticized TfL and the Mayor for underestimating and downplaying the severity of fare evasion.

title: SPOTIFY'S FRESH FINDS FAVOURITE FLO GALLOP IS COMING TO CARFEST 2026 - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
CarFest 2026 has a new addition to its Wigwam Stage lineup that is well worth circling in the diary. Flo Gallop, the South East London singer-songwriter who has spent the past few years becoming one of the most talked-about emerging pop acts in the UK, will be performing at Silverstone Circuit from 28 to 30 August. With CarFest making its debut at the home of British motorsport this August Bank Holiday, her set on the Wigwam Stage promises to be one to remember.
The Wigwam Stage has become one of CarFest’s best-loved destinations, a pub garden stage tucked within the BarFest Arms that trades headliners for something altogether more personal. Dedicated solely to handpicked rising talent and brilliant live sessions, it is where some of the weekend’s most memorable moments tend to happen.
Flo says: “I genuinely cannot wait for CarFest. Silverstone, a festival crowd, the Wigwam Stage, it is everything I love about playing live all in one place. It is going to be a good one.”
She has been named as one of Spotify’s Top 50 Fresh Finds artists in both 2023 and 2024, featured on the cover of Fresh Finds Pop, and added to major Spotify editorial playlists including Young and Free, Happy Pop Hits and POV: ur that girl. BBC Radio 1 Future Pop has supported her across all recent releases, and she was a featured artist on BBC Introducing in September 2025, racking up 255,000 Spotify listeners and 740,000 streams in 2025 alone.
On stage, she is just as hard to ignore. Festival appearances at Mighty Hoopla, Big Feastival, 110 Above and GoatFest sit alongside support slots for Sophie Ellis-Bextor and Netta, a spot on Allie Sherlock’s UK tour, two appearances on CBBC Saturday Mash-Up and three sold-out headline shows. She was also the official singer for the Beauty Awards 2024 and was invited to speak on the impact of AI in music at HowTheLightGetsIn Festival.
The biggest chapter is still ahead. Flo is set to release her debut EP later this year, produced with Nashville producer, Mark Siegel. Think, fun, chatty and unapologetically her, it is the fullest picture yet of an artist who has been building to this moment for years.
Flo adds: “This EP has been a long time coming and I genuinely cannot wait for people to hear it. Making it with Mark was one of those pinch-yourself moments. It feels like the most me thing I have ever made.”
Since launching in 2012, CarFest has raised over £28 million for UK children’s charities including BBC Children in Need, Ellen MacArthur Cancer Trust, Rainbow Trust Children’s Charity, Starlight Children’s Foundation, Teenage Cancer Trust and Young Epilepsy. This year, CarFest will also be raising money for five charities local to Silverstone – The Pace Centre, Helen & Douglas House, The Smallpiece Trust, Roald Dahl’s Marvellous Children’s Charity and Northamptonshire Community Foundation.
CarFest presented by bp takes place at Silverstone Circuit, Towcester, Northampton between 28-30 August 2026. Tickets are available from www.carfest.org
summary: Emerging UK singer-songwriter Flo Gallop will perform on the Wigwam Stage at CarFest 2026, which takes place at Silverstone Circuit from August 28 to 30. Gallop has gained recognition through Spotify's Fresh Finds, BBC Radio 1 support, and various festival appearances, and she is set to release her debut EP produced by Mark Siegel later this year. CarFest, established in 2012, raises funds for various national and local UK children's charities.
key_points: Flo Gallop is joining the Wigwam Stage lineup for CarFest 2026 at Silverstone Circuit.
She has been recognized as a Spotify Fresh Finds artist and received support from BBC Radio 1 and BBC Introducing.
Gallop plans to release her debut EP later this year, produced in collaboration with Mark Siegel.
CarFest 2026 runs from August 28 to 30 and raises funds for multiple children's charities.

title: Home and car destroyed in huge London house fire as 70 firefighters battle blaze
author: The Standard
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![UK set for 'warmest summer on record' as Europe preps for yet another heatwave](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/23/6/52/NewMaldenFire.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![Ten fire engines and around 70 firefighters were called to a house fire on Mount Pleasant Road in New Malden.](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/23/6/52/NewMaldenFire.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
A car parked in the front garden was also burnt out, but it is understood no one was injured.
Station Commander Steve McGhie, who was at the scene, said: "The fire was producing smoke that affected the local area, residents nearby were advised to keep their windows and doors closed where possible.
"One of the Brigade's 32-metre turntable ladders was deployed as a water tower, allowing crews to tackle the flames from above."
Firefighters were called at 9.36pm on Saturday and the blaze was under control by 1am.
A gas cylinder was removed from the property and “cooled to an ambient temperature as a precaution, as some cylinders can explode when exposed to heat”, the London Fire Brigade added.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
summary: A large house fire in New Malden, London, destroyed a home and a car parked in the front garden, though no injuries were reported. Approximately 70 firefighters and ten fire engines responded to the scene, bringing the blaze under control by 1am after being called at 9.36pm on Saturday. Crews deployed a 32-metre turntable ladder as a water tower and cooled a gas cylinder as a precaution while the cause of the fire remains under investigation.
key_points: Ten fire engines and around 70 firefighters battled the house fire on Mount Pleasant Road in New Malden.
A home and a car in the front garden were destroyed, but no injuries were reported.
Firefighters were called at 9.36pm on Saturday and had the blaze under control by 1am.
A gas cylinder was removed and cooled as a precaution against heat-induced explosions.
The cause of the fire is currently under investigation.

title: Inside London's data centres boom and the fierce local battles being waged
author: Niva Yadav; Luke Reevey
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/31/11/48/Brick_Lane_protest_pic_2.jpeg?trim=206,0,208,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Yet behind the capital’s digital infrastructure dominance lies a battle for the supply of the land, water, and electricity needed to tackle London’s housing crisis. The giant server houses have attracted criticism over high energy and water use, noise pollution and letting off harmful fumes, but few understand what the data centre boom means for the capital. In fact, few truly know what data centres do. Yet many know why they don’t want one in their backyard. ![

Save Brick Lane protest outside Truman Brewery

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/31/11/48/Brick_Lane_protest_pic_2.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has waved through several data centre developments, including sprawling campuses in Abbot’s Langley and Buckinghamshire, but critics say her embrace of Britain’s digital revolution is taking its toll on housing. According to research by the GLA, parts of the capital’s grid in Hillingdon, Hounslow, and Ealing have already reached full capacity, halting new housing developments. The power demand of energy-intensive sectors, like the data centre industry, could see demand rocket by more than 600% by 2050, placing strain on the grid. Tensions have reached breaking point in Tower Hamlets when Andy Burnham’s government gave the green light for the Truman Brewery data centre project. There are some 28,000 families on the council waiting list for social housing, so news of another data centre on a site which could have accommodated 350 homes has sparked pushback. “It’s a lost opportunity for a serious amount of housing,” says local campaigner Jonathan Moberly, member of the Save Brick Lane campaign. “You could activate the street by bringing housing into it, or kill it off for good by putting a data center there.” According to campaigners, the proposed 5.2MW facility, likely to be operated by US giant Digital Realty, will suck up enough electricity to power 15,000 homes. City traders based just minutes away will have access to ultra fast internet for high frequency trading. However, local residents won’t benefit from that - although the project, put forward by property owners Truman Estates and Zeloof LLP, is also delivering offices, a supermarket, a cinema and a number of homes. Read More Mr Moberly says that while ‘Big Tech’ promises plenty of new jobs, the reality is the majority of those are in the construction phase, with the average data centre only requires between 12 to 15 staff across a week. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/15/31/Screenshot-2026-08-21-at-14-33-59.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The impact on football could “erase the character and heritage” of an area like Brick Lane, says Faysal Ahmed, councillor for Spitalfields and Bangla Town. He received more than 7,000 objections from residents who fear for the future of the area - widely known as the curry capital of Europe. “We, the council, the Mayor, and this administration are firmly opposed to it, and so are the local businesses. Please listen to us, the residents, and review this decision and reverse it,” he said. Ms Rayner has said she has seen “no detailed evidence” on whether an alternative, housing-led development was feasible and the government said its decision was in line with the recommendations of the independent planning inspector. It claimed the harm to the area’s heritage will be “minor” and that the facility will help crackdown on anti-social behaviour in and among the derelict buildings, while highlighting the need for more data centres and the economic benefits that come with them. Living alongside these server houses can also pose serious concerns about quality of life. In Acton, families have said they feel “betrayed” by plans for a data centre facility on the Frogmore Estate, operated by Kao Data. Olivia Law-Zygadlo, a local parent, told the Standard she was concerned about the impact on her son’s severe breathing difficulties. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/15/27/Screenshot-2026-08-21-at-14-33-33.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Campaigners say data centres have a large impact on air quality - just one of Mr Moberly’s concerns. Every month diesel generators stored at data centre facilities are required to be tested, sending plumes of toxic gases into the air. Some data centres, like Kao Data, are trialling the use of vegetable fat generated from restaurant waste, which is a cleaner fuel with minimal greenhouse emissions. Other residents allege that they were not properly consulted ahead of local planning decisions. “We’ve been walked right over,” claims Hazel Garcia, who lives opposite the existing data centre operated by Vantage. She claims low-frequency humming from the facility and heat generation as just two of the problems that residents are facing. She fears another facility would only add to their anguish. But Adam Nethersole, the senior vice president of sales and marketing at Kao Data, insists that the operator wants to be a “positive neighbour” and a “responsible operator.” “We are taking a derelict industrial estate and we are going to turn it into a future-proof industry, which will provide inward investment, jobs, commerce and enterprise for the next 20 years,” he explained, adding that the operator is building a community centre and community gardens for the neighbourhood. He said Kao Data is trying “to do everything” it can to “be as transparent and open with the community as [it] possibly can be.” In response to concerns about water, Mr Nethersole said the data centre will run on a closed-loop, glycol-based system, minimising water usage concerns. In a statement, Vantage Data Centers said: “LHR2 was subject to full planning scrutiny and public consultation through the Old Oak and Park Royal Development Corporation, the independent planning authority for the area, and has been delivered in line with the permissions granted. We operate the facility in accordance with applicable planning, environmental and regulatory requirements, including those relating to noise, air quality and back-up power.” Ealing Council added that it was “listening to residents in North Acton” and was working with the Old Oak and Park Royal Development Corporation to address the issues raised. Experts have warned of the “data centre heat island effect”, when air-cooled data centres emit waste heat into the surrounding area, with some reports claiming local temperatures can rise by up to 9C. Such an increase is a stark prospect for Tower Hamlets, which is already recorded by Friends of the Earth as one of London’s warmest neighbourhoods. Plans to put excess heat into distribution networks has been mooted by the industry, but Owen Espley, community campaigns manager at Global Action Plan, explains that London lacks the “joint up system” to facilitate this. He adds that air-cooling can drive up electricity use. In districts like Slough - the world’s second largest data centre hub - standard water-cooling methods can consume up to 35 litres of water per second, the equivalent of the daily demand of 3,500 households, according to Affinity Water. But the tech sector rejects claims that data centres are sucking up vital water and electricity supplies. Sophie Greaves, associate director for digital infrastructure at TechUK, says that planning applications all join the same queue for grid connection, with no priority given to data centres. She noted that a survey carried out by TechUK showed that half of UK data centres employ waterless or closed-loop cooling systems. Nationally, the sector accounts for just 0.2% of non-household water usage in England - less than the volume lost daily through pipe leaks. Grow Places, development manager for the Truman Brewery, said it agreed with the decision to approve a data centre. Tom Larsson, CEO of Grow Places, said: "We are pleased to confirm that the Secretary of State has agreed with the Inspector's recommendations, granting planning permission for the three appeals, together with listed building consent, at the Truman Brewery. “This is a significant milestone and a testament to the efforts of everyone involved in this unique project. The Truman Brewery, Brick Lane, Spitalfields and Banglatown are ever evolving places, as all cities are, and we are proud to continue supporting this place growth.” With vacancy rates for server space hovering around 7%, according to CBRE, demand for data centres shows no sign of cooling down. But as they spread across London, the debate and disquiet in affected communities is only likely to get louder.
summary: London's rapid data centre boom is triggering intense local pushback and exacerbating concerns over land, water, and electricity resources. Projects like the Truman Brewery data centre in Tower Hamlets have faced severe criticism from campaigners and residents who argue that the facilities take up land desperately needed for housing, create pollution, and offer very few permanent jobs. While the government and industry representatives defend the digital developments for bringing economic benefits and implementing cleaner technologies, local communities remain worried about noise, air quality, and strain on the local power grid.
key_points: The approval of a data centre at the Truman Brewery in Tower Hamlets sparked strong local opposition because the site could have alternatively provided much-needed housing.
Parts of London's power grid, such as in Hillingdon, Hounslow, and Ealing, have reached full capacity, halting new housing developments as energy-intensive sectors like data centres drive up demand.
Residents near existing and proposed data centres have raised concerns about noise pollution, heat generation, air quality impacts from backup diesel generators, and a lack of proper consultation.
Industry representatives defend data centres by highlighting investments in closed-loop cooling systems, cleaner fuels, and the economic benefits and infrastructure the sector provides.

title: Video: Inside Rehearsals for TWENTY THOUSAND STREETS UNDER…
author: Rachel Stone
content:
Video: Inside Rehearsals for TWENTY THOUSAND STREETS UNDER THE SKY at Southwark Playhouse
Company members reflect on Patrick Hamilton's tale of three lonely Londoners searching for connection.
Southwark Playhouse has posted a rehearsal video giving audiences a first look inside the room for TWENTY THOUSAND STREETS UNDER THE SKY, ahead of its run from 10 September to 17 October. The footage features members of the company speaking about what drew them to the project, an adaptation the venue describes as both darkly funny and devastating.
The production is based on Patrick Hamilton's classic novel, following three lonely Londoners searching for connection amid the sprawling streets of 1920s London. The video captures the company discussing the world of the piece as rehearsals get underway.
Directed by Matthew Iliffe, whose previous credits include 'Bacon', the show is presented by Troupe, the company behind 'The Forsyte Saga Parts 1 and 2'. It marks the world premiere of the stage adaptation at Southwark Playhouse.
Casting for the production was previously confirmed in a report on the full cast set for TWENTY THOUSAND STREETS UNDER THE SKY, which detailed the ensemble now seen preparing for the run in this new rehearsal footage. The video was shot by Molly Osborne.
summary: Southwark Playhouse has released a rehearsal video for the world premiere of "Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky," running from September 10 to October 17. Adapted from Patrick Hamilton's novel, the production explores the lives of three lonely individuals in 1920s London. The play is directed by Matthew Iliffe and presented by Troupe.
key_points: Southwark Playhouse posted rehearsal footage for the upcoming production.
The play runs from September 10 to October 17 as a world premiere stage adaptation.
The story is based on Patrick Hamilton's novel about three lonely Londoners in the 1920s.
The production is directed by Matthew Iliffe and presented by the company Troupe.

title: Ah Trinidian In London - Where De Doubles - Soca News
author: Soca News Staff
content:
By Trini D
EPISODE 2: WHERE DE DOUBLES?
Now allyuh remember yesterday ah tell yuh ah reach London and people telling me Carnival coming.
Fine.
But before ah could deal with Carnival, Tube, £7 beer and all dem other London problems, ah had something more important to sort out.
Food.
And not just any food.
Ah wanted doubles.
Now somebody tell me, “D, if yuh looking for Caribbean food, go Brixton.”
Caribbean food?
Say no more.
Ah reach Brixton expecting doubles on every corner.
Friends, ah see jerk chicken.
Ah see patties.
Plantain.
Rice and peas.
Ackee and saltfish.
Chicken looking at me from every direction.
But doubles?
Nothing.
Ah walking through Brixton thinking, all dis Caribbean food around me and not one doubles have de decency to introduce itself.
Then ah walking down one little road and smell something.
Curry.
Now Trinidadians know curry have a way of calling yuh.
Yuh could be two streets away minding yuh own business and suddenly yuh nose saying:
“Turn left.”
So naturally ah follow meh nose.
Little takeaway.
Nothing fancy.
Couple tables.
Trinidad flag on de wall.
Soca playing low in de background.
And behind de counter is this young fella moving like he know exactly what he doing.
Then he look at me and say:
“Boss, yuh want slight, medium or plenty pepper?”
Ah stop.
“Wait nah… where yuh from?”
He smile.
“Trinidad.”
Now we talking.
Immediately ah forget ah come to buy food and start interviewing de man.
“Where in Trinidad?”
“How long yuh up here?”
“Who making de bara?”
“Pepper homemade?”
“Yuh mother know yuh selling doubles in London?”
He laugh and tell me he living in London years now.
Ah say, “Good. So yuh should know better.”
He say, “Know better about what?”
“About charging people London money for doubles!”
Because friends, then ah see de price.
Ah had to look twice.
Ah ask him:
“Boss… de doubles come over from Piarco Business Class or what?”
He start laughing.
“D, this is London. Rent high. Ingredients high. Everything high.”
Ah tell him, “Is two bara and channa we talking about, not ah mortgage.”
He say, “You want one or not?”
Now this is where principles become difficult.
Because de doubles smelling good.
Real good.
So ah order one.
Medium pepper.
Little tamarind.
He hand it over.
Ah look at it carefully because ah wasn’t letting London fool me.
Bara soft.
Channa looking right.
Pepper behaving itself.
Ah take one bite.
Friends…
Ah stop talking.
And allyuh know when I stop talking something serious happen.
De man behind de counter watching me with a big smile.
“Well?”
Ah chew.
Take another bite.
“Hmm.”
He say, “Good?”
Ah tell him, “It eh bad.”
He laugh.
“It eh bad? Look how fast you eating it!”
Ah tell him doh study my eating speed. That is private business.
Then ah order another one.
Yes.
Another one.
Ah still wasn’t happy with de price, but sometimes in life yuh have to separate economics from hunger.
Anyway, ah finish eating and ask him how ah getting back.
He say:
“Easy. Just jump on de Victoria Line.”
Ah look at him.
“Jump on what?”
“Victoria Line.”
“Who is Victoria?”
He start laughing again.
Apparently everybody in London find transportation confusion funny.
So tomorrow friends, ah going Underground.
Although somebody explain to me parts of de Underground actually run above ground.
Already ah don’t trust it.
I gone.
AH TRINIDADIAN IN LONDON — CARNIVAL 2026
7 days to Notting Hill Carnival.
summary: While visiting London ahead of Carnival, the author went on a quest to find traditional Trinidadian doubles instead of general Caribbean food. After searching Brixton, he followed the scent of curry to a small takeaway shop run by a fellow Trinidadian. Despite complaining about the high London prices, he thoroughly enjoyed the food and ultimately ordered a second portion.

title: Constance Marten granted permission to appeal sentence for killing her baby
author: PA News
content:
Constance Marten granted permission to appeal sentence for killing her baby
Aristocrat Constance Marten has been granted permission to appeal the 14-year jail sentence she was handed for her baby’s death while on the run with her partner.
Marten, 39, and convicted rapist Mark Gordon, 52, were in hiding when their baby daughter, Victoria, died in a tent on the South Downs in southern England in January 2023.
They had fled authorities to prevent Victoria being taken into care, as four other siblings had been before, their Old Bailey trial was told.
Marten and Gordon were found guilty of her manslaughter, child cruelty, concealing the birth of a child and perverting the course of justice following two trials spanning six months each.
Judge Mark Lucraft KC jailed them both for 14 years and handed Gordon a further four years on extended licence.
Marten has now been granted permission to appeal the sentence, and renewed her application for permission to appeal her gross negligence manslaughter conviction.
A court date is yet to be set.
Judge Lucraft accepted the prosecution case that baby Victoria died from hypothermia after being exposed to “significant cold stress”.
He rejected the defendants’ claims that Victoria was smothered in a “terrible accident” as they slept in the tent.
The offending was made worse because the baby was vulnerable and the defendants failed to listen to past warnings.
In a televised sentencing, Judge Lucraft told the defendants: “It is clear throughout the period neither of you gave much or any thought for the care or love for your baby.”
The judge said they had displayed “arrogance” and treated Victoria to “neglect of the most serious type”.
Police had launched a nationwide hunt after the couple’s car burst into flames on a motorway near Bolton, Greater Manchester, on January 5 2023.
The defendants travelled across England and went off-grid, sleeping in a tent on the South Downs where baby Victoria died days later.
After seven weeks on the run, the defendants were arrested in Brighton.
After a desperate search, police found their baby dead amid rubbish inside a Lidl bag in a disused shed nearby.
summary: Aristocrat Constance Marten has been granted permission to appeal her 14-year jail sentence for the manslaughter of her baby, Victoria, who died from hypothermia in a tent in January 2023. Marten and her partner, Mark Gordon, had fled authorities to prevent the child from being taken into care. She has also renewed her application to appeal her conviction.
key_points: Constance Marten received a 14-year sentence for the death of her baby daughter, Victoria.
Marten and Mark Gordon went on the run to avoid social services taking their baby into care.
The baby died from hypothermia after being exposed to significant cold stress in a tent.
Marten has been granted permission to appeal her sentence and applied to appeal her conviction.

title: Camden Fringe 2026: Dying To Meet You – Courtyard Theatre, London - The Reviews Hub
author: The Reviews Hub
content:
Writer: Agnieszka Wieclawska
Director: Keller O’Malley
In this cheerful comedy, Leta has a superpower, quite a good one, in fact. She can’t die. Or rather, she can die but comes back to life a few hours later, by which time she’s usually lying in a morgue somewhere. She dies a lot because someone is trying to kill her. Dying To Meet You is a rom-com with corpses.
Tess is Leta’s girlfriend, who, while waiting for Leta to escape from the morgue, cooks Bolognese. We discover that she is immortal, too. In the show’s early minutes, it seems as if writer Agnieszka Wieclawska is using the theme of resurrection as a way of discussing the fact that in spite of the violence against queer people in the world, queer people will continue to exist. However, as it turns out, Dying To Meet You is not a political play at all. Instead, it’s broad comedy with some meta bits thrown in for good measure.
The clownish comedy that runs through the whole of the 55-minute piece doesn’t always work as it should. Sometimes, there’s something too forced about the running around, the funny accents and the cheeky looks to the audience. And the tenor of the piece never changes, whether Leta is breaking out of her temporary drawer in the morgue, dodging bullets in a slow food restaurant or fighting her nemesis in an aeroplane hangar. When the five-strong cast are chasing each other in this last scene, the audience is fearful that Benny Hill music will suddenly erupt from the speakers. It doesn’t, but unfortunately the tune that does come is more or less the same.
There’s something quite film noirish about the plot, and it would be good if Wieclawska and director Keller O’Malley could lean into this darker side in the future. The comedy could then be wry rather than silly. But the actors are fully committed to showing off their clownish selves, especially Hannah Whyman with her range of accents, who, with Maeve Elmore and Olivia von Opel, dashes around the theatre, exiting and entering as if they are in a farce. Playing the leads are Wieclawska as Tess and Sarah Chamberlain as Leta. They both convince as the two lovers trying to find out the identity of their persistent killers.
It’s all very entertaining in a light-hearted way, but in a Fringe full of shows about masculinity, women’s rights, historical figures and grief, Dying To Meet You doesn’t feel that deep. Although some will welcome the slapstick as a tonic.
Runs until 23 August 2026
Camden Fringe 2026 runs until 30 August
summary: "Dying To Meet You" is a cheerful comedy playing at the Courtyard Theatre as part of the Camden Fringe 2026. Written by Agnieszka Wieclawska and directed by Keller O’Malley, the 55-minute play follows two immortal girlfriends, Leta and Tess, as they try to survive persistent attempts on their lives. While the show features film noir elements and committed performances from its five-strong cast, its broad, clownish slapstick can feel forced and lacks deeper thematic weight.
key_points: The play features Leta, who repeatedly comes back to life after being killed, and her immortal girlfriend Tess.
Despite early hints of political themes regarding queer survival, the production is ultimately a light-hearted, broad comedy.

title: 'As You Like It' review — a raucously entertaining take on this surpassingly sweet comedy | London Theatre
author: Matt Wolf
content:
![](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/7axg1x5lbWnZb0CYndPaZl/e7182597531ca9a5e065bd83bc05de67/Charlie_Josephine_as_Orlando_and_Lola_Shalam_as_Rosalind__in_As_You_Like_It_at_Shakespeare-s_Globe___c._Marc_Brenner_.jpg?h=550&fm=webp&q=90)
'As You Like It' review — a raucously entertaining take on this surpassingly sweet comedy
Read our review of As You Like It, co-directed by Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine, now in performances at Shakespeare's Globe to 25 October.
Summary
- As You Like It is playing at Shakespeare's Globe
- Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine co-direct a wonderfully entertaining production
- Lola Shalam is a fiercely determined Rosalind
- Peter Bourke is a touching Adam and Thomas Josling an unusually likeable Oliver
![Matt Wolf](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/1Cy2LDhf3IAIYeXD2TuPmD/f9c2d83eb6bd2f409c090ef6710bb912/Matt-Wolf-photo.jpg?w=32&h=32)
A rollicking summer at Shakespeare’s Globe continues with this raucously entertaining take on As You Like It, a surpassingly sweet play that seems here to take its cue from a passing reference near the end to “rustic revelry”.
Co-directed by Sean Holmes and Charlie Josephine, the latter of whom also appears as an especially gormless Orlando, the production shifts styles and period specificity without ever losing focus on the need to ensnare an audience by any means possible – and if that means leading them in a “hey nonny no” singalong or throwing in the odd ad lib along the way, so be it. (Katherine Pearce’s commendably casual Jacques at one point remarks “we never met” to one of the numerous lovers that make up the four couplings whose commingling ends the play.)
The start suggests high-aristo hijinks, as if an elaborately wigged and costumed company are about to embark upon The Marriage of Figaro: another defining piece, come to think of it, about the cross-currents of love. But once the plot sends its characters into the Forest of Arden, their disguises the stuff of self-revelation, we come to inhabit altogether funkier, more free-wheeling climes that can accommodate both an 11th-hour appearance as Hymen by the wonderful singer-songwriter Katie Richardson and a gasp-inducing backflip from Jonnie Broadbent’s show-devouring, as often as not barely clothed, Touchstone. Richardson, the play’s composer, lends a folk-inflected larkiness to the ebullient climax.
![As You Like It - LT - 1200](https://images.ctfassets.net/6pezt69ih962/4PRUWt0q5AxThKVYhswZJ7/84d5bc74e7bc18f5f0268e61d93f6c70/The_company_in_As_You_Like_It_at_Shakespeare-s_Globe___c._Marc_Brenner_.jpg)
No other Shakespeare comedy unites so many and disparate an assemblage of folks who to a person all see the light in time to share in love’s plenitude. Whereas Much Ado contains a putative death and Midsummer Night’s Dream seems suffused from the start with parental rage, As You Like It makes good on its title, delivering the audience into a pastoral idyll here visualised by a back wall of blank canvases that gets sketched in to stunning effect as the play continues: Arden’s coming into bloom accords with the passions it enfolds, and the sparseness is surely of a piece with a “forest” that is in fact several times referred to as a “desert”. (Paul Wills’s design shimmers in its simplicity.)
The shepherd Silvius pays obeisance to “the wounds that love’s sharp arrows make”, and As You Like It surpasses even Twelfth Night in making gender confusion a significant milestone in the sometimes pained courtship between Josephine’s wide-eyed, gawky Orlando and the rabid, feisty Rosalind of Lola Shalam. A onetime Juliet at this address, Shalam may not be “more than common tall”, as is indicated of Rosalind in the text. But that scarcely matters next to her Rottweiler-like determination, this duke’s daughter barking commandments of love at all and sundry, at one point fainting at the possibility of snaring some of that love for herself.
I’ve seen more wistful accounts of this play and certainly more moving ones, but it’s hard not to get caught up in the pell-mell energy that can agreeably accommodate Phoebe Naughton’s Audrey, a wench here born to work a room; Peter Bourke’s infinitely touching (and well-spoken) old Adam; and Thomas Josling as an unusually likeable Oliver, Adam’s master, whose behavioural about-face remains one of the most startling in all drama. (A shoutout, too, to the clarion-voiced Jordan Rhys as the late-arriving Jaques de Boys, an important stop on the story's route from riven families to wholesale restoration.)
In so deeply empathic a play, it’s surprising that not more is made of the deeply platonic love on view between Rosalind and her beloved “coz” Celia, who are jointly redefined as Ganymede and Aliena as the contortions of the plot work themselves out. You don’t get much sense here of Gracie Oddie-James’s comically inclined Celia feeling displaced by Rosalind’s newfound affections elsewhere – Celia’s plaintive “and I’ll sleep” here doesn’t count for much – but perhaps that, too, is of a piece with a production that has scant time for rest and wants instead to release the audience into a late-summer landscape of mischief and mirth.

title: Intriguing connections in Anja Bihlmaier & BBC Philharmonic's Prom including Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde with Jamie Barton & Clay Hilley, yet perhaps better heard on BBC Sounds
author: Planet Hugill
content:
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihilmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihilmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgpE8cuPNGWzJj_H7FaOaiS6zm7WzYqZPhPfHd2Bm2Fmrzg9eqh7gHWqD3jcgGQ2hNbyrIwGEa7y1mOrAoc8CjViwaVG78roIph-okWGwBlV-eb30zfj_Jpgs-gKMf9cRD-uZpUQNFkbohHrhjatEeqxbd9t-8opL1pnTzXBeHiGjEMGhBB1BlTUQ/w426-h640/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(7).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
Bushra El-Turk: Mosaic, Haydn: Symphony No. 45 in F sharp minor, 'Farewell', Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde; Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, Anja Bihlmaier
Reviewed 21 August 2026
A rare performance of one of Haydn's best-known early symphonies alongside Mahler's glorious final symphonic utterance in a concert full of links and references in performances that did not always quite overcome the challenges of the Royal Albert Hall
The BBC Prom at the Royal Albert Hall on Friday 21 August might, at first, have seemed a typical Proms programme presenting a diverse trio of works. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra and their principal guest conductor, Anja Bihlmaier presented us with Bushra El-Turk's Mosaic, Haydn's Farewell Symphony, and Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde with Jamie Barton and Clay Hilley.
Diverse works, to be sure, but scratch under the surface and we saw the connective tissues. The subject of a farewell linked Haydn and Mahler in a way that was sufficiently contrasting as to be intriguing. And then Bushra El-Turk's work addresses issues of cross-pollination between cultures, finding elements of the rootlessness and otherness that Mahler found in the Chinese poetry he set in Das Lied von der Erde. It was a lavish programme too, the huge orchestra for the Mahler not used in the first half. I did wonder whether Bihlmaier should have had the courage of her convictions and performed Haydn with Mahleresque forces (large body of strings, four oboes, five horns). Go on, it sounds intriguing and after all what are festival for?
Bushra El-Turk's Mosaic was written for the Manchester Camerata for the 2009/10 season. It began with a scurrying shimmer on the strings that was so quiet as to be almost inaudible in the Royal Albert Hall. Dramatic fragments and motifs emerged over, creating an anxious, almost unnerving feel. A gradual build-up led to denser textures but the fragments never quite coalesced, until at the end in ravishing quiet we heard a romantic, rather hymn-like figure emerge. I would have liked to hear the piece in more sympathetic circumstances to bring out the detail.
Because of the circumstances of its first performance, and the rather intriguing meta-theatre woven in to the music in a very contemporary manner, Haydn's Farewell Symphony is amongst the best known of his earlier ones. Yet it has not been performed at the Proms since 1938, and this was only its fourth performance! It was brave of Bihlmaier to decide to do it with a modern instrument orchestra and all credit to her. We should her more Haydn like this.
| ![Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiy-cuBhHWhlcYIEq0SHSWU_3MW-87dhtc7z8Ep161Ai8NS-45XqCmN4qBrcyJ4kdB5gwCnty3xs5hukMr1ydFI2AYRwBG-GufasQB409jjMC-DiD36bd6QSeSF0_tzTAaJD7ISQfQ2NbeVppMxY7Dyh_zLQRSrjDZ9wWzNXT6xZ1RqqeWYbKCG6A/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(10).jpg>) | 
| Haydn: Farewell Symphony - Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
In the first movement, the strings were strong, stylish yet completely modern. With a large-ish string body, the wind rather receded in the balance, yet there was urgency and dynamism to the performance with a lovely lyricism in the central episode. The slow movement was quiet with intimate detail, pointed motifs and lyrical moments. Yet there was harmonic uncertainty too, for all the standard feel of the movement the music was not obvious. I was worried about Bilhmaier's choice of tempo: not that slow, but with the repeats it made the movement too long for its surroundings, yet her tempos gave space for the detail. The Menuetto was full of contrasts, delicacy against strength, alongside the pull of the key relationships. All ending in wonderful midair. The finale was crisp and urgent, again full of contrasts with energetic impulse against elegant slow lyricism. As the instrumental body reduced (and the players did leave the stage) we went on a sort of time-lapse performance towards the modern day impulse for small scale performance. And the ending was as weird and mysterious as it should be.
Mahler's orchestra for Das Lied von der Erde is huge, with quadruple woodwind and much else besides including the mandolins. Throughout the performance the BBC Philharmonic was indeed resplendent. Bihlmaier took a disciplined almost classical approach, yet relishing all the tonal and timbral contrasts that Mahler implies. Speeds were steady-ish yet fluid with space for the singers. And yet... I suspect this is one of those performances that will sound better when rebalance for the radio. Somehow, neither singer quite dominated or cut through the orchestra when push came to shove. There were plenty of good moments, but you had to concentrate hard.
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiJUVK42I6euxXFnakG5FXpbtDiwgTn7xxZKOvzNumOMC0rtaIkxLGKvNwIdWkV0cMa2_Zm0lSCklhorXqRFa0iR0a8axQ6QzI-3uQuuVVgR3N3Mz_zTaO45zyNNH7n6qopA_OxsXfQXpLAgohUIqI2jidHjgCIwojbwflPx5CE_2XsrUK_crayWA/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(4).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) | 
For 'Drinking song of the earth's misery', Clay Hilley's approach leaned on a vivid dramatic presentation, and a clear histrionic effort to communicate the dramatic narrative of the song. By the end of the song, his anger was surprisingly fierce. Yet his unforced, focused tone meant that his voice was somewhat recessed in the balance. Hilley took so much care with the dramatic detail and narrative that I wished we could have been in closer contact. For 'The lonely on in Autumn', Bihlmaier began with barely there strings and a fabulous oboe solo. Jamie Barton was a dignified presence, and she seemed to choose emotion over simple beauty of tone. Towards the end there were moments of letting go, but mostly this was a contained yet intense account of the song. One which did not always cut through the orchestra.
Hilley brought a delightful lightness of touch to 'Youth' with very pointed words and the sense that he was telling a story. The orchestra was light and delicate for the opening of 'Beauty' contrasting with Barton's rather darker, steadier approach. She was telling a story and somewhat relished the contrast between voice and orchestra. I loved the way Bihlmaier got the orchestra to dip and dance, but her and later in the work I was rather wishing for some portamentos to enliven the clean string lines. In the faster, vivid sections, Barton's detail was rather lost in the hall though I loved the sense of impulse. In the moments when the orchestra relaxed and gave her space, her delight was palpable.
'The drunkard in Spring' featured Hilley back in storytelling mode, and oh boy was he vividly histrionic, yet some terrific detail was lost though the climaxes of the verses were terrific. We ended with bravura histrionics and came to appreciate his lively engaged storytelling. Then came 'Farewell' (Der Abschied). For the opening, Bihlmaier brought out the lower instruments and that tam tam to create some aural magic. There was space here for Barton, and she was artful yet affecting, but dignified too. I almost felt she was feeling the weight of the pressure of performing this work in this hall (following on from Janet Baker's four performance and Jessye Norman's one with Rattle and Jon Vickers!). Barton's dignified emoting was paired with some strong orchestral colours and a constant sense of impetus allied to fluid tempos. Towards the end of the first half we did get more expansive phrases, yet there was also the magic of her quiet intensity contrasting with just the solo flute. But at the end of the first part it was touch and go who won the loudness battle! In the second part, Barton was dignified, the music flowing yet with classical discipline. In the final stanza she did let do, though the repeated 'Ewig' was very internal and concentrated.
| ![Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou)](<https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhTZRZ-7Sh05ia_8ghebTfAU7xIz-Obsqqy_M3yQqoMyUCuN-ZRKJopDgmUO5RPr_iQgTlyE7RG86CutNEAMWHJxYhZLUChHCa6LCoRAHzvrhKCAy7lYVTqnO4-b7Sijc-aeuOIvrQwmuRYh32B7zui-cLfX7AGgq2te3kI3VahzFWMTInqMDCxqA/w640-h426/BBC%20Proms_Mahler%E2%80%99s%20%E2%80%98Song%20of%20the%20Earth%E2%80%99_photocredit%20BBC%20Chris%20Christodoulou_21.08.26%20(3).jpg>) | 
| Mahler: Das Lied von der Erde - Jamie Barton, Clay Hilley, Anja Bihlmaier, BBC Philharmonic - BBC Proms at Royal Albert Hall (Photo: BBC/Chris Cristodoulou) |
